HAZEN (Minister of Marine and Fisheries), moved that the House go into committee to consider the following resolution;
Resolved, that it is expedient to amend the Canada Shipping Act by providing (a) that certificates shall not be required for masters and mates upon sailing ships of not more than one hundred tons, registered tonnage, propelled by auxiliary power other than steam, employed partly in fishing and partly in the carriage of freight; and (b) that the Minister of Marine and Fisheries may fix the fee for replacing lost certificates.

He said; The principal necessity for this change in the shipping act arises out of the very great change which has taken place of late years with regard to the way in which the fishing industry is conducted. To-day nearly all the fishing vessels on the Atlantic coast and, to some extent, on the lakes and the Pacific coast as well, are propelled, not alone by sail, as was the case in days gone by, but by auxiliary power furnished by gasolene engines and nearly all of these vessels are being operated in violation of the present law because the law requires that vessels of over ten tons shall have properly certificated engineers. As the law stands it would be a very great hardship upon the fishermen, who find that the auxiliary power afforded to them by the gasolene engine, is of very great assistance enabling them to make their runs to and from the fishing grounds with a great deal more certainty and with a great deal, less labour than was the case when they depended upon sails and upon the wind alone. In addition to that there is no such number of certificated engineers, even if the fishermen were able to pay them for their services, to be obtained as would be necessary for the purpose of serving as engineers on board these boats. The proposed amendment to sec. 100 of the Canada Shipping Act consists of the addition of the following words to the law as it exists to-day:
Or to sailing ships of not more than one hundred tons, registered tonnage, propelled by auxiliary power, other than steam, employed partly in fishing and partly in the carriage of freight.	1
The reason for the amendment is that many of these auxiliary propelled ships are not employed solely in fishing. If they were, they would be exempt under the present law from having to have a certificated master in charge. They engage in fishing for three, six, or nine months only, and after that they carry cargo between the small ports in the maritime provinces.
Without the installation, of the gasolene engine, sailing boats are also exempt from the provisions requiring a certificated master to be in charge, if they are under 150 tons registered tonnage. (See section 5 of Chap. 65, Statutes 1903, raising such tonnage limit from 100 to 150 tons). But the usual custom to-day is to install a small gasolene engine in boats which are to all intents and purposes sailing boats so as to aid their movements in calm weather. As soon as a gasolene engine is put in they become steamships under the provisions of section 743 of the Imperial Merchant Shipping Act, which reads as follows:
743. Any previsions of this Aat applying to steamers or steamships shall apply to ships 164
propelled hy electricity or other mechanical power with such modifications as the Board of Trade may (prescribe for the purpose of adaptation.
The board of trade have advised the Department of Marine and Fisheries that it is their practice to classify gasolene propelled vessels as steamers, The reason why reference is made in this matter to the Imperial Merchant Shipping Act instead of to the Canada Shipping Act, is that the Canadian Act is silent in part 1, which relates to registration of shipping, as regards such ships. The department is advised that, in these circumstances, the provisions of the Imperial Act would govern. Unless, therefore, some provision is made to exempt these sailing Vessels with their small gasolene engines on board from the operation of Part II of the Canada Shipping Act, every one of them will require, under section 96 of the Canada Shipping Act to have a certified master in charge. There were 4,588 boats with gasolene engines engaged in the fisheries of Canada in 191011, (See answer in ' Hansard,' February 8, 1912, page 2722).
Unless some relief such as is proposed is given, these boats must either lay up when not employed in fishing, or if they engage in the cargo carrying business they must obtain a certified master. It is unnecessary to say that there is no such number of certified masters in the maritime provinces waiting employment. It is bad in principle to keep a provision in the law which it is out of the power of the people to comply with. The owners of these auxiliary sailing vessels could, of course, take out the gasolene engines and so bring themselves under the provisions of section 96 of the Canada Shipping Act which entitles sailing ships up to 150 tons registered tonnage to ply in Canadian waters or to 80 tons on a coasting voyage, (which voyage is defined in section 72 of the Act-and extends south as far as five degrees north latitude), without a certified master. But to remove these gasolene engines would be a retrograde movement, and the shipowners would naturally be opposed to any such step. '
The department has been asked to amend the law so as to meet the present day conditions. There is on file in the department a petition for such legislation. It is very numerously signed. It reads as follows:
To the Honourable the (Minister of Marine and Fisheries:
The petition of the undersigned owners of sailing vessels equipped with gasolene auxiliary power respectfully represents-
(1)	The tonnage of the vessels in which we are interested, and tile horse-power of the engines and speed developed by same is set opposite our respective names signed hereto.
(2)	Said vessels are equipped with auxiliary power for the following reasons: (a) To enable



those operating them to hare them under better control when entering harbours during light airs; (b) To expedite movements from dock to dock when in harbour, and save cost of towing; (c) To keep vessels in motion, and under steerage way in calm weather when on voyage from port to port, and thereby shorten the duration of voyage when fares carried consist of perishable commodities such as fresh fish; and (d) to supply in some measure a port to port service to aid in marketing commodities largely owned hy the operators of said vessels, rendered necessary owing to lack of other available means of transportation, thus enabling those engaged in the fresh fishing or carrying trade to market their fares in as prime condition as possible.
The regulations of the Department of Marine and Fisheries requiring the employment upon said auxiliary crafts of passed masters and engineers are burdensome and oppressive for the following reasons:-
(1) It would add seriously to the expense of operating, as they would have to be paid much higher wages than the ordinary men employed. (2) There are no such men available at present; and if there were any we would he unable to hire them, as we can make our vessels pay only by running them with ordinary men. (3) Men who have passed for steam engineers are not thereby qualified to run gasolene engines as they are so different. (4) Seventy-five per cent of the goods carried is owned by the parties operating said vessels, on which no insurance is carried, on either vessel or cargo. (5) The agents of insurance companies inform us that they will insure gasolene vessels for seven per cent, where without gasolene they charge thirteen per cent.
Therefore, your petitioners humbly pray that the Honourable Minister of Marine and Fisheries will favourably consider our request. And your petitioners as in duty bound will ever pray.
Those members of the House who last year were members of the Committee on Marine and Fisheries will recollect that when the Bill to amend the Canada Shipping Act was before that committee that this question of gasolene propelled sailing vessels came up for discussion. The members from the maritime provinces took very strong ground that something should be done at once to meet the requirements of the case. So firmly convinced was the committee of the justice of this claim that section 100 of the Act was recommended for amendment as follows:
100. The foregoing provisions as to masters and mates shall not apply to sailing ships of not more than one hundred tons gross tonnage having motive power of not more than eight nominal horse-power and employed solely in the carriage of freight; or ito any ship of less than fifty tons gross tonnage propelled by motive power and employed as a tug-boat or in the carriage of freight; or to pleasure yachts not carrying passengers or goods for hire; or to steamships carrying passengers not having a whole or fixed deck and of not more than twenty-nine feet in length at the light Mr. HA ZEN.
water line; or to ships employed solely in fishing; or to barges or other vessels having neither masts, sails or rigging and not being steamships.
Explanatory Note.-Sailing vessels with auxiliary engines and certain ships under 55 tons gross tonnage, are added to the list of exempted vessels.
Owing to the dissolution of parliament the Bill was never reported back to the House. It may be asked why not adhere to the amendment of last session? The reason is that many changes were to be made in the Act last session and this section was amended in line with others in other parts of the Act. As it is not now proposed to deal with the Act generally^ it is thought better to amend this section with the main view of affording relief during the present season to the class of shipowners referred to. Any elaborate amendment of the Act would make its consideration and enactment this session practically impossible. The proposed exemption appears to cover the case fully, and if after it has been in operation for a season or two it is found to be faulty in any respect the matter can be gone into again.
Clause 2 of the Bill is designed_ to remove what is felt to be a just grievance of the holders of certificates issued by the department. If a man loses his certificate he is cahed upon to pay one-half the fee that the original certificate cost. No matter how meritorious his claim to exemption from the payment of such fee may he, there is no power to grant it. Besides, the payment of six or seven dollars is often a serious tax on a master or mate who have, as a class, no reserve fund out of which to pay these extra expenses. The government does not want the money, and the certain knowledge that if a certificate is lost the owner of it will have to pay for a duplicate will not prevent its loss nor tend to make the holder more careful. Section 93 of the Act lays down the scale of fees as follows:-Master, competency, $15; mate, competency, seagoing, $8; mate, competency, inland, etc., $6; master, service, $8; mate, service, seagoing, $5; mate, service, inland, etc., $4.
Will the first part of this Bill apply merely to the coasting trade or to foreign trade as well?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: It will apply to all vessels of less than 100 tons engaged partly in fishing and partly in other business. If the vessels are engaged partly in fishing and partly in the carriage of freight, it is immaterial whether they carry the freight in the coastwise trade or otherwise.
I think the Minister will have to designate in the Bill whether the sections apply to the coasting trade or the foreign trade.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I shall consider that point when the Bill is under consideration.

Are there any provisions of the law which require certificated engineers for these motor boats, or is any amendment necessary to remove the difficulty?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: They do not require certificated engineers when engaged in fishing. But the fishing does not last during the whole year. At other times these boats are engaged in carrying products from one port to another; and at such times, if they were required to have certificated engineers they would be laid up, and would be of no use to their owners as earners of money.

The Bill, of course, is not restricted to any particular part of Canada. It will not in any way restrict the fishermen, but rather extend their rights to use these boats.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext:
This is a matter which was before the late government on several occasions, and the explanation given by the Minister of Finance is practically the explanation given to us. As I understand it the guarantee as proposed originally could not be accepted by the Edmonton and Yukon Pacific on account of the conditions existing. Consequently, in 1910, the company applied to the Railway Department asking to have a Bill passed not only to incorporate the Canadian Northern Alberta, but with that incorporation .to transfer from the Edmonton and Yukon Pacific the guarantee that had been given to that company. That guarantee must be all right, as I signed the document myself and noi person in this House took objection to it. I think the reason for the change was in connection with the amount of underlying security on one or other of the roads which was not compatible with the security going to the Edmonton and Yukon Pacific. That road was to start at or near Edmonton, and was to go to a point at Wolf Creek, and then down to the Brazeau coal mines, thirty-four miies. This Bill proposes that the road shall start from St, Albert, north of Edmonton, which is on the line of the Canadian Northern railway, and it runs through the same territory to Wolf Creek, /but it will! not interfere with the thirty-four miles branch line to the coal fields owing to the physical difficulties, but will continue along the main line towards the Yellowhead Pass. The meat of the objection, iff lobjectibn there shou-id be, in changing this, is that the line will parallel the Grand Trunk Pacific very closely for that distance. I istudied that question somewhat, and I know it is a difficult matter in the case of through lines to avoid paralleling, particularly when you are approaching the crossing of a river or a mountain pass where there is only one practical place to go through. In order to get the best results for a through line the companies have to be allowed to build as nearly to an air line as possible. If it were a local road for local purposes only, there would be strong objection to allowing the road to be removed from one point to another, thus getting away from serving one class of people perhaps to go to another point that would help the railway, but injure the people. In the present instance this is to become part of their through transcontinental line. For my part, I see no way to avoid what might be considered the difficulty of allowing the Canadian Northern to parallel approximately closely the Grand Trunk Pacific. The Canadian Northern people in discussing this matter with me on several occasions, rather chided the government . in this respect-and I give it to the House for what it is worth-that they always maintained that they were first on the
ground from (Edmonton to the Yellow-head Pass, and instead of them encroaching on the Grand Trunk Pacific, that it was the Grand Trunk Pacific that was encroaching on what they thought were their prior rights. Be that as it may, I cannot see any objection to the transfer of this guarantee, because if this government or the late government had been asked to guarantee the bonds of the Canadian Northern in the first place along this direct line, I think there would have been no objection. As I understand the situation they require legislation passed because under the guarantee of 1910, in which a special Act was passed also incorporating the Canadian Northern Alberta, bonds were practically sold or subscriptions received, and in order to protect those bondholders a trust deed had to be executed. Now, the route is to be changed, and although it might possibly have been all right if the transaction had been between private individuals to not introduce special legislation for the transferring of this road from one place to another, yet I think under the circumstances, not only to protect the bondholder-perhaps that is the smallest part of it because they would have been protected anyway-but in order that there may be no clashing of legislation, and that in the future there may be no opportunity at all for any person to raise the question that the Dominion of Canada was lax in protecting the capital that was sent into this country for the benefit of our railways. I am delighted to hear the Minister of Finance take the ground that the present government, and parliament I believe as well, will not be a party to any legislation, no matter what others may do, which will seem in any way to mar in any degree the securities held by capitalists on Dominion projects. We cannot afford to do that under any circumstances. I acquiesce cheerfully in this Bill, and I believe it is the only thing that can wisely and properly be done under the circumstances.	,

SUPPLY-POLLUTION OF THE RED RIVER.	-
Mr. WHITE (Leeds) moved that the House go into Committee of Sunoly.

Before you leave the Chair, Mr. Speaker I must crave the indulgence of the House for a few moments while I call the attention of

the 'government to a condition of things existing on the Red river north of the city of Winnipeg, that is fast becoming intolerable. Previous to some four years ago the river was open. At that time the government constructed what is known as the St. Andrew's dam across the. St. Andrew's rapids, and by so doing all current in that river was practically stopped and there has been created what might be called a large basin of dead water. That basin extends from the dam south to the city of Winnipeg some twelve miles. When the dam was built it raised the water some seventeen feet at the dam and about two feet at the city of Winnipeg. Previous to the construction of this dam the sewage from the great city of Winnipeg and the other cities south of the dam had been deposited in the river, but there was current enough to carry this sewage past the town of Selkirk towards the lake, and it was deposited in Lake Winnipeg. Although at that time we complained bitterly on account of the pollution of the Red river which made it impossible for the water to be used at Selkirk, or by any of the settlers along the river, we failed to obtain any redress from the city of Winnipeg, and up to the present time there has been no legislation (placed on the staAutejbook to make it impossible for this great city to pollute the river. And owing to the construction of this dam the conditions have become intolerable, and as I said a moment ago, property all along that river has been depreciated, and the health and the lives of tens of thousands of citizens of Manitoba are menaced by the conditions that exist in this basin of water. The construction of this dam stopped the current, as I stated a moment ago, and the city of Brandon, the city of Portage la Prairie, and all the municipalities down the As-siniboine river, and the great city of Winnipeg, with its 150,000 or nearly 200,000 people, with all its great stockyards, abattoirs and manufactories, have been pouring their sewage into this basin during the last four years, with the result that the Hives and health of the people are seriously menaced. I hold in my hand a letter from the secretary of the Board of Trade of the town of Selkirk, enclosing a small clipping which I desire to place on record. It is dated Selkirk, March 3:
Selkirk, Man., March 3.-Three cases of typhoid fever are reported at Lockport among the crew from the Dominion government publio works department engaged in blasting out a new ship channel at St. Andrew's locks. The men are working in bulkheads driven through the ice and their illness is said to he due to the bad condition of the river water under the ice. All winter difficulty has been experienced on account of t.he odours arising from the sewage-laden water.

The letter written to me indicates that the conditions are very bad at this place, and asks me to call the attention of parliament to it. I have a Bill on the order paper which I moved with the object of trying t-o get the sanction of this House, but I only succeeded in securing its first reading. The purpose of the Bill was to make it an offence to deposit sewage or poisonous waste in the river. There was another Bill which passed the Senate and came to this House, very similar to. my own, and owing to the emergency of the case I would have been very glad indeed to assist in passing that Bill into law. The town of Selkirk has from time to time petitioned the government asking that some legislation be passed. I hold in my hand several petitions that have been filed, asking that some action be taken to prevent the city of Winnipeg from using the Red river as an outlet for its sewage. I wish to place on record one of these resolutions. The memorandum reads:
The placing of the dam in the Red River at St. Andrew's causing the waters for a long distance above the dam to be raised has necessarily robbed the river of its current to such an extent that it does not carry away the dirt and waste being thrown into it. This waste falls to the bottom and remains.
The system of running the sewage into the river was objectionable before the construction of the locks, but under the present conditions it is a serious menace to the public health, and it becomes a vital necessity that a more sanitary method be found for the disposal of the Winnipeg sewage without any delay.
Then the Board of Trade passed the following resolution which was filed with the governmenlt:
Partial copy of resolution of the Board of Trade (passed at Selkirk, November 8, 1911:
Be it resolved that this board do emphatically and most strenuously protest against the disposal of the sewage of the great and growing city of Winnipeg without the interposal of a proper septic system for the purification of all sewage before it be discharged into the river.	.
That this board express it as their opinion that such procedure will cause 'the accumulation of practically all of the impurities of sewage for a greater portion of the year between the point of discharge and the St. Andrew's lock dam; and that the discharge of -all this sediment 'en masse' at certain seasons of the year will have the effect of largely increasing the menace to health that is presented by the sewage itself. That such action will be inimical to the lives of sixty million white fisli which are annually desoharged from the fish hatohery at Selkirk, and upon which the fishing industry of Lake Winnipeg and the perpetuity of the species in Lake Winnipeg is largely dependent.	_
That this board is deeply interested in the development, as an agricultural and residential

district, of .the lower Red River valley, and depreciates any action which will have the effect of arresting that development. . . That where the sewage of the city of Wininpeg, with the enormous increase to he expected from it, must depend upon so slow and shallow a discharging stream as is afforded by the Red River, the adoption of any permanent sewage disposal without purification would be suicidal in its tendencies, and work instant and incalculable harm upon this section of the province of Manitoba.
Now, there are several resolutions along the same line. The town of Selkirk, and the residents north of Winnipeg have been worked, up over this matter for some time, and something ought to be done by this parliament. We had an example in the city of Ottawa only one year ago, of the fatal effects on health arising from the pollution of a navigable stream, we had an epidemic raging through this city which filled all our hospitals., and an emergency hospital had to be equipped in order to take care of the sick. Hundreds of people weie ill in their own homes. We hadi over a thousand cases of typhoid fever in this city last year, and it cost the city the awful toll of 83 lives, owing to the crim-* inal neglect of the city o.f Ottawa to take proper care -of its sewage. I do. not think, this House and parliament can escape some of the responsibilities that Test upon us. This is the only body apparently that can intervene with the necessary legislation. While we have been sitting in this chamber during the last two or three months, working on financial and economic matters, and other public questions in which the people are interested, we have entirely neglected this extremely important matter which affects the.health and lives of the people of this, country. The prosperity of .this country dlepends largely on the health of its people, it is one of the greatest assets we have got, and still we allow this system of poisoning the source of our water supply to go on year after year, and apparently nothing is done to prevent it. I have just mentioned that the typhoid fever epidemic in this city resulted in 83 deaths. According to Dr. Wylie, one of the best authorities I believe on the American continent on sanitation, the average human life is worth $50,000 to the state. If that be the case, from an economic standpoint the city of Ottawa last year lost through that epidemic over $4,000,000. Less than $1,000,000, we are told, would provide a proper seiptic tank for the treatment of the sewage.
In the city of Winnipeg we have had the same experience. We have had epidemics there of the most serious nature and I have no hesitation in saying that, if some drastic measures are not taken to remove the source of danger, the great city oi Winnipeg will yet pay an awful price in the loss
of hundreds and perhaps thousands of the lives of its citizens for its neglect to provide modern methods for caring for its sewage. But, I am more interested in the residents of my own constituency. The property of these people is being depreciated in value, and the lives and health of hundreds o.f the residents along the river are endangered by the impure state of affairs existing on the river. I was told by a gentleman living on the banks of the Red river south of the dam that when the water was gradually let out last fall the deposit of sewage opposite his own door was over three feet deep, and the odour -arising from it was simply intolerable. The condition calls upon the government to take some drastic measure and I would ask the horn. Minister of .Public Works (lM-r. .Monk) now to see that there is a thorough investigation made of the conditions of the river especially where men .are working under his department. If we had that investigation made this coming spring perhaps we would be in a better position to deal with this matter effectively when the House meets again. I would urge the government in the meantime to take up one of the Bills that is on the order paper, make it -a law of this country, and thus prevent the pollution of our rivers. I have a record here that is appalling, showing exactly what has taken place from the pollution of rivers in Canada and giving the death rate. Thousands of our citizens have been stricken by typhoid fever all traceable to polluted waters and I think the time has come when this parliament should act in an effective manner in order to make it impossible for the great sources of our water supply to be polluted. The city of Winnipeg is surrounded by rivers. The Assiniboine comes from the west and discharges into the Red river. The Assiniboine carries along the sewage of Brandon, Portage la Prairie and all the adjoining municipalities and, since the water has been raised in the Red river, the Assiniboine, during the summer, is practically without any current, it is practically an open sewer and it is a menace not alone to the people of the city of Winnipeg but to the people living along that river. This great basin of water that has been created between Winnipeg and the dam is fast becoming in. the same condition. In my own town of Selkirk the residents dare not touch the water in the river. They cannot even give it to their stock with safety. The polluting of the water in the river has resulted in the pollution of Lake Winnipeg also. For ten or fifteen miles out from the mouth of the river a whitefish cannot live on account of the polluted condition of the water. I would ask the government to give this matter their earnest consideration and have

an immediate investigation made into the condition of the river north of Winnipeg, and take action at once to protect the health and lives of the people living north of Winnipeg on the Red river. We in Selkirk are determined to have this matter settled in the interest of the health of all concerned.

speechtext:
Well, the House is quite familiar with the provisions of Bill (No. 115) respecting the Manitoba boundaries, and I need not refer to that. This statute of 1893 contains the terms under which Prince Edward Island came into confederation, and the clause which deals with the subject in hand is as follows:
That as the government of Prince Edward Island holds no lands from the Crown and consequently enjoys no revenue from that . Source for the construction and maintenance of local works, the Dominion government Shall pay by half-yearly installments in advance to the government of Prince Edward Island $45,000 per annum, less interest at five per cent per annum upon any sum not exceeding $800,000 which the Dominion government may advance to the Prince Edward Island government for the purchase of lands now held by large proprietors.
That $45,000 is something less than 50 cents per head of the population of Prince Edward Island, and under the Manitoba Boundary Bill, passed this session, Manitoba wi'il receive $1.25 per head of her population for precisely the same reasons as Prince Edward Island receives only 50 cents per head, and the amount of $1.25 to Manitoba will, be increased as the population of that province increases. Now, Sir, I think this is a special discrimination against Prince Edward Island. Of course I do not think it was intended that injustice should be done Prince Edward Is. land in this matter, but justice can now be done to my province by treating it in the same way as Manitoba is treated. Then, as it is the only other province in the Dominion that stands in the same position, I believe that something should be done this session to remedy the injustice, and I would ask the Prime Minister if he will take it up and see that it is dealt with during the present session.

Mr. HUGHES (Kings, P.E.I.)

I desire to ask the attention of the committee for a moment or two, in connection with a very sad and [distressing incident which occurred in the early part of the year 1911, and which resulted in the death of four persons belonging to the Northwest Mounted Police. Ih the month of December, 1910, Inspector Fitzgerald, of the Northwest Mounted Police, in company with three other constables whose names were respectively, Carter, Taylor and Kinney, left Fort McPherson to patrol the route to Dawson. These members of the force endured great hardships and sufferings from the outset of their journey, and in the end lost their lives. I desire to read1 to the committee a portion of the official report of Commissioner Perry on this sad incident:
Inspector Fitzgerald in bis diary gives some inkling as to what was affecting bis mind; it seems to have been the anxiety to perform the patrol and not return to Fort McPherson defeated. His expression, ' My last hope is gone and the onlv thing I can do is do return,' seems to indicate this. Had he been a less experienced traveller than he was, he would surely, have turned back sooner.
The cause of the disaster may be summed up as follows:	_ _
1.	The small quantity of provisions taken.
2.	Want of an efficient guide.
3.	Delay in searching for the lost trail.
The heroic efforts to return to Fort McPherson have not been exceeded in the annals of Arctic travel.
Corporal Dempster's reports show that the unfortunate men had wasted to shadows. All were strong, powerful young men, and in the best of health and conditioh when they left on their ill-fated journey. That they should have lost their lives is greatly to be deplored. It is the greatest tragedy which has occurred in this force during its existence of thirty-seven years.
Their loss has been felt most keenly by every member of the force, hut we cannot hut feel a thrill of pride at the endeavour they made to carry out their duty, and their gallant struggle for their lives.
I oannot express it better than in the following extract from a letter addressed to me by His Honour the Lieutenant Governor of 'Saskatchewan ;
While the event brings deepest sadness to all, we feel that it is only an event such as this which can give greatest lustre and endur- [DOT] ing remembrance to the splendid Force.
My purpose in mentioning this sad event to the committee is to suggest the desir-? ability of voting an annuity to the mother and sisters of the late Inspector Fitzgerald, who now live in Halifax, and who were dependent upon the deceased son and brother. The last thoughts of Inspector Fitzgerald were for his mother, as shown in the brief and pathetic will written just
bl77

previous to his d'eath, and which was disi-covered in his pockets. It was, I am informed, the intention of Inspector Fitzgerald to retire from the force during the present year, when he would have been,
I believe, entitled to a superannuation of $1,000 per year. In the Halifax Public Garden, one of the most beautiful spots in all America, the citizens of Halifax have erected what is called the ' Fitzgerald Bridge,' as a mark of the esteem and high regard of the people of that city for Inspector Fitzgerald. I venture to make this suggestion to the committee, because the Prime Minister, representing as he does with myself, Halifax county, and which was the home of Inspector Fitzgerald, while no doubt very sympathetic in the matter, might feel reluctant on that account to establish a precedent and meet the suggestion I make to the committee. I think however, that this is a case in which parliament would be justified in voting a specific sum or an annuity to be paid to the mother of Inspector Fitzgerald during her lifetime, and I feel sure that, if the government can see their way clear to do so, it will meet with the support and commendation of the House. What I say respecting Inspector Fitzgerald is, of course, intended to apply to his companions in death.

I rise to express my sympathy with the hon. junior member for Halifax, who has just so well expressed his sentiments with regard to this tragedy of the north which resulted in the death of Inspector Fitzgerald and his party. It strikes me that it would be a moat fitting thing for this parliament to recognise the services rendered to Canada, and the empire by Inspector Fitzgerald, who laid down his life in those northern wilds in the discharge of what he considered to be his simple duty. The Northwest Mounted Police have done a great deal in conquering the wilds of the north and the west, and in giving to the people of those sections of our country peace, law and order. I have lived in the Yukon for some twelve years, and1 I can testify, as I do most enthusiastically, to the splendid work they have done, and are doing on our frontiers. Our boundary marches with that of the United States on the 141st meridian west from Mount St. Elias to the Arctic ocean, and the United States and Canada have settlements on either side of that boundary line, and also on the littoral of the Arctic ocean. It became necessary some years ago, in the opinion of those belonging to the Northwest Mounted Police, to establish a patrol annually from Dawson to Herschell Island.
This patrol leaves Dawson in December or January of each year usually. In the year in which Inspector Fitzgerald met his death that patrol left Herschell Island, or Fort McPherson, for Dawson. Inspector Fitzgerald was accompanied by three other men. It seems that on this particular patrol, the inspector neglected to take a proper guide. He had a guide with him whom he thought could guide him through that labyrinth of streams, mountains ana passes which exist on that trail, but his guide failed him. He continued his route thinking he could, with the knowledge he had of the trail, succeed in making Dawson, but we know now that he could not under the circumstances, have done so. His diary is a pathetic document in view of the events which finally cost him his life. Here is an entry dated 17th January:
Twenty-three below. Fine in a.m. with strong S.W. wind which turned 'to a gale in evening.
He goes on to explain what he did that day and continues:
I left at eight a.m. and followed a river running south, but could not see any cuttings on it.
That is he could see no marks.
Carter as completely lost and does not know one river from another. We have now only ten pounds of flour, and eight pounds of bacon and some dried fish. My last hope is gone, and the only thing I can do is to return, and kill some of the dogs to feed the others and ourselves, unless we can meet some Indians.
Unfortunately the party never met any Indians, and in eating the dogs they were taken down by a peculiar disease which sometimes comes to men who have to live on dog flesh as these poor fellows had to. Inspector Fitzgerald carried with him despatches from the police post on the Arctic Ocean, and customs revenues for our government. These were found intact in one of the last camps which he made. There is little more to add, Mr. Chairman, except, on my part to say, that I think it would be a most fitting thing for this parliament to recognize in some measure the services which inspector Fitzgerald performed. An hon. gentleman asks me what about the other three members of the party. They met their deaths a little earlier than Inspector Fitzgerald. The guide who went out to examine the trail, and if possible discover the bodies of the members of the patrol, found two of Inspector Fitzgerald's policemen dead and, cared for them as best could be done. Next they found another policeman, and finally Inspector Fitzgerald himself who was the last to die. I think that some fitting recognition should be made of the services of all four men, but

particularly of Inspector Fitzgerald himself who died in doing his duty.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
With regard to the estimates which are now asked for hy my right hon. friend (Mr. Borden) there are no comments to be made at all. The money will be cheerfully voted, it is well deserved by the force. I have read with some care the report of the Mounted Police which was brought down some time ago by the Prime Minister. In connection with that report two things struck me. One was the advisability of increasing the pay of the men.- The commissioner- of the force states how difficult it is to maintain the required quota of men on account of the inducements which are offered in the Northwest provinces to young men in good health and brains. It is natural to suppose that members of the Mounted Police,	whose	pay is rather scanty
may be induced to leave the force on account of the greater attractions other occupations offer, and of the even probability of their making a good deal more for themselves than they could if they were to remain in the force. I am very glad that the leader of the government, who has charge of the Mounted Police Department has already brought in a resolution to increase the pay of the Mounted Police which will give them more inducement to remain in the service, and when these resolutions are brought down the money called for will also be cheerfully voted. There is another thing which has struck me, as to the advisability, or otherwise, of extending the posts of the Mounted Police northward. Settlement is moving northward all the time. It has now reached the Athabasca river. It will reach by and by the Peace river district, and no doubt will extend, more or less, from that region up to the Arctic ocean. My hon. friend, I believe, will be compelled, as time goes on, to extend the police posts further north. Whether he can do that without increasing the force is a matter as to which I offer no opinion; but probably he will find it possible to decrease the number of posts in the well settled portions of the district of Athabasca and the provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta, and extend them farther northward. With regard to the tragedy which has just been referred to by my hon. friend from Halifax, and my hon. friend from the Yukon, for my part I will say, if my opinion counts for anything in the matter at all, that I will be very glad to see recognition given to the families of Inspector Fitzgerald and his companions. This is perhaps a little irregular, but the tragedy is one that is not likely to occur anywhere else. The patrolling done by the force in this northern region, from the Yukon to the mouth of the Mackenzie river Mr. THOMPSON (Yukon'
and to the Hudson's Bay Company posts, is a work which requires not only courage, ability and moral force, but all the qualities which may characterize the human mind and human intellect. In looking over the report of the tragedy as it occurred, it seems to me that Inspector Fitzgerald was imprudent in starting with so little provisions as he did, but this does not detract at all from his merit in responding to the call of duty. Inspector Fitzgerald and his party should have had another team of dogs, and carried more provisions, and had they done so they probably would have escaped the calamity which befell them. But this in no wise detracts from the heroism he displayed, and if the right hon. gentleman who is in charge of the force should ask for some testimonial to be given to his family, for my part I shall cheerfully support it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I would like to add a few words in [DOT]support _ of what has been already so well said by the junior member for Halifax with regard to the tragic death of Inspector Fitzgerald. It was my privilege to know Inspector Fitzgerald personally, being an old member of the Northwest Mounted Police-though before the time that Inspector Fitzgerald entered the force-and I have some knowledge of the duties which members of the Northwest Mounted Police are called upon to perforpi. There is an opinion in the western country, and particularly at the post at Fort Saskatchewan to which the late Inspector Fitzgerald belonged, that he was -called upon to perform an unnecessary duty. It is believed at least, that he was called upon, on account of his remarkable and distinguished record, to perform something that was altogether out of the ordinary, something beyond what is expected of the Northwest Mounted Police. It is believed in the district I have referred to by old associates and friends of Inspector Fitzgerald that it was perhaps to make a nice report that the police had such a complete system of patrol from the international boundary to the Arctic circle, that he was called upon to undertake that duty.
It is well known that they were not going out fox duty in the way of looking after criminals or to relieve settlers in distress because this is an uninhabited region, and I hope that the request of the hon. the junior member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean) will receive the consideration of the right hon. the Prime Minister. I do not know why it is but we have always found it very difficult to have anything done for the Northwest Mounted Police, one of the best military or semi-military organizations in the world. We read a great deal about the great things they have done, but members of that force who have been un-

fortunate enough to meet with accidents in the discharge of their duty have found since the organization of the police that they have received very little attention from the heads of the department in the east. The government has always been willing to recognize and reward members of other military corps for any service done. When the Royal Northwest Mounted Police were organized in 1874, they received 75c. a day, and at the end of their service they were given a free grant of land of 160 acres. In 1879, the Conservative party came into power, their pay was reduced to 50c. per day and their scrip was cut off, they lost the grant of land although at that time land was of no value whatever. During the rebellion of 1885 they were asked to do the hardest duties on the field, they did the scout duty, and as they had knowledge of the country the most dangerous work fell to them. But when it came to the rewards after the rebellion, although some corps that were under orders in the east received their scrip, the Northwest Mounted Police received no bounty at all. A great many companies that went to the west were sent to police posts and did garrison duty while the police went out to do the fighting; the eastern corps that did garrison duty at the posts received their scrip, while the police received no consideration at all.
I mention these facts simply to point out that for some reason or another the police have not been getting a square deal. They perform duties not performed by any other organization of the kind in the world. During the six years I served in the police force I was called on to act as sheriff for some months. I have acted as collector of customs, and the man who relieved me received $1,800 a year. There is a feeling among the mounted police that they are not receiving what they should receive, and I am glad to notice that a small increase of pay has been made, but, it is very small. There is an increase of only 15 cents a day, but that is not at all equal to the increase in wages in other walks- of life and in the cost of living. Wages of other men have nearly doubled since the police were first organized, and yet the police to-day receive only 75 cents a day for performing their difficult duties. A policeman when sent out on any particular duty has no option, he is not able to refuse the duty if he does not like it. I have known a man to receive a year in the cells for simply refusing to obey an order. When they are ordered to do any work they have to do it, and I think they are entitled to a greater increase than is proposed.
It would be a shame to see the mother of such a man as Inspector Fitzgerald have to suffer wait because her means of livelihood are taken away owing to the death of
her son. The government might well give her the pension that was earned by Inspector Fitzgerald for the 20 years he served, as a bounty as long as she may live, and, while I do not know the others, I think they also are entitled to some consideration. I hope the Prime Minister will look into this whole question, not only with reference to Inspector Fitzgerald, but to the police generally. It looks as if the deputy head of the department is anxious to demonstrate to the people of Canada how cheaply an organization of that kind can be kept up. The initial pay might well be increased to a dollar a day, and I do not think any one would think these men weTe even then being fairly paid.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I appreciate all that has teen said in commendation of the force, in which I have always taken a very great deal of interest. I can assure my hon. friend who has just taken his seat, and who, I understand, was a member of the force for some years, that so far as I am concerned the Northwest Mounted Police will always get fair-play and a square deal as far as I am able to give it to them. The statute fixes $1 as the maximum pay for constables. We are increasing the pay in the first year by the order in council lately passed to the extent of 25 per cent; it was 60 cents, it is now 75 cents per diem, end in the sixth year it reaches the maximum of $1. Formerly the constable did not reach the maximum until the ninth 3 ear . I am perfectly well aware that, compared with the rewards that come to men engaged in other vocations, this is not much, but still the pay now provided is iaiger than ever before, and I think it is practically the same as the pay in the permanent force	[DOT]
My right hon. friend has alluded to the probability that posts still further north will require to be established. I think that is very likeiy to be brought about. In the brief experience I have had, a great many applications have come to the department at Ottawa from time to time for the presence of a constable in new communities which are springing up so continuously and so rapidly in the great prairie provinces. We are endeavouring to supply these demands as rapidly as possible. I have heard it suggested in this House on more than one occasion that the force -might advantageously be reduced. Up to the present time I can see nothing that would lead me to such a conclusion. While I have not been able to give to that question the consideration which it would demand before taking action, the inclination in my mind at the present time, without speaking in a definite and conclusive way, would point to the opposite direction. I think, if any change is likely to be made in the constitution of the force.

it wouid be in the direction of increasing it rather than diminishing it.
Now, with respect to the very regrettable accident and loss of life which occurred two years ago on the Dawson and Mac-pherson patrol. This patrol, I understand was established about ten years ago, and the accident which took place a year ago was the first serious accident that has ever occurred in (connection with the patrol. This patrol has been made in the winter for several years past, with the object of keeping communication open with Fort Macpherson and the Mackenzie river, and carrying the mail between 'those places. Without it nothing could be heard from the Mackenzie river from the close of navigation of one season to the opening of the next-a matter of seven or eight months. The distance in direct line is 275 miles. Distance as travelled by patrol, 470 miles. The time usually taken is about 30 days each way. This year the patrol left Dawson on the 6th of January and returned on the 10th of March, making the round trip in 69 days.

speechtext:
It may be said of Inspector Fitzgerald that whatever error of judgment there may have been in respect of guides and_ supply of provisions, he bore his part in that journey to the grave in a way that will inspire the respect and admiration of every man in Canada. I feel especially proud because he was born and brought up in the constituency which my hon. friend and myself have the honour to represent in this House. It is impossible for me at the moment to make any definite announcement with regard to the subject my hon. friend from Halifax has brought to my attention to-day, and of which he has spoken to me in private. But I may say to him and to my right hon.^ friend, that I feel very earnestly the desirability of making some recognition to the families of these men who lost their lives under the circumstances I have mentioned. It is a matter to which I hope to give attention before the end of the present session.
So far as the members of this force are concerned, my hon. frienu from Victoria will remember that there is a provision made by way of pension which inures to thesd men after a certain service in the force. However, I want him to understand that as to giving these men every consideration possible, having regard to the usual practice in such eases, 1 am disposed to agree very much with what he has suggested. Let me say to him, however, that so far as the permanent officials of the Department of the Northwest Mounted Police are concerned, I do not think there is any room for the criticism that they are not inspired by a very sincere sympathy with the force. The Controller . of the Northwest Mounted Police, Coionel White, is disposed, so far as I know his character and disposition- and I think I know him pretty well, to give every possible consideration, under the law by which he is guided to the officers and men of the Royal Northwest Mounted Police. I know there is no man in Canada who has that force in higher regard than Colonel White, there is no man in Canada who is inspired by a more sincere sympathy with the officers and men of the force than the gentleman who is at the head of it at the present time. I think, therefore, there need be no idea in the mind of any hon. member of this House that, whether from the permanent head of the department or from myself, that force will not receive the utmost possible consideration and sympathy.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I do not think that the numbers of the force ought to be reduced. There has been an impression in the east that, as the new provinces are getting more populated and civil government is becoming better organized, the force might be dispensed with in those provinces. Anybody who takes the trouble to read the report which has been placed on the table of the House will come to the conclusion that it would be a misfortune if the protection which is given to the settlers should be withdrawn. Any man who reads this report will realise the protection, security and encouragement which are given to the settlers when they see the uniforms of the mounted police around them. If the settler has trouble of any kind he goes to the mounted police, and he is sure to have redress. In a multitude of circumstances the presence of the police gives to him a security which he could not have in any other way. The patrolling of the different sections which has been carried on by the police for many years has given to the country a security that otherwise it could not have had. In regard to the patrolling of the north, to which some exception, I understand, has been taken by my hon. friend from Victoria, Alberta (Mr. White), I think that, on the contrary, it has been of eminent service to the country. This service was organized some ten years ago, when I had the honour to have the police under my charge, and the chief reason which led the government to take that course was the desirability of asserting the authority of Canada in these northern regions. At the present time the mouth of the Mackenzie river is used by American whalers as the base of their operations in summer time. They are in contact with the settler. They took pelts away without any regard to law and it was advisable that we should have a force there, not only for the purpose of asserting our own authority, but also for the protection of the natives against the too close proximity of the American whalers. The force has done eminently good service in that respect. We have asserted that authority in these districts and that alone would be sufficient to warrant these yearly expeditions which have'taken place from the Yukon to the mouth of the Mackenzie river. In summer it is quite easy to communicate from Athabasca Landing with the mouth of the Mackenzie river, but in the winter it could not be done in any other way than that in *which it has been done, and in this respect the service is performing an important duty.
Mr. HUGHES (Victoria,Ont.) I desire to say a word in reference to one of the remarks made by the hon. member for Victoria, Alberta (Mr. White). The mounted police is not a military force, and at the
time of the (Northwest rebellion, and also previously, it had to perform the service of the regular troops. Immediately afterwards the volunteers received their land grants and recognition in the way of a medal. The mounted police never received any land grant, and yet all governments in Canada have refused to recognize them as a military body.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Although they were not a militia corps they were attached to and under militia officers, and performed military service.
Mr. HUGHES (Victoria, Ont.) Yes, that is the point I am making. Regular soldiers did the same thing. They were treated as regular soldiers and not as volunteers. The regular soldier got no land grant; all he got was a medal, and the mounted police were treated as regular soldiers. Supposing one of the officers of the mounted police happens to join the militia service of the country, all his service in the police counts for nothing, although in the past it was much more developing service than the militia' service as the mounted policeman in the old days, acted as sheriff, commissioner', inspector, and almost in every capacity from that of a judge down. This service is not counted at all in the militia service. I have always felt that the police have been rather hardly dealt with in hot having any credit given to them for their service in 1885.
