speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: We have three ice-breakers. The * Montcalm ' and the ' Lady Grey' are used for the purpose of breaking ice on the St. Lawrence river and the ' Earl Grey ' is engaged with the ' Minto ' in keeping open communication between Prince Edward Island and the mainland.
Are the boats engaged in the service between Pictou and Prince Edward Island?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes.
Is one of them exclusively an ice-breaker or does she carry passengers and freight and mail as well?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: She does.
What would be the policy of the minister respecting repairs to government steamers? Will he ask for tenders or will such work be assigned to persons whom his department may select?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I am informed that in many eases the work of repairing steamers eannot satisfactorily be done by tender. We have now at Halifax quite an extensive plant in connection with the naval yard there and a very considerable number of the vessels are now, I understand, being repaired at Halifax by the department. There are cases where it would be in the public interest to ask for tenders; there are other cases where it is inadvisable to do so, and there are other cases where it is much more in the public interest that we should have the repairs done by our own department at Halifax. I will always consult the officials of the department, who are better informed on the subject than I, and I shalll endeavour in every case to do what is best in the public interest.
Is it the policy of the present government to continue the system in force under the old government with regard to provisioning the government steamers?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I intend to continue the system now in force which is, that instead of the government purchasing the supplies itself, it makes a contract with the steward or some officer of the vessel under which he has a certain allowance for each officer and man to provide the meals on board the government steamers. I am told by the officers of the department that this has proven much more satisfactory than the system in vogue some years ago under which the department *employed a steward who purchased supplies for the department and fed the men. I am told that under the old system the meals were not as good and the cost much greater than under the present system. It is intended to continue the present system.

I am glad the minister has made that statement because I think the system in vogue for the last few years has been very satisfactory. Will the steward or the captain who has the contract to supply the meals to the officers and crew, be subject to the patronage committee, or will he have the privilege of buying his stores wherever he can buy them cheapest?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: He is not subject in the slightest degree to any patronage committee. A contract is entered into with him and he is free to buy the supplies where he can do so to the best advantage.

Have any steps been taken to get over the difficulty which occurred in St. John, where different people supplied goods to the steward of one of these steamers and have not been paid? The steward left the country without paying these merchants, and it has been as-Mr. MACLEAN (Halifax).
serted by quite a number of them that they thought when they were furnishing _ these goods they were furnishing them to the government and not to the steward personally.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I am sorry I cannot tell my hon. friend that that matter is finally disposed of. Mr. Doutre has been instructed by me to make a very careful investigation into the facts, and I expect to have a report from him in a short time. A man named Cogswell contracted to supply meals on one of the steamers under contract, and he ran up bills in different parts of the country where the steamer called, to the extent of over three thousand dollars, which have not been paid. The claim is made that those who supplied the goods to Cogswell believed that he was an official of the department, and that when they were supplying the goods they were really supplying them to the government. Of course, even though we are not liable legally, we may be liable in equity. There are instances in which it is hard to believe that those who supplied Cogswell thought they were supplying the government, because they went on month after month rendering bills to Cogswell himself, and not to the department. They contended that as Cogswell went to their places of business in the uniform of the service, that they got the idea they were selling direct to the government. We have taken means in the future to guard agains the recurrence of such a thing. We are insisting that every steward with whom a contract is made in the future will have to give the bonds of a surety company for the faithful performance of his contract, and also to indemnify against loss those who furnish him with goods. The Department of Justice has not yet approved of the form of bond submitted.

It would be a very natural thing for theft people to render bills to the steward, and that point ought not to be strongly insisted upon in their case. Prima facie it might he assumed that the suppliers thought they were dealing with the government through the stewards. Of course, it 'may be that some of them had knowledge, and I am very glad the minister is looking into the matter, and I am sure he will deal with it from an equitable standpoint. Of course, if they had a legal claim, I would not be making this appeal, because they could go to the Exchequer Court. [DOT]

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I do not feel justified in asking parliament to vote money for this purpose in the absence of a report of one of the responsible officials of the department, and I expect to have that report soon. For instance, one of the hanks claims $800 on the ground that it discounted notes which Cogswell had given to some of these mer-

chants for supplies. It is rather difficult to believe that the bank and the merchants who took Cogswell's personal notes believed they were dealing with the government.
Suppose Cogswell had said that parliament had not yet voted the money, as is often the case.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: There might be something in that.

I am glad to hear the hon. minister is giving the matter consideration. I know that people in Yarmouth supposed at the time that the department would be liable for the Bill. Of course, there was no necessity for Mr. Sanders or any one else making a claim on the department until the steward defaulted. I hope the minister will see his way clear to pay the bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: My disposition is to pay it if I can justly and fairly do so, guarding the future by requiring bonds to be given.
As a matter of fact, in the ordinary course of business, do any of the accounts for supplies that have been obtained by the stewards reach the department?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No. A contract is made with the steward, under which he supplies each officer and man on the ship at so* much a meal. The number of meals, I presume, is certified to by the purser, and the department pays the steward on that basis.

As a matter of common knowledge, parties who would supply goods under the circumstances mentioned in this case would do so under the idea that the steward was only a medium between the government and them for the purpose of purchasing. The fact that the stewards made those contracts has not been specially understood by the general public unless it was drawn to their attention. I wish to refer to another matter, to which I called the attention of the minister in the early part of the session, namely, that a man had been employed as pilot on one of the winter boats plying between Pictou and Georgetown who held no certificate as pilot. The answer given to me by the minister was that he was only employed temporarily. I am informed that this man Boute is. a man who had no qualifications whatever. I do not think he was a certificated master. He had only been floating about on sailing vessels in the Gulf of St. Lawrence, and he was appointed pilot on this government steamer. Of course, the law is very clear that to be employed on any other kind of steamer he would have to be a regularly licensed pilot.
I know that down to the early part of Feb-165
ruary this man, who had no right to be there at all, was still acting as pilot on this steamer. If the steamer had gone ashore or there had been any other difficulty, the minister would have been in an unfortunate position before the House.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I asked my deputy to look into the law on the subject after my hon. friend had called my attention to the matter, and I was informed by the deputy that there was no law whatever making it necessary that the pilot should have a. certificate or a license, but that all that was necessary was to appoint a man who was qualified for the position. This man, I may say, was recommended as being highly and thoroughly qualified for the position before he was appointed by the department. After the hon. gentleman called attention to the matter in the House, further inquiry was made, and the department was satisfied that the man was qualified to discharge the duties he was called upon to discharge. It may be that my hon. friend is right that there was an omission in the law, and that it might be desirable that a man should be required to have a certificate for the discharge of the ordinary duties of a pilot. But a man who has been in the habit of going to and fro between the same ports every day as an officer on a ship could perhaps be as safely trusted to guide the ship in case of a storm or fog as any pilot.

I think the Minister is stronger in the first part of his answer than in the last. If .he believes his conclusion, there is no need of anv vessel being piloted. The great difficulty of handling these steamers in wintertime is that they may run aground; and while a man may know the headlands and the lighthouses from going around in a schoon-in the summer-time, it cannot be argued that such a person would have the accurate knowledge that a pilot would have who was specially examined for the purpose and with long experience of taking vessels through harbour entrances. It may be that government steamers have hitherto been exempted from the provisions of the pilotage law, and I am aware that in summer time they do not employ pilots; but in the winter season, when they are navigating waters which are not free from danger, in regard to the depth, and where therp are three pilotage districts running upon one another, it seems to me that the Minister is running a great risk in taking the recommendation of his political friends in Prince Edward Island, who said, we will not give you a pilot, but we will give you one who suits us politically. In Captain Brown of the 'Minto' the Minister has an officer of long experience, who knows the conditions there; but instead of promoting



to the place of Captain Finlayson, as he should have done, the first mate, who had experience there for a great number of years, who knew the conditions that have obtained in later years, and who had the advantage of close; communication with Captain Finlayson, the Minister again listened to the voice of the tempters from Charlottetown, and sent to British Columbia for a man who had been employed on those steamers 15 or 16 years ago, but had nothing to do with winter navigation in the meantime, and practically tells the thoroughly competent and well-trained men on the vessel that he will not have them at all. There was a rule that obtained in the Marine and Fisheries Department, which I am sorry to see the Minister breaking, that was, "that in regard to all officials in this branch of the service, promotion should be based upon seniority.	_
A man who entered the service of the government in any one of these steamers in any responsible capacity connected with sailing the vessel, or in the engineering department, was promoted according to seniority. My hon. friend (Mr. Hazen) due, I take it, to the great pressure that was exerted upon him at the inception of his career in the department, broke through that rule. He accepted the re-Icommendatiion of the two members for Queens county, sent to British Columbia and brought down a man who had not been near the Gulf of St. Lawrence^ for the last 15 years. I hope the Minister will not violate the rule as to promotion by seniority again 'in regard to these matters. This year the department has been very fortunate, although my information is that a few weeks ago Captain Murchison, the man who was brought from British Columbia was on the point of leaving the vessel, she being in such great peril. The conditions were such that he made all preparations for leaving the ship, and had not the wind fortunately changed and the ice begun to move the other way, this vessel commanded by the man just mentioned would have been a complete loss. I refer to these matters because I want to urge upon the minister the continuance of the prudent policy that was adopted by the late administration of making promotion by seniority, and of voicing the complaint, which I think I have a right to make, as being in the public interest, that the minister did net retain Mr. McPherson. I do not know what answer the Minister would have been able to make to the 'country if this vessel had been lost in consequence of his disregarding a well understood rule, and appointing to the command a man who had been absent from the service for ten or fifteen years.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I may say to my hon. friend that from my observation, and from Mr. MACDONALD
what I can learn, if there ever was such a rule as he speaks of with regard to promotions, it was quite as much honoured in the breach as in the observance.
Oh no, not at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
That is my information, and I think it is quite correct. With regard to Captain Murchison, I received the information that he was in every way qualified for the position to which he was appointed. He held the necessary certificates of qualification, he had had very large experience, and his whole record was that of a man who was thoroughly competent to discharge the duties of the position to which he was appointed. I do not think it was a matter of luck on my part, but because we had a very careful and competent navigator in the person of Captain Murchison, that the service has been as successful this year as it has been m the past. My information further is that Captain Murchison was previously in the service of the government, but that a number of years ago he felt that he was being very unfairly treated, and he was forced practically to resign his position. Restoring him to the service and giving him Command was, I think, a mere act of justice and the righting of an injustice which he had suffered in the past. That would not have been sufficient reason for making the appointment, had he not been well qualified for the position not only by possessing the necessary certificates, but by his standing as a navigator and as an experienced man.
Mr. HUGHES (Kings, P.E.I.) Has the first officer on the ' Minto ' resigned his position?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
What is his name?
Mr. HUGHES (Kings, P. E. I.), McPherson, I think, and I am told that he resigned in consequence of being passed over. I would like also to know who has been appointed in his place.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I understand that Mr. McPherson, who is the man referred to by my hon. friend, practically resigned. He asked for a very long leave of absence, suggesting, I believe, that it was not his intention to return to the ship.
Because of another man being appointed ?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No, I am told he gave no reason. There is nothing on the files of the department to show that he received other than fair treatment.

I endorse to a large extent, the remarks made by the member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald), that having in mind the success

of this service nothing will take the place of experience; and while Captain Murchison may be a very good man, yet it must be understood he has been out of the service for quite a number of years. Whether or not he has had as large experience as the man who was in charge of the vessel, is just a question. The principle of promoting men in the service-that service at all events-is certainly a sound one, and it should be kept in view in the appointment of the junior officers. In the event of the sickness of the captain or his absence through any cause, or his removal by death, the next officer ought to be qualified to take his place and thus the principle of promotion should go into effect. The officers, in order to get the best service from them, should be given to understand that promotion will come by seniority. Now, I understand that the steamer ' Minto ' was in a very precarious position at one time during the winter season although it may have been through no fault of the captain. I would ask the minister if the vessel at that time sustained any particular damage, and if it will be necessary to send her to Great Britain to receive the necessarv repairs?	J

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The ' Minto ' has sustained no special damage at all.
But some repairs will be necessary ?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I think every season repairs are necessary to every boat in the service.
,,Mr- HUGHES (Kings, P. E. I.). Will there be any more repairs required during the coming season than are ordinarily called for ?	J

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No.
And the repairs can be made on this side of the Atlantic ?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes.
Was any change made in the departmental regulations last year respecting the uniform to be worn by seamen on the government steamers employed in the fisheries protection service ?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I do not think so. Certainly I never heard of it. No change has been made in that regard since I have been at the head of the department.

There were no regulations to the effect that when on shore, or off duty, the men were prohibited from wearing the ship's uniform?
165J

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Not in any of the ships that are under the control of the Marine Department.
Perhaps I am mistaken.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: In saying this I am speaking of the Marine and Fisheries Department, not of the Naval Service.
Has the minister been making any inquiries regarding the points between which the car ferry service is to run ?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I may say to my hon. friend, that matter is being dealt with by the Railway Department, not by the Marine Department. I can tell him, however, that full inquiry will be made as to what is the most desirable location for the car ferry before a decision is come to.
Perhaps the minister can tell me who the marine expert of the Railway Department is ?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I am afraid I shall have to refer the hon. gentleman to the Minister of Railways for an answer. I do not know of any marine expert in the Railway Department.

It is rather anomalous that when this government is starting upon a proposition to run a car ferry across the straits of Northumberland involving such a large expenditure, they are doing so without having any information whatever as to the conditions, or any information from the proper source from which we should hpve it.
The Minister of Marine and Fisheries knows that no one in the Railway Department has had anything to do with this question of a winter service. The question of obstruction to navigation here can only arise with reference to the winter months. One would suppose that the government before undertaking this expenditure would have taken steps to obtain all the information procurable and I am surprised that the officials of the Marine Department have not been called upon to deal with it.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
It does not seem important which department deals with this question so long as it- is dealt with intelligently and _ thoroughly. As this car ferry will be simply a part of the government railway system, connecting the railway on the island with the Intercolonial railway on the main land, it is right that it should be managed by the Railway Department. While the inquiry is not being made by my department ali sources of information possessed by the Marine Department are being placed at the disposal of the Railway Department. A

former professor at Queen's University, Professor Kirkpatrick, has been appointed to gather all information with reference to the selection of a route for the proposed' car ferry. Professor Kirkpatrick is thoroughly qualified and has no local feeling. He is in touch now with the captains of the government boats running between Prince Edward Island and the mainland and other navigators with experience in those waters, and I am sure that he will submit to Council information upon which Council can come to a correct and sane conclusion.

The gov-eminent decided to undertake this project without getting information even from the hon. gentleman's own department. I do not hesitate, with full responsibility, to make the prediction that the car ferry in winter time will be a lamentable failure and the government will have to take the full responsibility of it. They should have looked into the question before deciding to commit the country to this expenditure.
Does the hon. member object to the car ferry?

I say that the expenditure of the money of this country for the construction of a car ferry in winter is one of the grossest errors this country ever made, and I predict it will be a failure and that the government will repent it. My complaint is that the government put the cart before the horse, they decided to spend the money and then to find out whether it could be spent. I had the papers showing the information the government had before them when they reached their decision and if these papers are accurate the government went blindly into this project.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: My hon. friend is entirely in error. It is admitted that the car ferry would be of great value to Prince Edward Island. The information which the government is obtaining now is information to decide as to the proper route on which to establish a car ferry in order to make the connection between the railway and the island and the mainland.

Does the minister undertake the responsibility of stating as a minister that he or his government had anything before them that would show that they had the slightest ground for believing 'that the operation of a winter car ferry there would be a feasible proposition in January, February and March?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I am surprised to hear my hon. friend opposing this proposition.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service

speechtext: Time will Vindicate me.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: My hon. friend has before indulged in the pastime of putting on the veil of prophecy. That is not a safe occupation for a public man. No great public work has yet been undertaken in Canada without some member in this House prophesying that it would be an utter failure, yet all our public works have turned oiit to the benefit of the country. I do not want my hon. friend to be placed in that class of false political prophets by any rash utterances he may make on this question-. However, that has little to do with the estimates before the House.

It has something to do with them, we are voting money for winter communication. My hon. friend is quite welcome to the feeling that it is a very dangerous thing for an hon. member to make a prophecy in regard to a question of this kind. It is one proposition to make a prophecy as to whether a great public enterprise can be constructed -over land and what it will cost, and another as to a question of this kind. I have lived all my life alongside the Straits of Northumberland, and I have seen the conditions there for the last 45 years. It would have been prudent and wise for this government not to have put the cart before the horse, but to have made some inquiry as to the possibility of operating a car ferry in the Straits of Northumberland in the winter months before committing this country to that expenditure.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Does my hon. friend not think it would be an enormous advantage to the island to have a car ferry if only in the season of the year during which there is no danger of the interruption of communication so as to avoid the three breakings of bulk in the shipment of the products of the island?

My hon. friend is running away from the point, as he very well knows. The question as to whether a car ferry would be a good thing in summer is an entirely different thing from the question as to whether it could be operated in winter. 1 venture to say that, he cannot find among his friends who live along the shores of the Straits of Northumberland, not even in the province of Prince Edward Island, who will tell him that a car ferry is possible in those straits in the winter months. The correspondence shows that the Department of Railways had nothing whatever before them.
Why is the hon. gentleman opposed to it?

My Lon. friend (Mr. McLean) knows that the reason why this proposal is being imposed upon the people of this country was in order to influence the elections in the province of Prince Edward Island. The correspondence shows that the Department of Railways had nothing whatever before them which would lead any one to believe that it was feasible. I say again that the government should be condemned, because they are committing the country to a great expense for what is supposed to be a substitute for this vote, this vote for maintaining winter communication with Prince Edward Island by the steamers 'Earl Grey'and the 'Minto' which have, within the last few years, performed that service as well as it could possibly be performed. The time lost and the inconvenience have been of the smallest possible char-'acter, having regard to the conditions that exist and will exist as long as nature creates them. I say we have here evidence that the government is proposing to make a substitution for this vote without having taken the opinion of any man, of any one in the Marine and Fisheries Department, or any one of those who have had to do with the navigation of these straits during the last twenty-five years. But after having decided to embark upon this enterprise, after they have initiated this thing, then they say, we will look around and see whether it is possible to do this business, and although it is assigned to the Minister of Railways to deal with the question the Minister of Railways has no marine experts in his department. Professor Kirkpatrick of Kingston may be a very good civil engineer, but civil engineers are not people you would think of consulting whether a car ferry can cross the straits of Northumberland in the winter months. I say that professor Kirkpatrick, who has lived in Kingston all his life, and who has not been accustomed to ice navigation, would not be a man who is equipped in the slightest degree with the knowledge to state as to whether any kind of a steamer could operate in the Straits of Northumberland during the winter months. I say before the government decided anything they should have sent for Captain Brown, for Captain Murchison, for Captain Finlayson, men who know the conditions, and if they, had sent for them and got their opinion before the government had started upon this enterprise, they would have told- him that such a thing as a car ferry carrying freight and passengers crossing that tide during the winter months is simply absurd and grotesque. I am astounded that the minister should have told us that the matter was in this position, that not a single one of his officials were ever asked
their opinion as to whether this thing is possible. They tell us that there is a ferry running on the straits of Mackinaw, which are not comparable at all to these straits, the conditions are entirely different. When the correspondence moved for by my hon. friend from Westmorland (Mr. Emmerson) the other day was brought down, it appeared that outside some representations made by my hon. friend from Queens, Prince Edward Island (Mr. McLean) to the Prime Minister, it was because some statement had been made at a meeting at the market hall before the election last year, that this whole problem of winter navigation could be solved by the operation of a car ferry in the winter months, that the government proceeded to commit the country to the expense and solution of the problem in that way without Shaving asked the opinion of a single man who knew anything about the subject whatever.

speechtext: House in committee on Bill (No. 114), to incorporate Reviilon Freres Trading Company.-Mr. Barker.

Reviilon Freres is a great French trading company, having very large interests in the wilds of northern Canada, where hunting has been carried on, for the purpose of fur trading. They have had a large establishment for years in Montreal, they nave another in Paris, France, and I believe they have a branch in the United States. They got a charter here some ten years ago through the office of the Secretary of State, and carried on business under the impression that they were a duly authorized corporation. Later they found it necessary to get an Act passed. But the banks through which they carried on their business in looking into the authority of the directors, discovered that in the original charter no provision had been made for first or subsequent directors, and that there was really no person to represent the company. Last session a Bill was introduced to incorporate Reviilon Feres, it went before the committee of the House, and was then referred to a special committee to look into all the facts. The Bill was reported to the House and passed by the House. It then went to the Senate; but unfortunately, owing to the sudden termination of the session, it did not pass. So once again this company found itself without any legal authority. They introduced their Bill again this session, this time in the Senate. It has now passed the Senate practically as it passed this House last year, with the exception of a word or two of a merely formal character. in section 5 and a new clause, section 11, which was introduced in the Senate committee t-o provide for the method by which this company shall have representation of the board in Paris as well as here. The section as introduced was accepted by the company, but the law clerks of the two Houses thought that the words now added to section 11 are more appropriate and more fitly express what was intended. With that exception, the Bill is as it was passed by this House last year. The story of the company is simply that years ago Reviilon Freres, large furriers in Paris, obtained large properties in our north in carrying on their fur business, and as the game disappears, they propose to colonize and sell their properties

to settlers. That is the whole object of the Bill. The company has four directors, of whom two live in Paris and two in Montreal, and the clause added by the Senate provides that the company may by by-law settle what are the particular functions of the section of the board in Paris and what are the particular functions of the section in Montreal, and where there should be representation of both sections.
How does it come that a trading company of this kind has a Dominion charter?

I understand that it occurred in this way. Revillon Freres were enterprising French furriers, and looking abroad, they concluded that the northern wilds of Canada would furnish them with a supply of furs, and they started a company. They are enow a very wealthy concern, owning large districts, and they desire that these shall be held in the name of a company properly organized.
On section 11,

I notice that this company have the power to make bylaws. Will those by-laws have the force of law, or have they to be sanctioned by the Governor in Council? My reason foT asking the question is, that I understand the practice to be that by-laws made by companies or corporations require the sanction of the Governor in Council. That is the practice of the provincial legislature.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: It is not the practice in all the provincial legislatures.

The practice is not invariable. There are certain by-laws made expressly subject to the Governor in Council for a particular reason. I would not object in the least to putting such a provision in the Bill, but all this proposes to do is to divide the work of the board; that certain work must be done by the whole board, and certain other work may be divided between the Montreal section.and the Paris section. This is a trading corporation that has been in existence for 10 or 12 years, and it is not desirable to put in any restrictions that are not absolutely necessary.

It is not unusual to do this in the part of the country that I come from. In this case the ccmpany is a trading corporation, and any by-law they pass may be binding upon the people that deal with them and have the force of law. It is not right that the company, or their directors, should be able to make laws binding upon the world that deals with them on their own motion with-cut any restriction whatever.

These people have been trying for ten years to get incorporated and will agree to almost anything. At the same time, I may point out to the hon. gentleman, who is a lawyer himself and therefore knows the custom, that whenever a bank or business body wants to deal with this company they will inquire as to what their powers are under their by-laws. That is the ordinary routine in the case of all these legal questions. It is very undesirable, I should say, that a trading corporation like this should be hampered in any way.
If it is not customary, I do not- want to press any objection.

It is certainly not customary in Ontario, except where a by-law may be for the purpose of altering the capitalization of the company. There is nothing of that kind in this Bill at all.
Bill reported, read the third time and passed.

speechtext: House in committee on Bill (No. 119), respecting certain patents of the Continental Can Company.-Mr. Fripp.
This Bill renews a patent, and therefore I would like to have it explained.

The object of the Bill is to remove the patent from the operation of section 38 of the Patent Act to section 44, a very simple matter. Under section 38 of the Act a patent that is not manufactured continuously expires. Section 44 gives the patentee the opportunity to appear before the commissioner and revive the patent, or have a chance to hold it at all events. There is nothing unusual about the purpose of the Bill.

My hon. friend is mistaken in the theory that this proposition is not an unusual one. It is a case in which a foreigner obtained a patent in this country and did not carry out the conditions of "the patent. He did not begin to manufacture in Canada within the time limit. After he has failed to comply with these conditions, which are only reasonable, I fail to see any reason why we in Canada should give any special treatment to an outside patentee who does not observe the provisions of the law. It is not the usual practice by legislation to permit the patentee to come in and claim rights and privileges under another section of the law. In previous parliaments Bills of this kind have always been viewed with the greatest possible suspicion, and some evidence had to be presented that there had at least been some effort on the part of the patentee to comply with the provisions of the law before he received consideration. There have been

cases where men had initiated arrangements that would ensure the manufacture of the article patented, hut difficulties have intervened. This fact parliament has taken into consideration, and some leniency has been shown to the patentees and their rights have been preserved, but it is not such a matter-of-course proposition as the hon. member for Ottawa suggests. I think the case he has made out 's no case at all. We ought to have more facts in regard to the Bill before we pass it.
My hon. friend is mistaken. The facts weTe all laid before the committee, all possible objections were considered and the committee decided to report the Bill without amendment.
When the Bill was read a second time the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Carvell) and I both refused to be bound by the report of the committee.
My instructions from the solicitor in charge of the Bill are that they have manufactured in Canada but have not manufactured continuously in Canada as the Act requires.
I am opposed to the renewing of patents unless some very good reason is given. We should certainly have some better explanation than the hon. member (Mr. Fripp) has given.

This is not a case of renewal. It seems that this patent was issued under section 26 of the Patent Act and the patentee desires to come under section 44 of the Patent Act where he thinks his patent should have come originally.

Then there must have been an error in the Patent Office and we should hear from the Minister of Agriculture. It is not desirable that a practice should be established that patentees who have forfeited their rights may come to this House for relief.

The statute expressly provides by section 44 for such a case as this, where an article has not been continuously manufactured. Then the Commissioners shall have an opportunity to hear both the patentee and any person desiring to use the patent under license, and after hearing both sides, he may decide whether the patent is forfeited or is to continue.
But this man did not come within the time prescribed by the statute and now comes to parliament . for a restoration of his rights.
No, I think not. But he does not want to have his patent declared null and void, he wants section 44 invoked in his favour.

I do not understand what is wanted, we have had no clear explanation of what has happened. If the patentee has complied with the law there is nothing necessary now. I know the department are not in favour of this tinkering with the law. It is the policy of the department to make them comply with the statutes unless there is. strong reason to the contrary.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
The hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) thought they should have a statement from the Minister of Agriculture. The Minister of Agriculture, of course, does not profess to be an expert on patents. I frankly say that I do not know all the details of this Bill. But I point out to my hon. friends opposite that they are exercising, I think, a certain amount of virtuous indignation on patent Bills of this kind, and within my knowledge of this House it has been the practice to put through a larger number of these Bills when my hon. friends were in power than it is during the present session. I do not say that I am in favour of it, as hon. gentlemen opposite know perfectly well the stand of the department is generally against special Bills, and I think rightly. If there were too wide a gate left open it would mean that everybody would get careless about their patents, knowing they could come here and get a Bill shoved through without any bother. For that reason, I think the policy generally should be not to put through Bills of this kind without valid reason. I will say this, that it is a customary thing, after a reference of all these Bills to the Private Bills Committee, to have the Deputy Commissioner of Patents there, or one of the officials, who generally takes a stand against the Bill. It has also always been customary, when there are special reasons or special hardships involved in a particular case, to deal with it on its iherits, and it is usual, I think, to get the judgment of that committee to say whether these reasons are sufficiently strong, and if that is the case, to waive the general procedure of the committee. I am not aware of any cases, certainly not any that I can recall, of a Bill of that kind passing the Private Bills Committee being turned down by the House. Unless it is pointed out to me that this is a particularly weak case, I do not know that it should be turned down. I would point out, however, that in nearly all these cases reported from the committee to the whole House, the report is almost always formal, and I think I only recall one instance during my experience of four sessions when the report of the committee on a Bill has been rejected or turned down, and there has been a report throwing it back on the committee again. I think the leader of the opposition, when he was the leader of the government, enunciated as a 1 general principle that Bills which have

passed a committee of this House, without some extraordinary reason, should be allowed to pass the House.
But the committee has been reduced in the meantime.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Still, it appears to work fairly satisfactorily. The attendance at all of these committees is sometimes slim. But I think he will acknowledge that if there are strong objections they -are generally put up in that committee before the Bill comes to the House. However, I have no strong feeling in the matter, and I am willing to let it stand if the committee desires it.
I am sure we are obliged to the minister for his explanation that because certain patents were renewed under the old government, that is reason why this patent should be renewed.
We have already passed three Bills of this kind during the present session.

There was a Bill brought in the other day by the hon. member for St. Antoine (Mr. Ames) that was amended in committee. So the reference of the Standing Committee is not always taken by the House Committee. I do not suppose there would have been any trouble about this Bill had the hon. gentleman explained to us why he wanted to get it. I do not know myself why he should apply under section 44.

Mr. MclLEAN (Queens, P.E.I.). Before recess the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) made the broad statement that a car-ferry across the Straits of Northumberland was not feasible in the winter time. I do not know where he gets his information. I suppose, if he has been observing the ice in Pictou harbour or along the southern coast of Nova Scotia, *he has come to the conclusion that a car-ferry would not be possible in that part 'of the Straits of Northumberland. But surely other people besides the hon. gentleman have been observing conditions there. For over thirty years the captains of the ice-boat at Cape Tormentine and Cape Travers, and the captains of the government ice-breaking steamers, have sent daily reports of the condition of the straits to Otfawa, and that information is to-day in the possession of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries.
If the hon. gentleman will take the trouble of going over to the Department of Marine and Fisheries he will find there a daily report of the conditions in the Straits of Northumberland from the year, I think, 1881, or previous to that. The conditions are not as he has stated1 them to this House. We have had, for many years, ice-breaking steamers. Those steamers have very fairly conducted the business between Prince Edward Island and Pictou, and between Charlottetown and Pictou. There have been this year very few stoppages. But, those steamers have not the power or the strength that we say they should have, and they do not constitute a fulfilment of the terms of confederation between Prince Edward' Island and the Dominion that we should have continuous steam communication between the railway on Prince Edward Island and the railway on the mainland. My right hon. friend the leader of the government (Mr. Borden), speaking in Charlottetown on the 8th of September last, made the statement that if he were returned to power he would fulfil to tlie letter the terms which were entered into between the Dominion and the province in 1873. I will read for the information of the committee the language which was used by the right hon. gentleman on that occasion:
And now, Mr. Chairman, Ladies and Gentlemen, I come to a question of vital importance to your prosperity. I refer to the transportation question. You can never fully enjoy the benefits of the market of Canada and the outside world under your present dislocated traffics arrangement. I believe the conditions at the present existing are not such as you anticipated when you gave up your status as an independent colony and became part of the Dominion. A solemn compact was then entered into, binding as well on the government of Canada as on you as a province, and the hardship is manifest that whilst the Dominion have exacted a strict performance on your part they have not in my judgment used reasonable diligence to obviate your insular disadvantages in this regard. I believed that instead of this subject being controlled by different departments it should be under the supervision of one department only, and your steam communication with the mainland should be arranged in conjunction with the island railway and the Intercolonial railway thus doing away with the exasperation of the three short hauls.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: MAINTENANCE AND REPAIRS TO GOVERNMENT STEAMERS AND ICEBREAKERS.
speechtext: Now, the only way that this can be effected is by having a car-ferry or by the construction of a tunnel. We found when we came up here and were in conference with eminent engineers that it would take something like twelve years to construct the tunjiel. We thought that was too long to wait, a third of a lifetime, and we asked the government to give, in fulfilment of this promise made by the right hon. Prime Minister, a car-ferry. The government immediately acceded to our request. I was in this House between 1904 and1 1908, .and on many occasions during that time I and my colleague (Mr. Martin), brought this question before the consideration of the House. The right hon. leader of the opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier), had made a promise to the people of Prince Edward Island in 1891, that if he should be elected at the election which was then ensuing he would see that our transportation problem would1 be solved. Although he sat in this House from 1891 and was leader of the government for fifteen years, .he never raised his voice to say anything for the people of Prince Edward Island, But, when my right hon. friend the leader of the government (Mr. Borden), came into power, although he had made this promise exactly in the same words, that the right hon. leader of the opposition had made it, he immediately fulfilled his promise, and the people of Prince Edward Island are getting the justice now that they ought to have got thirty years ago. It is only fair that this government should fulfil the promise made by the Prime Minister to the people of Prince Edward Island especially when they' know now that it is a feasible matter provided1 the government give us a car-ferry of sufficient power. If we have a boat of 10,000 horse-power strongly enough constructed to force its way through the ice, our transportation problem will be solved whether the boat is run to Pictou or not. The question has been raised as to where this ferry will be run to. I .have no doubt that my hon. friend from Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) would like to see it run to Pictou, because I suppose. if it does not run there Pictou will be a dead issue in so far as anything material coming out of the traffic 'between that point and Prince Edward Island is concerned. To-day the business in Pictou practically all comes from Prince Edward Island, and if this car ferry is put in operation within the next two years possibly it may run between Charlottetown and Tatamagouche or between Cape Traverse and Cape Tormentine, and that is why the hon. member for Pictou denounces the government for giving the people of Prince Edward Island the justice they should have had years and years ago.

speechtext:
I do not propose to continue this discussion very much longer at this stage because, while this matter is perfectly in order in regard to this item, it being to provide for the boat which is being constructed in connection with winter navigation, I shall discuss it at greater length when the estimates of the Minister of Railways come before the House. My only reason for introducing this matter at this stage was to ascertain from the Minister of Marine and Fisheries whether any of his officials, or anybody connected with his department, had ever made any report to the government previously to the government deciding upon a policy in this regard so as to find out whether or not the government had any information before them when they decided upon their policy. I have learned to-night that, in so far as the people who ought to know anything about this matter are concerned, the government had no report from them and, against the enthusiasm of the hon. member for Queens, P.E.I. (Mr. McLean) and those who say that my opinion about this matter is not worth anything, I might tell them that I have before me all the papers connected with it which have been brought down, and I may say that I cannot find from any engineer, or any public official, responsible or otherwise, in any department of the government, any report that would justify the theory that a car-ferry can be operated in the Straits of Northumberland in the winter-time. Indeed, in the discussion that went on before six o'clock, I felt that perhaps I was unfair to the minister in discussing the question at this stage, and I went and looked through all the papers cai'efully to see whether it was really proposed that the car-ferry should be operated in the winter-time. If the proposition involved simplv the operating of a car-ferry during certain months of the summer that was one thing, but if the government, in asking this vote for winter steamers, intended to substitute other means of communication during a part of the year, that was another matter. I took the responsibility of saying before dinner that the -proposition to operate a car ferry during the winter-time would result in absolute failure. I am supported in that view by the only official of any department of the government that ever looked at the question and took the responsibility of making any report upon it. I have in my hand this letter from the former Deputy Minister of Railways. Mr. M. J. Butler, who writes on the subject as follows r-
Your letter of the 16th instant addressed to the hon. the minister, re proposition to put on a modern and powerful icebreaker and car carrying system steamer, across the strait of

Northumberland, has been referred by him to me for reply.
I am of the opinion that no such steamer ran be designed, at any reasonable cost, to do the service during the winter months, nor do I think it possible to make such a project pay its way.
That is the only opinion of any official in regard to this matter that is before the government, and when the Prime Minister wired my ho.n. friend ('Mr. McLean, Queens, P.E.i.) on the eve of a provincial election, that they proposed to inaugurate this car-ferry scheme, the Prime Minister wired without any report from anybody who knew anything on the subject which enabled him to justify any such policy. We have here a report from Mr. Bowden, chief engineer, who tells us that he had not time to look into the matter. When we look into the statements of my hon. friend we find that his estimates are based upon the assumption that one ferry steamer will be sufficient for the purpose. The hon. gentleman has given up the tunnel, he has given up the winter steamer proposed to be built in addition to the ' Earl Grey ' and * Minto,' which would give the people of Prince Edward a complete winter iseTvice, and he is willing to have one ferry steamer as an experiment.-and which he will be bound to admit is an experiment of the first order-when he has not a single person on record in this government or in the 'departments of the government to say whether this scheme will be in any degree adequate. I should apologize to the Minister for going into this discussion on his estimates when this question is perhaps more germane to the Railway Department which is supposed to deal with it.
Will the minister be good enough to get one a statement of the number of passengers carried by the winter boats during the season of 1910-11 ?

But, I fear my hon. friend forgets that the people of Prince Edward. Island not only want to get better communications during the winter, but they also have the very vital grievance that in shipping their products from the island at all times of year there are practically three different hauls: the haul over the island railway to the steamer, the steamer carriage to Pictou or Cape Tormentine or Shediac as the case may he, the haul on the Intercolonial railway through to destination and the loading and unloading at each transfer. That is a substantial grievance which the people of the island want to have remedied. It would be of enormous advantage to them if a train ferry were established so that they could put. their freight and products on the car on the island and not have to break bulk until that car reaches its -destination in Canada or in the United States. Such a system would of course enable them to have cars equipped with cold storage compartments so that their perishable products would be carried in good condition direct to the consuming markets. That is one great advantage which will be- accomplished by the car-ferry. My hon. friend (Mr. Macdonald) says that the government acted in this matter without information, but I do not think it is open to the hon. member to say that. It is true the papers before the House are rather meagre in the information they contain, but there are reports in the Department of Marine and Fisheries showing day by day the condition for the last 30 years so far as navigation between Prince

Edward Island and the mainland is concerned. I think my hon. friend (Mr. Macdonald) may fairly give the government credit for having some knowledge of these reports and he might also bear in mind that there are men around the Council Board who live close to the island and who have been for years interested in this very important question. Ice-breakers are not a new thing; every year there is more work done by them; they are making progress on the St. Lawrence river, where navigation is open ' earlier now than in the past owing to their operations between Montreal and Quebec. My hon. friend may be easily within the range of probability when he says that if an ice-breaker is constructed1 as a steam ferry, with proper power and proper weight, then during the greater part of the winter season that ferry can give continuous communication between the island and the mainland.

speechtext:
I referred to the hon. member for Queens, P.E.I., not to the minister. The minister is breaking away from

his usual custom, he is free from party politics to-night, and 1 congratulate him upon it. It" was not, I think, in the very best taste for the hon. member (Mr. McLean, Queen's, P.E.I.) to associate with this question the strongest terms that could be employed in connection with party politics. I think he can rest satisfied that from Seatarie to Amherst, in fact throughout the whole province of Nova Scotia, he will find the greatest possible sympathy for Prince Edward Island, and the greatest possible desire to give that province the very best accommodation that is available. But the bon. gentleman has made the statement that the leader of the opposition, although he had been 15 years in power, had never raised his little finger to improve the conditions in regard to the ferry service or the connection between Prince Edward Island and the mainland.
That leads me from a party standpoint to ask the minister to give a statement of the improvements that were made in the transportation service between Pictou and Charlottetown, and generally between the mainland and the Island, by the construction of boats, etc., during the regime of the late administration. It may be a little cumbersome and involve the giving of figures that -would not be necessary, but the statement of he hon. member for Queens is of such a sweeping character and. such an indictment against the late government, that it is only fair to the Liberal party that we should have some knowledge of what was done by the late government to improve the communication between Prince Edward Island and the mainland by means of new and powerful steamers.

speechtext:
I aliso want to make a few remarks that have been called for by the observations of the hon. member for Queens, P.E.I. The fact of the matter is that the car-ferry was first mooted, so far as I remember and so far as the papers show, by a gentleman named George E. Pull, who came here on a delegation, I think in 1906 or 1907, and strongly advocated that project. The hon. member for Queens, P.E.I., was a .member of the House at that time, and I am satisfied that the proposition was not treated seriously then by the great majority of the people of Prince Edward island, and a great majority of the people interested in the subject; it was treated rather as a ridiculous proposition. I am inclined to think my hon. .friend from Queens, P.E.I., likewise took that view ot it at that time, because being a member of the House he would be alive to the importance of bringing forward any proposition of an advantageous character to the province and to the people whom he represented, and it would be his duty to do so. I am quite sure he would do his duty in that respect, and the fact that he did not bring the matter up tends to convince me that neither he nor anybody else thought this car-ferry service would be practicable between Prince Edward Island and the mainland. I hope that it will be practicable, and that it will be found to be of great advantage;

and to a certain extent I am quite -willing to give the government a good deal of credit for taking up any proposition that would remove the difficulties under which Prince Edward Island has laboured so long in regard to transportation. But I do not know that this car-ferry service will be a solution of the difficulty, in fact I may frankly state that I am afraid it will not. I hope that it will, but the conditions under which the project was taken up and the haste with which it was announced last fall tend to arouse suspicion.

speechtext: There is no question about the feasibility of a car-ferry as they are in successful operation in other places. subtopic: MAINTENANCE AND REPAIRS TO GOVERNMENT STEAMERS AND ICEBREAKERS.
speechtext:
This subject, which is not a new one, has claimed considerable attention at my hands and, early in December, I gave notice of a motion to the effect that in the judgment of the House it was desirable to establish a car service between the mainland and the island and at the same time to widen the gauge of the Prince Edward Island railway. I was unable to reach a discussion of that motion owing to delay in bringing down certain information for which I had moved. That information has since come down, but it was then too late to reach the motion on the ,paper and so I withdrew it in order that the matter might be discussed on some other occasion.
In 1905 a Bill was passed by this House having for its object the connection of the Prince Edward Island railway with the Intercolonial railway and the establishment of a car-ferry service between Tor-mentine and Carleton Head. That Bill, however, was killed in the Senate. The fact that a car-ferry service of this kind has not been established is largely attributable to the people of Prince Edward Island themselves. The Bill to which I have referred was strongly opposed by certain members from the island in this House and in the Senate it was killed largely through the influence of Prince Edward Island senators. The reasons are obvious. We must recognize the fact that there are sectional differences and jealousies on the island as in other provinces and Charlottetown and Summerside have vied with each other in an effort to secure every possible advantage in the way of communication with the mainland and because of the influences and prejudices of the eastern and western sections of the island against any means of communication being established in the centre of the island, as between Carleton Head and the mainland at Tormentine, the scheme fell through. I had a strong view with respect to the matter at the time

that the government should acquire the railway which runs from Sackville to Cane Tormentine, known as the New Brunswick and .Prince Edward Island railway, and should establish a car ferry service such as has been established at other points ton this continent, and such as is now in operation on a smaller scale at the Strait of Oanso, on the Intercolonial railway.
I think that eventually the government should acquire that road, and that they should establish a car-ferry service and operate it as part of the government system of railways. I believe that is the only solution of the difficulty. For many years the representatives of Prince Edward Island in this parliament have talked of a tunnel, they have brought it before the House time and again, but no one seemed to take them seriously, in fact sometimes it was thought they were not serious themselves; not that the proposition is not feasible from an engineering standpoint, but that the undertaking was too large to be considered seriously at the present time in our history. In June last I was in Prince Edward Island in connection with an election campaign, in a way, and I discussed with the people the matter of a car-ferry service. I strongly advocated it then, and I advocate it now. I mink it is perfectly feasible, and that it will be a success if established. It may interfere with the constituency of my hon. friend from Pictou, it may interfere with some interests in my constituency; but what are these interests as compared with the greater interest of improved transportation facilities between Prince Edward Island and the rest of the Dominion?
My hon. friend says there are suspicious circumstances in the haste with which this matter has been taken up. This parliament met in November, but there was no mention of it in the speech from the Throne, although the leader of the government had discussed it in Prince Edward Island in September. There was no mention of it by representatives from the Island after the opening of parliament. It was brought to the notice of parliament on the 7th of December, when I took occasion to give a notice of motion with respect to it. I notice in a return which was laid upon the table of the House, that there was a communication addressed on the 22nd of November to the right hon. the Prime Minister, which was signed by the two representatives from Queens, P.E.I. The matter apparently did not claim much further consideration until the 23rd of December, on the eve of a local election in Prince Edward Island. On the 28th of December the Prime Minister and the Minister of Railways appear to have taken certain steps in the way of sending telegrams and writing letters to Prince Edward Island. The elections were held in the early days of January, 1 166
I think these telegrams reached Prince Edward Island two days before the polling. Well, of course people are suspicious; sometimes those who are hit are supersensitive with respect to letters and telegrams on occasions of this kind. These letters and telegrams may not have been written with any idea of influencing the provincial elections, it may have been a mere coincidence that they were sent down to the Island at that particular moment. Of course, I do not mean to insinuate that there was any connection between the telegrams and the election, I am only mentioning the facts. It is no doubt unfair to impugn the motives of ministers of the .Crown in such matters.
Now some reference has been made to the lack of estimates. I do not think the government at that time did have any estimates with respect to the matter, and I am bound to say that we could hardly expect them to have. I do not think they should be condemned because they did not have such estimates, although it might be a fair matter of comment that they should have made such positive declarations as to what should be done before they had any estimates of the probable cost. I favour the proposition, and I will support it. It is not only in the interest of Prince Edward Island and of the Prince Edward Island Tailway, but it is in the interest of the Intercolonial and of all Canada. The people of the maritime provinces as a whole are peculiarly interested in it, and the people of Quebec, Ontario and of the distant west are to a large degree interested in the proper solution of this question. In July last I told the people of Prince Edward Island that a tunnel might be feasible. In years to eome conditions may prevail in Canada which will make the construction of a tunn.el possible. But in the meantime what should be done? Try at least this experiment. I _ think it will be successful during the major portion of the year, even during the winter months. Between the nearest points, Cape Tormentine and Carleton Head, a distance of between six and seven miles, I am told by those who are familiar with the navigation of the straits, that during the winter months, once during every twenty-four hours in the day-time, there is practically a clear channel between those two points. It is caused by the tide bringing the ice together, and when the tide recedes one portion of the ice goes out on the eastern end of the island, and the other goes to the western end, the ice separates, leaving a channel. I am told this by people who have no object in misrepresenting the circumstances. I have not seen it myself, but the people in that section of New Brunswick who are familiar with the conditions prevailing there say that is the case.



There is a short period in which there is open and continuous communication between these two points. During the greater portion of the year you could1 have communication between the island and the mainland without extra cost six or seven times during the day. It would be possible to convey trains across. It could have been done last year at these points. It would obviate the three freight charges, it would place the people of Prince Edward Island on a parity with the people of Cape Breton in respect to transportation charges, there would be no break and1 there would be the continuous mileage haul from the point of embarkation to the point of destination. Under these circumstances I think it is commendable for the government to undertake this. 1 may say that in the past I have called the attention of the preceding government to this very matter. I have invited their consideration to it, and I invited their consideration to the subject not later than last July. Regardless of which government is in power, regardless of party affiliations, I believe that the representatives in this House whether they be from the east or from the west, should1 join hands in aiding to give the best possible communication between Prince Edward Island and the mainland. Perhaps the discussion of this matter is not relative to this particular item, other than that as references are made to winter communication between the island and the mainland, it may be relevant. But this is a subject that might more properly be discussed when the Minister of Railways has his estimates under consideration. It belongs to the government system of railways, and it is a part and parcel of the branch line proposition which has been before this House for many years. The branch line proposition could not be effectively carried out without the establishment of a steam-ferry service at these points-I do not say at these particular points because I am not sectional1 in regard to the matter. It has been said that a very good route might be established between the western end of Prince Edward Island and Riohibucto, or some point in the county of Kent. Let it be determined wherever the best route is to be found, there place your ferry, there establish it in the interest, not of any particular locality, not of any particular province or county, but in the interest of the whole Dominion and bring the people of Prince Edward Island into touch with their fellow countrymen throughout the rest of Canada.

I cannot allow this item to carry until I have had an opportunity of bringing to the notice of the minister what I regard as a matter of very great Mr. EMMERSON.
importance to the section of the country from which I come. This particular item gives me a, legitimate opportunity of bringing up matters that I Tegard1 as important to the harbour of North Sydney and Sydney, and if I allowed it to pass without doing so I might not have the opportunity again. We all take more or less pride in the places from which we come and dwell with delight upon their advantages and beauties. I am sure that any person who has the good fortune of living on the shores of the harbour of Sydney or North Sydney, or, as my hon. friend says, the Bras d'Or lakes, can have nothing but pride in the great beauty and commercial advantages of these harbours. Without saying anything against any other harbour in the world, I do not think that Sydney harbour, particularly the harbour of North Sydney, is second to any. That is a big thing to say, but I think it is true. A harbour in Australia, Halifax harbour, and Sydney harbour are regarded1 as the three finest harbours in the world with the preference given to North Sydney and Sydney. There are a few things that should be done for the harbour of Sydney and North Sydney. When I tell the minister that there is in the neighbourhood of 2,000,000 or 3,000,000 of tonnage coming into that harbour every summer he will get some idea of the shipping that is frequenting it, and when I tell him that never a dollar in the world has been spent for the betterment of that harbour he will understand that we are not coming too often or asking too much. It is true that a few dollars may have been expended in building wharfs and breakwaters. While upon general harbour improvements millions are being spent in other 'parts of Canada, there never -has been a dollar spent on this magnificent harbour of Sydney and North Sydney. The outgoing of iron and steel, the incoming of iron ore, and the shipping of 6,000,000 or 7,000,000 tons of coal out of this harbour every year will give the minister some idea of its imnortance. I take this opportunity of bringing to -hi|a notice this magnificent harbour and the splendid facilities which it offers for transportation. We hear a great deal about St. John. It seems to me that the Minister must have heard of the harbour of St. John, he has heard of Courtenay Bay, and he has heard of some $7,000,000, or $10,000,000, or $15,000,000 being spent in the woods at Courtenay Bay in order to make a harbour which when completed will be nothing like as .magnificent a harbour as that at North Sydney. I am surprised when we are talking about the ereat points of transportation in this country where elevators are to be built, where millions of dollars are to be expended in the betterment of transports-

There is a continual growth in this trade. I saw her tracks in Sydney harbour last year, just enough to show us what she could do if she kept at the work. She came to Sydney harbour and without any difficulty made tracks in the ice but she went away and has never come back.

speechtext:
Last winter. I do not know what she came there for except it ivas to give an exhibition of her power, and then she fled and we never have seen her since. Now, the service is three trips a week, but after the first of May there will be a daily boat and with this daily service established, we hope to make connection with the mail boats so that the maritime province mails can be caught up by the ' Bruce ' from the steamers coming up the St. Lawrence and landed at North Sydney by which means the million people in the maritime provinces would get their mail much quicker than by the Rimouski route. speechtext: I endorse what my hon. friend (Mr. McKenzie) has said in reference to the necessity for having an icebreaker at certain times of the year in the harbour of North Sydney and Sydney, which after all is the one harbour. The hon. gentleman (Mr. McKenzie) has not exaggerated the importance of this matter. Unfortunately in some years, in January and February the harbour is frozen over, and I am sure it would not take a large expenditure to have an icebreaker there for a couple of months. This year the harbour froze over a good deal earlier than usual. I think it only justice to the county I represent that I should supplement what has been said by the hon^ member for North Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie. When we are spending millions of dollars in making ports all over the country which are not natural harbours at all, I do not think it is too much to ask the government to assist in this small way the splendid natural harbour of Sydney so as to make it available for shipping at all times during the winter months. I trust that the minister will make inquiry as to the cost of keeping an ice-breaker there during a certain portion of the winter, and I am sure if he puts an ice-breaker there he will do good Work not only for the port of Sydney but for the shipping interests of the Dominion generally.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service

speechtext:

But, after the description given of its beauties and potentialities by my hon. friend (Mr, McKenzie), I shall not delay that visit longer than I possibly can help. I may say, however, that although I have not visited Sydney I possibly have as good an idea of it as my hon. friend (Mr. McKenzie) seems to have of Courtney Bay which he speaks of as being situated in the woods. I would invite my hon. friend

(Mr. McKenzie), to drop off at St. John some time, and I would like to take him around to have a look at Courtenay Bay, and then I am sure he will come back next session and be ready to withdraw the disparaging things he said about it.

subtopic: MAINTENANCE AND REPAIRS TO GOVERNMENT STEAMERS AND ICEBREAKERS.
speechtext: I think it would be hopeless for me to find it without the guidance of my hon. friend the minister.

subtopic: MAINTENANCE AND REPAIRS TO GOVERNMENT STEAMERS AND ICEBREAKERS.
speechtext: There are none so blind as those who will not isee, but I am sure that with the beautifully clear air and exhilarating atmosphere of St. John my hon. friend (Mr. McKenzie) will be able to see further than when his vision is bounded by the four walls of this chamber. I may say that this year we sent the ' Stanley ' to Sydney harbour at the request of some shipping interests with a view of opening the channel so that vessels could get out, and that experiment was very successful. Only last week we sent an ice-breaker there again for the purpose of making a channel up to the pier of the Dominion Coal Company, and as a result of our laudable efforts to assist the port of Sydnev, the ' Stanley ' is now firmly bound in the ice' off Sydney harbour, and I am afraid it will be some days before we can get her released. The question of ice-breaking is every year becoming more and more important, and people are beginning to realize that it has the effect ot helping shipping and trade. I shall be very glad to give my attention to the representations made by my hon. friends and to accede to them so far as it is possible for the department to do so with the steamers and plant now at its command.
