It was we'll known that Dr. Murray w'as a poacher, along with some other men who did not regard it as a heinous offence. Wherever they could get a salmon, they took it, to the injury of the fishing. Dr. Murray was of course no more guilty than the men who participated with him in the amusement. But about the 8th or 9th of October, when this government was safely installed in

power, he went up the river and announced to his fellow poachers that no more Grits were to be allowed to poach on the river, and that he and his friends were going to take all the fish that fall. Later on this new guardian of poachers, in company with some other men were setting nets on the river and he proceeded to telephone into town to Inspector Hockin, that men were poaching on the river, and that he should send out a policeman, which he did, another good Conservative; and he, along with Doctor Murray, took a net from a man who was not fishing, but who was on the road, and who happened to be a Grit, and brought it into town in triumph. As this man complained next day that there was going to be trouble about .this thing, Ghafiles <E. Tanner, writes to the minister, and develops a new phrase of the matter, that employment was to be furnished to no less than three Conservative lawyers in the county. Mr. Tanner writes:
Inspector Hockin of -this place has in hand important cases of salmon poaching on the West River. There has been a lot of poaching, hut the law was never enforced against certain people. The catch the other night involves some people who ought to he severely punished. One of them is a special guardian DeWolf McLean. Other important people are named Porters. _
It is very much in the interest of the public that the cases be thoroughly prosecuted. The example will have a most wholesome effect; and theTe is great need of lan example. These people have been making a business of poaching.

It may be unnecessary in cases at times to have counsel; but in this instance, at this time, having regard to general conditions and the people involved, it is most desirable that speoial dare should be taken to have the prosecutions conducted to a satisfactory conclusion;

All I can say to my hon. friend is that he will not get one official m the Department of Marine and Fisheries hut will say that Mr. Hockin has been a most successful and excellent fishery officer and his record in the department is as high as that of any other official in Canada. That is the departmental record which Mr. Hockin has. He has been a fishery official I think for over a quarter of a century, he has been there under different governments, and his record as fishery officer is. an excellent one in the department, so I am informed by the officials whom I find in the department. Now Mr. Hockin very properly reported to the department that men had been arrested charged with poaching, and surely it is a desirable thing that the fishery laws of the country should be enforced, and that poaching should be stopped. Mr. Hockin writes to the department, having been informed that my hon. friend is going to appear as counsel for the defence,
and recommends that counsel be employed on' the other side. The Department of Justice was asked to name counsel, and they named Mr. Fitzpatrick. Now my hon. friend, having reflected on Dr. Murray and having reflected on Mr. Hockin, now comes down and reflects on the professional conduct of Mr. Fitzpatrick, who is not here to-night to defend himself, either. My hon. friend seems to think that Mr. Fitzpatrick has shown himself to be a party to a conspiracy because he did not cross-examine Dr. Murray. I want to tell him that that fact indicated nothing of the sort. Time and again when I have been acting as counsel I have refrained from cross-examining witnesses where I believed it would do my case more harm than good. One cannot tel] whether Mr. Fitzpatrick was acting well or not from the mere fact that he did not cross-examine witnesses. I do not think it is fair for my hon. friend, who is himself , a member of the profession to reflect upon the professional conduct of a brother member of the profession merely because he did not judge it prudent to cross-examine a witness, who my hon. frieqd thinks he should have cross-examined. I have not seen the evidence in the case, therefore, I cannot give an opinion. All I say is that the fact that he did not crossexamine the witness would not, to my mind, be conclusive evidence or any evidence at all, that he had neglected the case. Then a prosecution is commenced against Dr. Murray in the county court. The opinion of the fishery inspector is that it originated in spite, because of Dr. Murray's action in laying the information against these people, and the fishery inspector advises that Dr. Murray should be defended by the department, and the department has acted upon his advice. Is there anything wrong or improper about that? Then we come down to the fact that an appeal is being taken, and counsel of course are necessary to argue that appeal. Now I would ask my hon. friend if he really thinks on reflection there is anything improper or wrong about it, and if he does not think that he is making a mountain out of a mole hill. I would not like to suggest anything improper,^ but it seems to me that my hon. friend is influenced by his political feeling against Dr. Murray and Mr. Hockin, and possibly against Mr. Fitzpatrick, in the charges he is making. Now it is incredible to me that in a county like the county of Pictou, you will find three men of such leading, standing, and repute-

speechtext: Then, in reference to the first item, I presume it has to do with 'he dismissal of overseers and inspectors appointed by the late government. I am not going to defend the appointment of those officers or attack the dismissal of any gentleman, but I would like to point out that if it were possible for some understanding to be arrived at between the provinces and the Do-minion by which this .vork and the regulations would be under the jurisdiction of one or the other, it would be greatly to the benefit of everybody. The minister may not be aware of it now, but if he happens to continue as minister, he will find out that political advantage is taken of the conditions as they at present exist. Fishermen on the lakes in Ontario especially will apply for an extension of the fishing season to the Dominion. The Dominion officers will be stiff and say: No, the request cannot be granted, while the provincial officers will go to the fishermen and say: We would be delighted to give you an extension but the Dominion will not allow us to do it. That leads to constant friction. That is one of the reasons why I presume the minister's predecessor found it necessary to have a staff of inspectors. He desired to get information as to whether these applications should be -complied with and as to whether the regulations were properly enforced toy the provincial governments. If some arrangement could be made by which the province, or the Dominion-I do not care which-would have absolute control of the regulations and their enforcement, it would relieve a very trying and irritating situation, and I have no doubt rwould be welcomed by both the Dominion and provincial authorities.

I think everybody who has given any thought to the question at all will agree with what my hon. friend (Mr. Graham) has said about the unsatisfactory condition of things as they at present exist. The authority apparently is divided between the two governments. If some arrangement could be made by which the control of the fisheries could be taken ever by one government or the other, it would be very much in the interest of the fisheries, and it would promote the public interest generally.
Every one agrees about this, and it is not a party question by any means. Buff, in the past, it has been found impossible to work the matter out satisfactorily, and I am not prepared to say that even had I



had the time to consider it carefully and thoroughly I would have been more successful than my predecessors have been. Certain questions with regard to the jurisdiction of the provinces and the Dominion at the fisheries are being submitted to the courts in a stated case, and it may be that the decision given by the Privy Council will clarify the situation.

The hon. gentleman suggested that if you had a government in Ottawa of a different political1 stripe from the government of the provinces there would be more difficulty, but I may say that in my short experience with the government of the province of Quebec which is of a different political stripe from the government in power nere, I have had no 'difficulty whatever. Trouble perhaps may come in the future, but it certainly has not come yet. I think every one will agree that if some arrangement can be made for the administration of the fisheries from the one central authority it would be much in the public interest.

speechtext: I beg to call the attention of the Minister of Marine (Mr. Hazen) to a serious accident which occurred recently at Birds Rock Lighthouse in the Gulf of St. Lawrence when the lightkeeper was drowned. Bird Rocks is a very dangerous spot and many accidents have happened in years past, this being the third lightkeeper, in my recollection, who has met with a violent death there. The body of the lightkeeper has been found and is now on Bird Rocks where his wife and his assistant are living in the lighthouse. The father of ,the young man who is an old elector of mine has written me to ask the Minister of Marine to send one of the government steamers to bring the foody to the Magdalen Tslands. The father is an experienced navigator and he says that one of the government steamers, especially the ' Montcalm,' could reach Bird Rocks at this season of the year without any difficulty. It would be a humane act on the part of the Minister if he could comply with the desire of the father of the deceased.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:

I beg to move that the words 'preliminary or qualifying' be inserted before the word * examination.,
BENNETT (Calgary). I certainly think that the provision of the section should be so extended as to provide for the case of graduates within the British Empire. As it now stands it merely allows advancement to those who are graduates of the Royal Military College or of any university in Canada. There are a large number of valuable civil servants that I know of in Canada who are graduates of English universities, some of Cambridge, some of Oxford, and from other leading universities of the world, and I think the privilege should be extended so as to cover the case of graduates in the Royal Military College or of any university in the British Empire. I cannot see why it should be otherwise.

subtopic: CIVIL SERVICE ACT AMENDMENT-POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext: Is there reciprocity in that?

subtopic: CIVIL SERVICE ACT AMENDMENT-POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext: No, there is something better than reciprocity; there is something that concerns true imperialism.

subtopic: CIVIL SERVICE ACT AMENDMENT-POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext: What is it?

subtopic: CIVIL SERVICE ACT AMENDMENT-POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext: Let those who are graduates of the universities of Oxford and Cambridge, who are already in the civil service, and who desire promotion, obtain that promotion by extending this privilege to them.

subtopic: CIVIL SERVICE ACT AMENDMENT-POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext: What I meant by reciprocity was whether the same privilege will be extended to graduates of Canadian universities in the English civil service.

subtopic: CIVIL SERVICE ACT AMENDMENT-POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext: Practically it has been so. Members of our professions go over to England and all they have to do is to go through a very formal examination.

subtopic: CIVIL SERVICE ACT AMENDMENT-POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext:
Does not my hon. friend (Mr. Bennett, Calgary) think that if our people have to go through a formal examination in England in law or in medicine the same thing should take place in Canada? I am not against giving the

privilege to any graduate from. Great Britain, or,any other part of the British Empire, but even in this country the same rulle exactly exists as between the different provinces. There are no reciprocity degrees. Some few years ago a Bill was passed with this object of bringing about reciprocity in this respect, hut the principle involved in Dr. Roddick's Bill was not acceded to by some of the provinces. My hon. friend, I am afraid, is opening up a much wider issue than he thinks. We all stand for the British Empire, but our home is Canada and we want to give first chance to our own people in Canada, In England Donald MaoMaster, K.C., one of the ablest lawyers in this country, had to undergo an examination.

subtopic: CIVIL SERVICE ACT AMENDMENT-POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext:
Purely formal.
Mr. LEMIET1X. Well, let the same formal examination be prescribed for those who come from England, South Africa, Australia or New Zealand. This is a very serious matter. If we extend this privilege to the graduates of any university in the empire the same privilege must be extended to our own people in any part of the empire.

subtopic: CIVIL SERVICE ACT AMENDMENT-POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext: I take exactly the view of this -question that has been expressed by my hon. friend from Rou-ville (Mr. Lemieux). The first duty of this parliament, as I conceive, is towards Canada, and I think that in a matter of this kind we should not be called upon to give rights to Britain which Britain would not give to us. Mv hon. friend (Mr. Bennett, Calgary)' is proposing, if I am not mistaken, what my hon. friend from Brantford (Mr. Cockshutt) would call a jack-handled preference. It is to reconcile myself with the hon. member for Brantford in this matter

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: CIVIL SERVICE ACT AMENDMENT-POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: CIVIL SERVICE ACT AMENDMENT-POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT.

subtopic: CIVIL SERVICE ACT AMENDMENT-POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext: Well, I am not particular about the term; it means the same thing. I think the position of the hon. member for Rouville is sound with regard to this question.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
subtopic: CIVIL SERVICE ACT AMENDMENT-POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext:
The question raised by my hon. friend from Calgary (Mr. Bennett) is one which deserves consideration, and it ought to be looked into, but I think my hon. friend will admit with me that we should not go into this matter on this section of the Civil Service Act. This Bill refers to the third class employees of the Post Office Department. The wording of the clause is that which is adopted by all the other departments If we were to
adopt the principle which -my hon. friend advocates, and advocates so well, we should make the change not only with reference to the third class employees of one department, but with reference to the employees of all the other departments. I think this will appeal to my hon. friend. For the moment, we are only passing a clause which says that no third class clerk shall be eligible for promotion for a higher class until he passes the -qualifying examination, or unless he is a graduate of the Royal Military College, or of a university in Canada.	Even if we were satisfied
it is quite possible that he is right on the iqu-estion-1 would not like to make that provision in -a clause which deals specially with one class in one department. Consequently, I would ask my hon. friend to .allow this amendment to pass as it is. The question whether this ought or ought not to -be put into the Civil Service Act is one well worthy of consideration, -but. we will have to consider it in connection with all the departments and not only in connection with one department. <

subtopic: CIVIL SERVICE ACT AMENDMENT-POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext: This is a question which might well come before the next imperial conference, and I might say to my hon. friend (Mr Bennett, -Calgary) that, sooner or later, he may have to exercise his faculties in the British House of Commons. There will be a good chance for him to advocate these imperial schemes which, for my part, I consider the nobler kind. He might at the same, time, when he is in the British House of Commons, ask the British authorities of free trade doctrine to remove the cattle embargo and to amend the naturalization laws.

subtopic: CIVIL SERVICE ACT AMENDMENT-POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext:
Both the hon. members for Rouville (Mr. Lemieux) and Red Deer (Mr. Clark) entirely misapprehend the point I -make. The hon. member for Red Beer speaks of our first duty being to Canada, but allow -me to remind him that the class of people who would be affected by this proposed change are those who are Canadians, because they are living in Canada and are British subjects by reason of their birth. My understanding is that when one comes and takes up his residence here and finds employment he is a Canadian. I would, therefore, ask the hon. member for Red Deer what he means when he refers to these gentlemen as not being Canadians. Pernaps he might be able, in his usual voluble style, to explain. This clause deals with those who are in the employ of the government of Canada already, and it merely provides for their promotion. To enter that employment they have to pass an examination. In the western provinces any person who desires to study law is allowed the status of a student if a graduate of

the Royal Military College, or any university in the United Kingdom or Canada. We in the western provinces provide that any one may become an articled student at law without examination if he is a graduate of a university in the United Kingdom or of a Canadian university. This young man referred to in this section 3 is already in the employment of the government; the time comes for his promotion and he may be promoted by reason of passing an examination or by reason of his academic attainments, these attainments having been acquired before he became a citizen of Canada.
I submit that any one who has passed the examination and obtained the degree of B.A. in any of the universities of the United Kingdom may just as well be spared that examination as one who is a Canadian and obtains his education in the Royal Military College or in a university in Canada. They are both Canadians, but by an accident of circumstances one got his education in the United Kingdom and the other in Canada; one came to Canada in his youth or was born in Canada and obtained his education here; the other came after he obtained his education in the United Kingdom, and they should be on the same footing because they are both Canadians. The position taken by the hon. member from Rouville (Mr. Lemieux), and by the hon. member from Red Deer (Mr. Clark) was beside the question and had to deal with a case not now before the committee. As the Minister of Marine has suggested, a man born in Canada might have obtained his degree in Oxford or Cambridge, and I know of one particular case where under the Rhodes scholarship system a young man in western Canada so obtained his degree.

subtopic: CIVIL SERVICE ACT AMENDMENT-POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext: A young man who goes to Oxford as a Rhodes scholar must, before doing so, obtain his degree in Canada?

subtopic: CIVIL SERVICE ACT AMENDMENT-POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext: That is not so. I know of two men personnally who did not obtain Canadian degrees. They got the Rhodes scholarship, one in the junior year and the other in the sophomore year.

subtopic: CIVIL SERVICE ACT AMENDMENT-POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext: I know three Rhodes scholars who went from Quebec and each had previously obtained his university degree. '

subtopic: CIVIL SERVICE ACT AMENDMENT-POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext: I know the rules very well and they do not have to obtain a degree here before getting the scholarship.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: CIVIL SERVICE ACT AMENDMENT-POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext: As a matter of fact most of them do have their degrees before getting the Rhodes scholarship.

subtopic: CIVIL SERVICE ACT AMENDMENT-POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext:
Quite so, but it is not essential.
Mr. BENNETT lOalaarv).

subtopic: CIVIL SERVICE ACT AMENDMENT-POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext: My hon. friend (Mr. Bennett) referred to me as having in my usual voluble style referred to someone as not being a Canadian. A compliment from my hon. friend (Mr. Bennett) on volubility of style, I rate extremely high, but my hon. friend seems not only to be voluble in his style of speech but defective in his style of hearing, because I never used the words he attributed to me. I never referred to any one not being a Canadian, as he will find when he reduces his volubility to reading in ' Hansard ' what I actually said.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
subtopic: CIVIL SERVICE ACT AMENDMENT-POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext: I would ask my hon. friend from Red Deer not to forget my Bill.

subtopic: CIVIL SERVICE ACT AMENDMENT-POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext: There is no fear of any one in this House forgetting either the hon. Minister or his Bill. To come to the Bill, as I was doing, I do not think my hon. friend (Mr. Bennett) has touched the argument in this case. If I proceeded actually on his style of argument, I should think that a man who learned his economics in England should be allowed to introduce English goods free of duty because he was born in Canada. It is not the man we are dealing with in this case; it is the degree, it is the qualification. The question is as between a Canadian and an English qualification; the man is not in the question at all. I did not mention him; my hon. friend thought I did, but I did not say anything about the man.

subtopic: CIVIL SERVICE ACT AMENDMENT-POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext: Did not the hon. gentleman say the first duty of this parliament was to legislate for Canadians?

subtopic: CIVIL SERVICE ACT AMENDMENT-POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext: I said the first duty of this parliament was to Canada. There is a very great difference be tween a Canadian and Canada. There may be some Canadians who would not make the distinction, but there is a great distinction between any given minority of Canadians and ' Canada '. I repeat that the first duty of this parliament is to Canada, and I don't think my hon. friend will disagree with me in that.

subtopic: CIVIL SERVICE ACT AMENDMENT-POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext: We agree.

subtopic: CIVIL SERVICE ACT AMENDMENT-POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT.
speechtext: The question is as between degrees and I think we are on safe ground in dealing out to a British degree exactly the consideration which Britain gives to a Canadian degree.

speechtext: I have an amendment to offer, and I might mention it now. _ This resolution is founded on the description contained in the resolution of 1908. The question will probably soon be decided by the Privy Counci) It is true that some years ago a test case
was prepared by the Department of Justice for submission to that court, and I do not know for what reason it was not submitted; hut I am informed by the Attorney General of Quebec, 'Sir Lomer Gouin, that proceedings have been taken against some of the poachers who for some years have had so-called authority from Newfoundland to cut timber in the district which is supposed to _ pertain to the province of Quebec and in some parts of Ungava. When this resolution is passed and Ungava is ceded to Quebec, I am quite sure that the provincial authorities will see that the jurisdiction of both governments is clearly established by the Privy Council. May I ask the right hon. the Prime Minister if he has communicated with the government of Quebec as regards the exact territory which it is proposed to add to the province of Quebec? I understand that the Prime Minister of Quebec has been quite willing to accept the territory of Ungava, but he claims that not only the mainland but also the islands bordering on Ungava, should be given to Quebec; and I would like to know from the right hon. gentleman if the islands will be included in the territory to be ceded to that province.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council

We determined not to include the islands for the present. One reason was the difficulty of giving a description of the islands adjacent to those _ territories which would be sufficiently definite. Then, the islands may be necessary for Dominion purposes in connection with navigation and defence.
Will my right hon. friend kindly inform the House what is the population of Ungava-Indians, Esquimaux and white men-if he has the information at hand?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I have not the information before me at this moment, but I will give it to my hon. friend on the second reading of the Bill.
