speakerposition: subtopic
stagedirection
speechtext: Mr. HAZEN moved the second reading of Bill (No. 140) to amend the Fisheries Act.
Will the minister be kind enough to explain this Bill?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The measure was explained upon its being introduced on .Thursday. My hon. friend (Mr. Sinclair) was, I think absent on that occasion, but it will only take a few moments to again explain the Bill. Owing to the uncertainty as to the question of fishery rights in tidal waters, following the Privy Council decision of 1898, the Department of Marine and Fisheries discontinued the granting of new leases of areas on which to carry on oyster culture and cultivation, and while some of the provinces at first arranged to take up the matter, as it was felt that leases of a satisfactory nature could not be given by the provinces without the consent of the Dominion, it was dropped and things were drifting on in this way up to two years ago when the Inspector of Fisheries took up the question of a modus vivendi with Mr. BORDEN.
the maritime provinces, under which this department would issue leases pending the settlement of the outstanding question of fishery rights, and without prejudice to the claims of the provinces in any way. Nova Scotia and New Brunswick agreed to this modus vivendi, although up to the present time the government of the latter province has not signed it, and of late I think there has been a disposition on its part not to do so; but Prince Edward Island, after first expressing anxiety to enter into such an arrangement, finally declined to do so, and the premier of the province, Mr. Matheson, *who has been in Ottawa for some weeks past, states that the local government is not prepared to enter into any arrangement which would hand over rights which it considers it possesses; but on the other hand is anxious to itself issue lease on the policy that it is in a position to place the industry on a flourishing basis. The question has been taken up with the Department of Justice, and the deputy minister of that department advises the desirability of amending the Fisheries Act, to enable a suitable agreement to be entered into with the province, and states that such an agreement would not in any way prejudice or affect the questions now pending, looking to a decision regarding fishery rights. The matter is important, because as my hon. friend knows the oyster industry in the lower provinces has been falling off year after year. If the hon. gentleman will look at the report of the oyster fisheries on the Atlantic coast prepared by Mr. Wm. A. Found, the Inspector of Fisheries, and published in 1910, he will find a table at page 23 which shows the following state of affairs so far as the oyster industry is concerned:	The oyster fishery some years
ago was one of very great importance. We find, for instance, that in the year 1890 54,926 barrels of oysters were produced in the three lower provinces. The year before that, the quantity was 61,549 barrels. From that time down to the present there has been a continuous falling off in the production year by year until in 1910-11, the last year for which I have statistics, there were only 27,005 barrels of oysters produced in those provinoes, of which 14,045 barrels were produced in New Brunswick, 11,264 barrels in Prince Edward Island, and only 1,696 barrels in Nova Scotia. This discloses a very alarming state of affairs, and it is perfectly clear that unless something is done the oyster fishery will become an industry entirely of the past. There is every opportunity in the maritime provinces for a very large production of oysters. The natural producing beds are situated about as follows:	In New Brunswick 5,000
aojres, in Prince Edward Island 4,300

acres, and iti Nova Scotia 1,250 acres. The area that might be made to produce oysters has been variously estimated at from 1,000,000 to 3,000,000 acres. Hon. gentlemen know that oyster culture is now carried on on the Atlantic coast of the United States to such a large extent that it yields approximately $15,000,000 per annum, though oysters sell for from one quarter to one-third the price they do at the Canadian beds. Under artificial culture, [DOT]oyster beds would yield about 250 bushels per acre per annum, and even as high as 500 bushels per acre might be obtained. Unless oyster culture is taken up in an intelligent way the Canadian oyster fishery must soon be practically wiped out. The regulations have become more and more restrictive, until at the present time fishing is not allowed to begin until October 1 so that it usually lasts about four weeks each season, and as the number of oysters is being year by year reduced, the quantity of spat is being proportionately minimized, so that the beds will have less and less chance of being seeded. When oyster culture is taken up the regulations will have to be so arranged as to enable it to be carried on to the [DOT]best advantage. The department, without the consent of the provinces, was unable to do anything because in view of the condition of the fishery laws at the present time, parties could not accept leases from us unless those leases had been approved of by the provinces concerned. Under these circumstances it has been thought better to pass this law empowering the government of Canada to grant permission to the provinces to make leases of these oyster areas, under rules and regulations and under terms and conditions to be determined upon by the Department of Marine and Fisheries and. the different provincial governments. If that is done it is believed that these oyster areas, which are not now yielding, can 'be leased in blocks of from five to ten acres, as the case may be. The result will be that the person who leases areas will replant the beds, and we hope there may be an increased production in this industry which is such a desirable one to perpetuate and develop. The Bill simply authorizes the Governor icn Council, under terms and conditions that may be [DOT]agreed upon, to empower the provinces to grant leases of these oyster beds.

I am very much obliged to the minister for the very interesting [DOT]account he has given us of the purposes of the Bill. My own view is that it will be much better to leave the management of the oyster industry in the hands of the Dominion government, and that is the view held by the people of Nova Scotia
generally. The other provinces are more interested in this fishery, as they have larger areas capable of cultivating than have the people of Nova Scotia. In Nova Scotia we have no Minister of Fisheries, and no officers to look after these matters; but there is no doubt, at all in my mind that so far as the maritime provinces are concerned it would be much better for the industry and for everybody else concerned, if the Dominion government should continue to take charge of the oyster industry. I presume from what the minister has said that it will not be compulsory on the part of any government to accept the management of the oyster industrv from the Dominion unless they wish to do so. It will still be open, I presume, for the province of Nova Scotia to leave the conduct of the oyster industry in the hands of the federal government, as has been the case in the past, should the province wish to do so. I trust if that should be done, the minister will take an interest in this important question, and carry out such a policy as will have the effect of conserving the oyster industry.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I am very glad to hear the hon. gentleman's views because they entirely concur with my own. I think without doubt it is more in the interest of the oyster industry that it should be managed by the Department of Marine and Fisheries at Ottawa. This Bill is simply introduced to meet a difficulty which faces us in the case of Prince Edward Island, and I fear also in the case of New Brunswick. Nova Scotia has, however, consented to our carrying on the management of the industry in that province, and we are prepared to have the oyster areas delimited and lease them to certain people under the regulations to be established. But there is no intention of throwing any burden in connection with this matter on the provincial governments. To my mind the other governments are making a mistake which will involve them in a certain amount of expenditure in the way of stocking and delimiting the beds, and in other Tespects. However, that is a matter for the provinces themselves to decide. If Nova Scotia is still willing ito agree to the modus vivendi, we are prepared to go ahead and do our share.

In the county I have the honour to represent there is some business done in the cultivation of oysters and this industry is of considerable importance to a couple of the districts there. On that account I am emboldened to say, I think it would be a mistake to transfer the cultivation of the oyster to the ! provincial government. As my hon. friend

from Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair) pointed out, they have not the machinery down there for the cultivation of the oyster, and I fear if the whole thing is transferred to the province, the result may be ultimately the entire neglect of this industry. As it is, there has been a serious falling off. I think that the department here should devote a little more attention to the matter of oyster cultivation. The beds in my county, to which I refer, are in Tracadie harbour. I have asked the department to have some cultivation done there; and I take this opportunity of calling the attention of the minister to this place. It was proposed, I think, last year, that Mr. Kemp should go down and do some work there, as he did fifteen years ago, but owing to the fact that he was engaged in 'Prince Eidward Island, it was impossible for him to go. I had good reason to expect, however, that this matter would receive attention at an early date and I hope that the assurances given will be borne in mind by the present minister.

I understood that under this proposed arrangement, the Dominion government would still retain the management and regulation of the fisheries and the local government would have the power to grant leases and receive the rents from those leases.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: As in practically all fisheries, we make the regulations.
And the local government has the rents-

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Well, the effect would be that we would allow the local government subject to conditions which may be agreed upon, to grant the leases and to get the benefit of what revenues there -may be. I do not expect that there will be a large revenue. The license fee is merely nominal, a dollar or two an -acre. These licenses would be controlled by the commissioner. But I think that there is no question that under the law, the power to regulate in relation to close seasons and so on, is vested in the Dominion government. Even where it has been decided, as in the case of the rivers, where the provinces are the riparian proprietors, that they have the rights to lease those riveTS to anglers and to collect the fees, yet the regulations regarding the close season and all that sort of thing are made here at Ottawa.
And enforced by the officers of this government?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes.

I assume that the minister intends to make appropriations for the promotion of the oyster business. I understand that in Nova Scotia, assuming that Mr. CHISHOLM (Antigonish)
these beds are left under the control of the federal government, something will be done. But if in Prince Edward Island they do not agree to leave the beds under control of the federal government, will the minister spend money to assist the oyster propagation there?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Under the Bill, we will not spend money anywhere in oyster propagation. The proposition is, that worn-out bottoms, capable of producing oysters, but now sterile, will be leased to private individuals and these private individuals will practically farm below the sea as the farmers do in the land. They will lease these areas, plant them, and reap the profits.
Will the local government have the right to determine the length of time?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Under the Bill everything is subject to terms and conditions that may be agreed upon between the two provinces, and that will be a matter of agreement having regard to conditions that are desirable.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Motion agreed to, and Bill read a second time, and the House went into committee thereon.

If the provinces avail themselves of the benefit of this measure, will that mean that the Dominion government will abandon the work it has been carrying on recently, in connection with oyster culture? An officer of the hon. gentleman's (Mr. Hazen) department has been doing work in the different parts of the maritime provinces in this connection. For the last few years, I believe he has been operating in Prince Edward Island-Some years ago, .this expert of the department, Mr. Kemp, was in the neighbourhood of my own riding, and planted some oysters in the Annapolis river at Goat Island. I have not been able to get a report on that experiment to learn whether it turned out satisfactorily or whether it was a failure. Is it proposed to abandon work of this character? Or is this work to go on and are we to have reports of the progress made?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: We must be able to get reports in the department. If the hon. gentleman will let me know what report he desires, I will expedite the furnishing of it. Mr. Kemp is now in Ottawa, I believe. There must be reports on file, I assume, though, as my attention has not been called to the matter, I cannot say that IJrave seen those reports.
No, there is no report.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Then I should think it w mid be desirable that my hon. friend

should call for a report, and I will be glad to have it furnished. Even though this work is being carried on by arrangement with the provinces, as undoubtedly it will be in Prince Edward Island, and maybe in other provinces, I think that from the national standpoint, and having in view the importance of this matter, it is only right and proper that the department should continue, as far as it can, to assist in the development of the industry by placing the services of its expert in oyster culture at the disposal of any province to assist that province by advice and consultation. If the government here are to carry on the work then, in addition to the leasing of these areas, it might be well for us also to carry on experimental work to furnish object lessons to those leasing areas from the government as to the best methods of oyster culture. I do not see why we should cease our work here even although under this Bill we enable the provinces to extend their work.
Bill reported, read the third time and passed.

speakerposition: subtopic
stagedirection
speechtext:
Bill (No. 100) for the aid and encouragement of agriculture-Mr. Burrell-read the second time and House went into committee thereon.
On section 2-annual grant to encourage; agriculture,

It seems to me that this clause is fairly subject to criticism in that it proposes to leave to the Governor in Council very wide discretion as to the granting of subsidies. A subsidy may be granted to one province which is not in proportion to its population or needs. Subsidies granted to provinces ought to be based upon some principle, as nearly as possible on the principle to be found in the British North America Act. If this Bill passes, it will give the Governor in Council absolute discretion, without consulting parliament, to do what the Governor in Council pleases with the money which may be voted for this purpose. 1 do not know whether it is intended that when the estimates are brought down a separate amount should be voted for each province or a lump sum for the whole Dominion to 'be used at the pleasure of the Minister of Agriculture. Perhaps my hon. friend the Minister of Agriculture might enlighten the committee as to what is intended in that respect.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
There is absolutely no desire on the part of the government to divide the money in any way except what is absolutely fair and equitable. I stated in introducing the Bill that the money would
be granted according to the population of the various provinces, and I think there would be no objection to bringing down the supplementary estimates divided as they would be according to the populations of the various provinces.
Well, why should that not be provided in the Bill?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: I do not see why.

It is a wrong principle. If the Minister of Public Works were to come down with a Bill providing that moneys appropriated to public works might be divided in the discretion of the Governor in Council we would all be shocked. It is true we have the statement of my hon. friend, and I have no doubt that the intimation he has given will be carried out in good faith, but parliament is passing a law which presumably is to remain permanently upon the statute-book, and I think we ought to recognize the principle upon which subsidies are to be given namely, in proportion to the population of the different provinces.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I have no doubt that the practical working out of this will result in the amount voted by parliament being apportioned practically in proportion to the population of the different provinces, but I do not think parliament should lay down a hard and fast rule that that should be the case. There may be years when one province will need for agricultural purposes more than another. Regard must be had to the conditions in the different provinces. It would be better to leave it as it is, allowing some small measure of discretion with the Governor in Council that he may have regard to the different conditions. My hon. friend will see that there should be some elasticity and a certain amount of discretion although the probable result will be that the provinces will all get their fair share.

Of course that could all be done under a special Act. When the estimates are brought down and passed they become a statute of the Dominion of Canada, and you can give aid to any province for any purposes for anything within the constitution. This is a general principle laid down providing for an amount of money to be expended annually and there should be some basis as to how the money will be divided. To put it on a sordid ground, it is possible that in one province, where a provincial election may be taking place, the government might intimate, as certain gentlemen did in a riding recently, that if the people want a lot of money expended in that province, they had better put in a certain party. In a riding recently they were told that if they wanted a lot of money spent on agriculture it would be

well for them to vote for a certain candidate. That is what was said by a very prominent member of this House.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I have heard that statement frequently in the last fifteen years.
Very frequently.

The hon. gentleman seems to want to hang on to it. With that experience, there should1 be some standard established when a general principle is being laid down. Special circumstances can be met, by special legislation, and special estimates, as they arise. But, this is for the distribution of an amount to be voted annually and the government are asking us to place in their hands the sayso of where this money will go without any regard to the population of the different provinces.
Mr. HUGHES (Victoria;. It may not go to a province at all; it may go beyond a province.

This Act, unfortunately, says it shall be confined to the provinces. If we are going to hand this over to a department of the government we shall lay down the general principle upon which the division shall be made. I say this all the more strongly coming from the province of Ontario which has the largest population, and I think ought to have some consideration, particularly wnen the government had such a large support from that province.

The statement of my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Hazen), which is quite at variance with the statement of my hon. friend the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Burrell), shows the necessity for having some provision in this Bill. The Minister of Agriculture made the statement, as if it were the settled policy of the government, that whatever money as voted should be distributed among the different provinces in proportion to population. The Minister of Marine and Fisheries, having an eye perhaps to the condition of affairs suggested by my hon. friend on my right (Mr. Graham), says: Oh, it will not do to declare that it shall be distributed according to population because we must have some discretion; there must be a certain leeway left to us; we must be allowed to pick out the different provinces, and to say how much money shall be given to each; circumstances may arise which might make it desirable for the Governor in Council to give larger proportion to one province than to another. That shows that the government has not settled upon its policy. The Minister of Agriculture, with Mr. GRAHAM
the very best intentions might be outvoted by the Minister of Marine and Fisheries when the matter comes before council. It is proposed to increase the subsidies to the different provinces. That is the basis of the provision, and nothing else. Section 2 says:
The Governor in Council may grant . . . to any province, for the encouragement of agriculture, a subsidy not exceeding such sum as may in such year be voted, by parliament for that purpose.
The Fathers of Confederation, haJving had in mind what would be the necessity of the different provinces, what they would require for education, roads, bridges, and other provincial purposes, felt that, in order to guard against dissatisfaction in the future, in order to guard against difficulties as between the different provinces and in order to prevent the spectacle of the provinces being obliged to come to the federal treasury

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: If my hon. friend is going to dwell on the Fathers of Confederation, probably we had better take lunch first.

I rather think so too.
At one o'clock House took recess.
House resumed at three o'clock.

Before the recess, when the Minister of Trade and Commerce seemed to think that the principles of the Fathers of Confederation should be subordinated to bis desire to get an early luncheon, I was proceeding to speak of the agreement of confederation, with regard to the subsidies, and I showed, I think, that it was considered in the highest degree desirable that the provinces should know exactly what subsidies they were going to receive, and that the allowance to the provinces should be made upon a fixed and definite basis, so that the people of any one province would not feel that they were in any way subject to control by or dependent upon the generosity of the federal government. The idea was to make them in every possible respect independent of the federal authorities. That was the same plan which was adopted as the result of the interprovincial conference in 1906. The governments of the different provinces met together at the request of the federal government and increases were made to all the provinces, but they were made upon a fixed and definite principle. It is now proposed to do by this Bill, what the government asked parliament to do in reference to the Highways Act, that is: to vote subsidies to the different provinces, but

to 'leave it in the discretion of the Governor in Council as to how those moneys would be apportioned. We know very well that one of the most important subjects with which the governments of the provinces have to deal is the subject of agriculture. All the provinces give aid for the encouragement of agriculture, and by this Bill it is proposed to add to the subsidies of the provinces sums to be devoted to this special object. I submit that in the interests of all the provinces, in the interests of the whole people of Canada, this Bill should provide that these additional subsidies should be granted upon a fixed and definite principle. The Minister of Agriculture admitted that was right and he said it was intended to apportion these amounts according to population. But that the government has not any definite policy upon the subject, is evident from the remarks of the Minister of Marine, who apparently took distinct issue with the Minister of Agriculture and said that there might be circumstances which would render it desirable not to grant the aid according to population, but to leave it to the discretion of the Governor in Council. In the absence of any definite statement from the Prime Minister, that shows the government has no definite policy upon this subject. I submit that the principle in this Bill is most objectionable. It was bad enough to do this sort of thing in respect to the highways, and the only excuse the Prime Minister gave for that was that the Bill had been drawn in a hurry and they had not had time to work out the details. Let me ask the Minister of Agriculture if that is the excuse in this case. Has there been no opportunity to work out the details of this measure, so that it is necessary to come to Parliament with this skeleton of a Bill and ask Parliament, with respect to these moneys for the promotion of agriculture, to give to the Governor in Council an absolutely free hand to deal with these grants just as they please? I can hardly imagine a case arising where there would be any difficulty if the Bill provided that these subsidies be given to the different provinces according to the population of each. All the provinces of Canada are agricultural provinces; they are equally interested in the matter of agriculture, they are all spending large sums of money for the encouragement of agriculture. Therefore, I cannot imagine that any possible difficulty will arise if the government should amend this Bill so as to provide that these subsidies should be given just as are subsidies provided by the British Worth America Act, on the basis of the population of each province. This Bill! purposes yielding to the Governor in Coun-t cil that power over the expenditure of money which parliament has always been jealous of retaining. In the estimates there
are almost thousands of items in respect to which parliament is asked to give its ap-( proval or disapproval for all kinds of public works which are specified in detail, but in this case, it is proposed simply to pass the Bill in blanket form, giving to the Governor in Council, which means the Minister of Agriculture, the right to be generous to one province and niggardly to another, and to depart from the principles laid down in the British North America Act.

election times to discriminate as between one province which favours the government and another province which does not. My hon. friend is full of good intentions, I know; but let us make it dear in this legislation that there shall be no discrimination but that all the -provinces shall be treated alike, and that the grants shall be really in the interest of the farmers and not- in the interest of one political party.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
There seems to be some rather strange misconception in regard to this Bill. I am almost led to think that the ibon. member for St. John (Mr.Pugsley) and the hon. member for Rouville (Mr. Lemieux) were not in the House when I asked leave to introduce the Bill, for I took particular pains to state accurately and clearly what was the purport of the measure and what were the lines on which the government were going to proceed. I know that my hon. friend from St. John has a very fertile and expansive mind, and he has probably put into his remarks some statements in regard to which he was not very serious. He said that it was to be left to the Governor in Council to apportion the money among the different provinces. What the Bill refers to the Governor in Council is not the allotment of the money, but to devise the ways in which the respective amounts shall be expended, so as to ensure their being expended on agriculture and in such a way as not to induce the provinces to knock off their own agricultural grants, but rather to stimulate them along those lines. This is done because we had not time to formulate an exact policy under which we could spend this money ourselves, and in order to implement the promise of the leader of the government to give some aid to agriculture this year. I am perfectly in sympathy with what the hon. member for Rouville (Mr. Lemieux) says in regard to the work done by Macdonald College and other educational institutions, and I believe the money which this parliament may vote for agriculture would be well expended if devoted to the objects aimed at by these institutions. I might point out that in the province of Ontario, of about half a million dollars per year which the provincial government spends on agriculture, nearly 30 per cent is spent on agricultural education; and in Nova Scotia nearly 40 per cent of the money spent by the provincial government on agriculture is spent on agricultural education. The Dominion government would be amply justified in helping the provinces along these lines. But to relieve the mind of my hon. friend from St. John, I may say that when the votes are brought down, they will be divided among the different provinces according to population, so that eaoh province will know Mr. LEMIEUX.
exactly what proportion will be allotted to it. Perhaps I may be allowed to quote the closing lines of the remarks I made in introducing the Bill, and which will make this quite clear:
The principle upon which grants will be apportioned will be that of division based on population, the census of 1911 -governing. The government has given a good deal of consideration to this phase of the matter, and has arrived at the conclusion that the population basis is one which is open to the fewest objections. . . I may add that there is no desire in this matter to favour -this or that of the various provincial governments. We recognize that in every provinoe a government has been placed there by the people, and I am voicing the sentiments of the Prime Minister and his colleagues in saying that the sole purport of this measure is to do what the title declares it is designed for, viz.: to aid and encourage agriculture.
Would that include aid to annual exhibitions?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: It would be done in any way, upon agreement between the provincial governments and the Minister of Agriculture, so long as it will assist in agricultural development. These details must be left to this government, which is giving a grant which is rather unusual. The hon. member for St. John intimated that there was some difference of opinion in the government on this matter. I do not think so. What the Minister of Marine said was that owing to natural conditions of an extraordinary character, it might be advisable in one year to spend more in one province than in another. We can all understand that; but this year at any rate we do not propose to take that into consideration. There is going to be a straight division -according to population.
What about next year?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: In introducing this Bill I pointed out that it was more or less of a temporary measure. The idea of the government was to work- out this year a thorough knowledge of agricultural conditions in the whole country. The British North America Act has slightly confused the jurisdiction as between the provinces and the Dominion as to agriculture. We would prefer to do this work ourselves, but we want to work out the scheme this year on lines that will be fair and that will be approved by the provinces.

When an amount will be put in the estimates in accordance with this Bill, will that amount invariably apply to all the provinces, or will the government be in a position one year to exclude three or four provinces, and in another year to exclude others, or will

any amount put in the estimates be applied to all the provinces?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Not one dollar can be spent, under this Bill until it has been voted by parliament, and parliament has to be satisfied.

Can the expenditure be withheld without the consent of the province? Suppose 'a certain amount is voted to a province and the province and the Dominion government do not agree, could it be withheld at the dictation of this government?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: If the province could not satisfy the government that the amount would be expended c-n agriculture, it would not be proper for the government to hand it over.
Apart from that there would be no conflict?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No.

Would it not be very much better to have the distribution provided for in the Bill? Of course, we will all take the word of the present Minister of Agriculture, that if he is Minister of Agriculture next year, he will divide the money among the provinces according to population; but there might be a condition of things under which the Minister of Marine and Fisheries would feel that it would not be in the interest of the Dominion to expend this money according _ to population. That is what we on this side of the House fear. Therefore, I think it would be better for the minister to frame an amendment providing that the total amount to be divided under this Act must be divided among the provinces pro rata, allowing this government to exercise some control as to the manner in which it should be expended under proper arrangements with the provincial governments,

I do not at all object to the provisions of section 3, which provides for the making of an agreement between the federal and the provincial governments. I think that is very proper, but it does seem to me that my hon. Mend the Minister of Agriculture has not shown any reason for not putting in the Bill a provision that the moneys shall ibe divided according to the population of the different provinces. My hon. friend (Mt. Burrell) says that this year the government aTe experimenting in oTder to ascertain whether it is desirable to expend the moneys themselves instead of through the provincial government, but I would remind the hon. gentleman that if that decision should be come to, they will have to apply to parliament to amend this Bill because the measure provides for subsi-168
dies to the provinces. Therefore, before the Dominion government could take charge of the expenditure to be made under this Bill, the Bill would have to be amended.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Why?

Because section 2 provides :
The Governor in Council may, in any year, and upon such terms and subject to such conditions as are prescribed by order in council, grant to any province, for the encouragement of agriculture, a subsidy not exceeding such sum as may in such year be voted by parliament for that purpose.
Now, I take it, Mr. Chairman, that means the granting of a money subsidy to the governments of the different provinces. It would not be making a grant to a province if the government themselves expended the money by giving aid to exhibitions or giving aid to agricultural colleges; that would not be in accordance with the terms of this Bill. The Bill provides and provides only, for a subsidy to different provinces. The expression subsidy to a province is well understood. We had it first in the British North America Act, and we have had it in all the Acts in amendment to the British North America Act, which have been, passed since that time. I am going to suggest an amendment which I think my hon. friend (Mr. Burrell) would have inserted in the Bill if he had had time to think the matter over before introducing the measure. I will move that the following be added as a subsection to section 2:
All moneys voted in any year, if expended under this Act shall be .apportioned among, and paid to, the governments of the different provinces of the Dominion according to the respective population of the said provinces as established by the last census for the time being.
Now that carries out what my hon. friend says he would do if he had control over the matter as Minister of Agriculture, but he should put it clearly upon the statute- book that that shall be done. It would be a declaration by this parliament that where an arrangement is made for voting moneys in the way of subsidies, these payments shall be founded upon the principle of population so far as the different provinces are concerned, and it prevents an Act going on the *st'atue-foook which is imdefinaite in its character, and which would be a declaration by parliament that it was willing to vote moneys in the way of subsidies, leaving it to the government to do as they pleased with the money as between the different provinces.

It is perfectly apparent that if the scheme outlined by the hon, member for St. John were carried



into effect it would be perfectly useless. For instance, take the two provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan:	It must be
apparent that at times we _ might have an excellent crop in one province and not in the other. It therefore, becomes necessary to provide seed grain in consequence of hail falling in certain localities. The hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) knows perfectly well that in some sections of the province of Alberta during the present year the crop was entirely destroyed by reason of hail, while in other sections there was no destruction at all. In the province of Saskatchewan no loss was experienced. It therefore, becomes essential that in the distribution of this money there should be no fixed principle, but rather regard should be paid to the demands from the several provinces by. reason of their necessities. That should be the governing consideration, I submit to this committee, in determining how the money should be divided. For example I think the province of Saskatchewan this year, having regard' to seed grain requires little or no money at all; but I happen to know that in the province of Alberta large sums of money will be required to meet the demands of the settlers not only by reason of hail, but owing to the early frost, a condition which has not arisen in the other provinces. If you divide the money according to population then the necessities of at least one of the provinces may not be properly met. There is this, point further. As the interests of the provinces are presented to the Governor m Council, the government of Canada should practically determine how that money should be apportioned and divided.

The hon. gentleman who has just spoken evidently did not hear the remarks of the Minister of Agriculture, who stated most positively that although not mentioned in this Bill, the estimate brought in would provide that the money should be divided, under this measure, between the provinces according to population. What the amendment proposes to do is to embody in the present Bill the suggestion and the promise of the Minister of Agriculture. The amendment simply proposes to place in the Statute what the Minister of Agriculture says is the policy of the government. My hon. friend (Mr. Bennett, Calgary) says that he objects to it being divided on any fixed principle. But that is what we on this side are contending for. We think it would be wise to do that. It does not at all affect, and would not and could not affect, the Act referring to the distribution of seed grain, or any other distribution to meet any misfortune that might occur. When special cases arise, this parliament has unlimited power to deal with such cases by special Mr. BENNETT (Calgary).
legislation, and it always has done so. Should any requirements appear or be needed in any province, this parliament has always been, I think, fairly generous in meeting the emergency and providing money in the estimates to so satisfy such a demand. But this Act is to provide practically a subsidy to each province, and that subsidy is to be expended' along certain lines, and it has no connection whatever with any special conditions that may arise. The Minister of Agriculture has taken the ground, and taken it wisely, that when this money comes to be distributed under this Bill, which is nothing less than a subsidy, it will be divided according to population among the various provinces; and when estimates are brought down for the money to he expended under this Bill, those estimates will be provided among the various provinces according to the population. Now all we are asking is this: That there be embalmed in the statute a clause which shall carry out the promise of the minister to the House this afternoon.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: My hon friends on the other side are threshing out exactly the same question that was debated at very great length in connection with the Highways Act. There is not the slightest objection to setting forth the proposed division of the appropriation in a statute, but we are not going to put the division m this Bill because there is no necessity for it. The division will appear in the Supply Act in both cases, and there is no need whatever for putting it in this Act as well, so far as I can understand. Up to the present time no good reason has been shown to me why we should do that. If we were providing in this Bill a certain sum of money whicn need not therefore be voted by parliament, everything that has been said on the other side would be absolutely logical and absolutely reasonable, and we would accept it at once. But we have already assured the House, and it remains to be seen whether our assurance will be borne out, that the moneys provided for assistance to highways, and the moneys provided for assistance to agriculture, will be brought into the estimates in the way my hon. friend (Mr. Burrell) has mentioned this afternoon, and will therefore appear in the Statute, and that Statute will be just as binding as if the same provision were made in this Bill. It seems to me therefore that there is no good reason why the division should appear in both places.

It is all very well when my right hon. friend gives us the assurance that the division will take place in the supplementary estimates this year, but we have no guarantee that it will take

place the next year or the year after. If that be the intention what good reason can be urged against putting it in the present Bill, and then we will know what will occur not only next year but some other year when another gentleman perhaps may be leading the government. We do not know what conditions may obtain in the future, and we would like to have this safeguard inserted in the Bill so that we may know what is going to happen. It has been said by the hon. member for Calgary (Mr. Bennett) that in the west this is going to be distributed in providing seed grain. For my part I can well conceive what might happen if my hon. friends were able to go to any particular province in Canada and say: ' We will give you so many bushels of seed grain this year.' My right hon. friend (Mr. Borden) says, 'We do not intend to do that.' But we on this side would like to have the amendment of my hon. friend from St. John (Mr. Pugsley) inserted in the statute so that we may know what will be done in future.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: My hon. friend seems to forget that every year parliament has the matter in its own hands. A vote must be brought down, and parliament will have a perfect right, before the appropriation is made, to point out any injustice to any particular province. And that appropriation must be embodied in the Supply Bill. It seems to me there cannot possibly be any danger such as my hon. friend has alluded to. He speaks of the great advantage-I do not know if he speaks from experience-
No, I never distributed seed-grain.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
My hon. friend seems to have very impressive ideas with regard to this measure. The proposal in this Bill, as m the Highways Bill, is to utilize such provincial machinery as can effectively be utilized in connection with the subject. I need hardly remind my hon. friend from St. John (Mr. Pugsley), that af this parliament isaw fit to make a general appropriation for aid to agriculture, it would not be necessary to have any such Bill as this at all. He knows that under section 95 of the 'British North America Act, the laws of this Dominion relating to agriculture override any provincial laws that are inconsistent with them. This parliament has the primary right, the dominant right, to legislate in respect of agriculture; so that if we saw fit to depart from the proposal which we are making now-which I think is a very good proposal-of co-operation with the provinces we should not need any legislation at all. But it has seemed to us that co-operation with the provinces and the 168}
utilization of provincial machinery is a good principle. At all events, we are disposed to try it, and to try it on terms that will be absolutely fair and just to every province of Canada. It is perfectly obvious that we must have assurance that the money in each province will be expended judiciously, economically, and acceptably, and for the purposes for which parliament has voted it. That is the only qualification we make with regard to the matter. So far as the distribution is concerned it will be on the fairest basis we can propose, the basis suggested by my right hon. friend the leader of the opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier), the basis of population, the basis of existing subsidies.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
If everything
contemplated in this Bill can be done by an appropriation Bill, what is the object of this measure? The object is that intimated by my right hon. friend (Mr. Borden), to provide a system of co-operation with the provinces. So far, we all agree with him. The object is a good one, and we do not oppose it-quite the contrary. But if the object is to lay a foundation for cooperation between the Dominion and the provinces, it seems to me obvious-and I submit it to my right hon. friend (Mr. Borden)-that \ye should have a complete law which the provinces will know and understand, and which will not be changed by an appropriation Act to be voted year by year. To this end the method of appropriation among the different provinces should be laid down. I confess that I view with some alarm the statement of the (Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Burrell), When he said that this year it was intended that the money should be apportioned among the different provinces. But he was not looking to the future.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: The right hon. gentleman must have misunderstood' me.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I am very glad of that. Will the hon. gentleman (Mr. Burrell) then please tell me what he said ? I understood him to take the view expressed by the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Hazen) that it might be necessary to give to one locality more than to another. On the Highways Bill we heard the same thing from my hon. friend from South Simcoe (Mr. Lennox)-that he hoped the policy would not be pursued of making an even distribution among the provinces, because one province might require more than another. That is exactly the kind of thing we object to, and I understand that this is the sentiment of the House, and that everybody is satisfied that this money should be distributed on the basis of population, which, I think, is

the fairest basis. If that be so, then why not have it stated in the Bill. Then, happen what may afterwards, the distribution of the money voted by parliament, for the purpose of aiding agriculture would be given in a proportion that is known and understood. I would not insist so much on this amendment but for the statement made by two prominent members of the majority, the hon. member for South Sim-coe (Mr. Lennox) and the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Hazen), that there may be occasion when it would ba advisable to give more money to one province than to another. This makes it absolutely indispensable that this should be in the Bill.

May I remind the right hon. gentleman (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) when he speaks of distributing this money according to population, that to distribute it on the basis of a decennial census would not be fair to the west, inasmuch 'as in the new provinces we have a census every five years.
The amendment does not say ' the last decennial census,' but the ' last census.'

But, the hon. gentleman (Mr. Pugsley) knows that you have to read the law by the special provisions in regard to Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta. The population of one province may increase by 100,000, while another may increase only 10,000. Mani-| toba, probably, will not increase as rapidly as the other western provinces. The government will have the information before them by reason of the immigration returns. They should be free to distribute the money according to the necessities of the case, the climatic and other conditions that may arise from year to year.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: There may be something in what is stated by my hon., friend (Mr. Bennett, Calgary). Everybody is aware that the population of the western provinces increases more rapidly than that of the eastern provinces. But that does not take from the principle that the money ought to be distributed according to population, and if according to population, it should be according to population as shown by the census.

I had not intended to speak on this subject, although it is one in which I am very much interested. But the leader of the opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) happened to mention my attitude in regard to a former Bill, the one relating to the highways. I realize that I am in a hopeless minority, as it. might be expressed, at this time. I am' Sir WILFRID LAURIER
entirely in harmony with the government's attitude that there is no reason whatever for incorporating this proposed amendment in the Bill; I am opposed to that amendment at all events. I am exceedingly glad that the government has decided to aid agriculture. As I said the other, day in reference to the Highway Bill, it is a step in the right direction.
I think I will stand alone in the position I take in regard to the system of distribution. The government's policy is that, they shall distribute this money absolutely upon the basis of population. The at-tiude of the opposition leader is also that it should be distributed upon the basis of population. The only difference between them is whether that principle should be incorporated in the Bill now. I do not want it incorporated in the present Bill, because I do not think it would be right to incorporate it, but since the matter has been mentioned, I would rather like to place on record, my view upon this question as to the system of distribution. My view ts that neither the money under the Road Act nor those under this Act, should be distributed upon the basis of population, and I hope, as I said the other day, that the government, having taken this step in advance, will yet come to realize that, whatever party may be in power, the true basis of distribution is the needs of the localities, and not population or conformity to provincial boundaries. I believe that the less sectionalism wre have, the better. I believe that we should throw aside all parish politics, and parish legislation, that we should leave to the county councils the duty of providing for the needs of counties, and to the provinces, the duty of providing for the special needs of the provinces; that when we come into this House, whether it is in the selection of cabinet ministers, or as far as may be in the selection of senators, and as far as may be in everything, that we should realize that it is not a question of county or locality or province, but it is a question of the whole of Canada, and that we are legislating for the whole of Canada. I can see that cases will arise and must arise, when it would be more in the interest of Canada as a whole, more for the general advantage of Canada, that we should distribute this money upon the basis of the needs of localities altogether aside from the question of provincial boundaries.
It has been suggested that this may be used for political purposes. I am not afraid of that, I would not be deterred from my course even if the right hon. the leader of the opposition were in power (which God prevent for a long series of years, at all events) because I think the true principle is, that this government have been chosen

by the people, upon them has been cast the duty of legislating and providing for the needs of Canada; and they have the right to take upon themselves the duty of determining, and it is their duty to determine from time to time what shall be the basis of the distribution of this money. My answer would be, if I had the power to make the answer:	Do not trouble yourselves gentlemen, we are in power, and we are asked by the people to administer this fund, we will take the responsibility and to the people we will be responsible. I would not be afraid of criticism in that position. My view is, that certain portions of Canada are especially adapted for agriculture. Certain other portions of Canada are not so manifestly adapted for agriculture and the government of this country takes a large view of the whole situation, not provincially, but they say: Here is a locality that particularly needs the distribution of a certain amount of money; we are charged with the responsibility of distributing the funds of the people of Canada and whether the criticism is favourable or unfavourable, we will decide that this particular locality, whether it be in Quebec or in Manitoba, shall have this assistance out of this public fund. That position would be subject to criticism. Hon. gentlemen opposite, would perhaps think it was not honestly done, because they have not been accustomed to that sort of thing to any great extent; but wrapt in the consciousness of honesty, knowing I was doing what I absolutely believed to be right, I would" disregard the criticism of the opposition and I feel confident that the time will come when we will have sufficiently enlarged ideas in Canada, as to the necessity of obliterating provincial lines to distribute public funds as regards railways and this fund, on the basis of the greatest need of the population and having regard to the general advantage of Canada.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: And suppressing the provinces also.

Not suppressing the provinces to any degree, but endeavouring that every province shall devote its energies to that particular line of industry best adapted to develop the greatest good for the greatest number of the whole Dominion of Canada and where a section of Canada is especially adapted to mining or fishing or agriculture, we shall bend our energies to develop it along; the lines of least resistance, and so seek to promote the general welfare of all without regard to provincial boundaries or local boundaries of any kind.

to say that this money should Ibe handled	in	the different provinces
on conditions to be fixed by the Dominion government? Why should not the money be handed over to the provinces to be disbursed on the responsibility of the provinces? Why are not the government and legislature of the province just as responsible to the people of the province as this parliament and this government are to the people of the whole Dominion? It would almost seem as though the idea of this legislation was that the provincial legislatures and governments were in some sense inferior, or less intelligent, or less responsible, than this government is. That is an assumption that is entirely unwarranted. The provincial legislature represent the people of the province just as the members of this parliament represent the people of the Dominion and the government o.f each of the provinces represent the people of the province just as this government represent the people of the Dominion. Then why should there be any hesitation, considering that it is right to hand back to the provincial governments for exspenditure by them, money taken out of the Dominion revenue which is not provided for in the Confederation Act? Why should there be any hesitation about doing it and saying that we are doing it for that reason and that purpose? Why should this government want to exercise some sort of directive control over the proper functions of government in the various provinces? Why should we assume that they do not know how to build their own roads or aid agriculture within their own limits? Such an assumption is entirely uncalled for. So, I say that if we do intend to follow the principle that we are handing back to the various provinces money that in equity, though not in law, is theirs, let us put it in the Act and say that that is the principle in accordance with the amendment of my hon. friend from St. John. As long as the government refuse to do that, as long as the Bill contains the words and phrases appearing in it as it comes to the House, I must say that the government are asking too much in asking the people to consider that the fixed policy of the government is such as the premier has undertaken to state here to-day. The very fact that there are supporters of his own who hold diametrically opposite views to those he has expressed is a reason for urging that the principle, if there is a principle, should be embodied in the Act.

Mr. Chairman, the hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. 'Burrell) has admitted again and again in the course of his remarks that it is the intention to distribnte this money according to population. What objection can there be to inserting that in the Act? Is it not Mr. OLIVER.
more satisfactory to all concerned that that should be embodied in the Act itself? The aright hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Borden) has said that there is no occasion for it. Yet, at the risk of being regarded as provincial by the hon. member for South Simeon (Mr. Lennox), and at the risk of talking parish politics, I venture to say that there are people who are not quite as confident of justice being done in the distribution of this money by Die present government, or perhaps by succeeding governments, as the hon. member for South Simcoe appears to be. I can understand that the maritime provinces, without any possibility of their territory being enlarged and without any possibility of their population growing proportionately with that of the other provinces, will necessarily become relatively an insignificant part of Canada; that is that their influence will be relatively insignificant. Whilst we have the Premier and the Minister of Marine and Fisheries as the commanding influences in the Cabinet, we have every confidence that justice will be done each year, but they are not to be there always and we know not the day nor the hour when perhaps one, or both, of them will disappear from his present position. We feel that it would be only right and fair that the principle should be set forth in the Bill itself, that each and every province, the smaller as well as the larger, those that are not influential as well as those who have influence, should have an assurance of its fair share of this money. The people of the various provinces are entitled to their relative share of this distribution. There is a surplus of nearly $40,000,000, the treasury is full to overflowing, the different provinces have contributed to this money, and it is only right that each and every one of them should receive its share. We had the budget brought down a short time ago. There was no relief to the farmers of the country in the way of giving them a reduction of taxation. It is a very laudable thing that the government should spend a portion of this large sum in the improvement of roads and encouragement of agriculture. What are they going to do with the surplus taxation taken from the pockets of the people? They do not propose to reduce the customs tariff; the interests will not let them. So no thanks to them if they increase the subsidies to the provinces for the promotion of agriculture and the improvement of roads. If the government lessened the burdens of the people by a reduction in the customs tariff it would be very acceptable to the farmers of the country, but, inasmuch as they will not do that, it is only right that the farmers should be guaranteed their proportionate share of this money by having a section in the Act giving to each

province its share in proportion to its population and not leaving it dependant on the sweet will of the government. I think the amendment is a reasonable one.
Amendment (Mr. Pugsley) negatived on division.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall section 2 be agreed to?

Perhaps this might be a suitable time to get some information from the hon.'Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Burrell). 1 wish to ask him whether it is the intention to increase the acreage at the experimental station at Charlottetown, P. E. I. Perhaps I might ask the question by reading a letter.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: I think it will he as well to bring that upon the estimates. My hon. friend will have an opportunity when the estimates are brought up and perhaps he will defer the matter until then.

Could not the hon. gentleman give the practical object of the legislation and tell us how he intends to encourage agriculture? These are broad terms. Could he specify a little more than he did before?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
It has been made very plain so far. If the government had had in mind some of the considerations that seem to have influenced hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House it could have brought in a large appropriation in general terms and spent it anywhere throughout the country that it saw fit. But it did not think that the wisest or best course, so it proposes to use this Bill as a means of arriving at an arrangement with the provincial governments by which there can be co-operation between the provincial and federal governments. The government proposes to distribute the money, which it will ask parliament to vote for this purpose, in accordance with the population of the various provinces. Hon. gentlemen on the other side ask us upon what principle? The principle is a very plain one; each of the provinces of 'Canada has or is supposed to have an agricultural department under which money is expended in the interest of the people of the province for aid to agriculture and for agricultural education. We are endeavouring, by means of this statute, to provide that the money voted by this parliament and to be distributed under this .Bill shall he expended by the provincial government under such regulations and under such conditions as will ensure to the government and parliament of Canada that it is expended for the purpose for which it is intended. We propose to try that principle here and if that does not
succeed we may try some other principle another year. We may try the principle which hon. gentlemen on the other side seem to be fighting for-although I must confess that I cannot understand why they are fighting for it-of giving up the principle of co-operation, and of bringing down instead a grant in aid of agriculture expending it ourselves in the various provinces. We have not thought that was the best course, but there is so much objection to our proposal and so much argument in favour of this other course that perhaps we might take that into consideration. I would suppose that the principle which we have adopted and by which we would call the provincial governments into co-operation, would have commended itself to every man in this House without distinction of party. Instead of that, the proposal of the government made in an eminently fair spirit and to be embodied, so far as the division is concerned, in a plain statute, seems to be viewed with suspicion and distrust. I must confess I cannot understand why. The principle is the encouragement of agriculture by the utilization of provincial machinery and by cooperation with the nrovincial governments. It-seems to me that this is a very easily understood principle; it is a principle I believe from which good results may he expected, but I am bound to say that the other suggestion which 'seems to be urged so strongly by hon. gentlemen on the other *side of the House is worthy of being taken into consideration.

I think my right hon. friend is extremely unfair to members on this side of the House. I did not hear a single member on this side speak against this government co-operating with the provincial governments in encouraging agriculture. My hon. friend must have got angry at some of his own followers because they were not disposed to accept the suggestion of the Minister of Agriculture, that these moneys should be divided on the basis of population. My right hon. friend surely did not hear us on this side correctly. All of us who spoke weTe in favour of co-operation with the provincial governments, but what we said was: that if it is proposed, as the Minister of Agriculture admits it is the correct thing to do-to apportion these moneys among the different provinces on the basis of population, that parliament in this statute should now lay down the principle on which this money is to be divided. That is all we were arguing for. And surely we have the more reason to argue for that when we find the Minister of Marine rising in his place and saying that he was opposed, to binding the government to distribute these moneys according to population, because, he said, there might be cases in which in one province or another it would

be necessary to appropriate a larger amount than would be justified on the basis of population. In view of that statement it is hard to believe that this policy was settled upon, as my right hon. friend says it was, by the government before the Bill was brought down. If the policy was settled upon, how is it possible that an influential member of the government could say it is true that so far as we reasonably can we will apportion these moneys on the basis of population, but we want elasticity so that from time to time we may depart from that principle in cases where in the judgment of the Governor in Council it would be necessary to do so. There is no ground whatever for the statement of the Prime Minister that we have opposed liberal encouragement to agriculture or that we have opposed the federal government granting aid to the different provinces and acting in co-operation with the governments of these provinces.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I move that item 248, for a grant of $100,000 to the National Battlefields Commission, be struck out, as I intend to have the vote brought down in the supplementary estimates, with appropriate wording to meet the requirements of the statute.

There are the old forts of Beau 'Sejour and Gaspereaux in New Brunswick, and Fort Lawrence in the county of Cumberland in Nova Scotia, and a number of others, and I hope he will take into consideration the preservation of -all these old battlefields and forts, which certainly have been too long neglected.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: At present I -am dealing only with this Battlefields Commission with respect to Quebec. The other matters to which my hon. friend has referred w-illl have our consideration, but it is not possible for us to deal with them this year. I do not say that it will be possible for us to deal with them at any particular time in the future, but the matter to which my hon. friend has called attention, is, I am sure, one in which we are all interested.
I do not suppose it is the intention of the government to change the present personnel of the commission?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have no information to give my hon. friend as to that.

The Finance Minister says that nothing can be -done this year, and he cannot give any assurance when anything can be done, as to these odd forts and historic battlefields. I want to impress upon him this fact, that unless -something is done soon, the day will have gone when anything can be done. Fort Cumberland or Fort- Beau Sejour are fast crumb-lig, and unless something is done speedily, they will simply be a memory. At Fort Lawrence and at Fort Gaspereaux on Baie Vert-e similar -conditions -prevail. If -anything is to be done to wrest these places from the process of decay, it must be done speedily. I think the attention of this government has been called to this matter. I know that the attention of the former government was called to it, and it w-as put off, as- is too -often the case with all governments. If the government would make some announcement with respect to taking early action in this matter, I think the -country would hear it with pleasure and gratification.

I may say that the late government had this matter under consideration, and a proposition was made to enlarge the scope of the National Battlefields Commission. There did not seem to be any reason why that should not be done. The -gentlemen who are serving the country very acceptably on -this commission do not get any compensation for their services, and it seems to me that it will be pre-eminently the work of the -commission to take charge of the matters outlined by the hon. member for Westmorland. Several months ago I brought this matter before the House, and the hon. Minister of Militia referred to it as a matter of great importance on which the government would take early action. He -expressed unbounded enthusiasm at the idea, and I would have thought that the Minister of Finance would have been prepared to have enlarged the scope of this commission. A few words put in the Bill would be all that would be necessary.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think that the commission should be consulted with regard to such a matter. Individually, I am in entire sympathy with -the preservation of our battlefields and all -historic points in Canada. I have had in mind the possibility of enlarging the -scope of the commission, but as the expenditure for this year is comparatively large, it -is probably as much -as the government may feel called upon to make this ye-ar. The question of enlarging the -scope of the commission is a matter which will have to be left for future consideration, as there is not a great deal of time left this session.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
I may say that the proposition meets with my very

hearty endorsation, but inasmuch as we 'have a Battlefields Commission, I presume it would be more appropriate that such an item should be placed at the disposal of that commission. Whatever items may be set apart for dealing with our Canadian battlefields belong, I should imagine, to that commission.
Let us get the item first.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: The item, of course, will have to be considered. The matter has not yet been discussed in council, but as soon as it is in shape my hon. friend will have full information in connection with it. Whatever has been said in regard to the matter has been most sympathetically received by my colleagues, to whom I have spoken.
Sympathy is cheap, it is money we want.
Sympathy is a good thing to start with.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: There are certain persons who like to indulge in promises without performing them, I need not say that it is not our intention to proceed along those lines.

I may say to my hon. friend the reason we were greatly discouraged when he was absent from the chamber was that the Minister of Finance, with that care for the treasury which of course, it is proper he should have, rather led us to believe that nothing would be done this year.

While this matter is before the House I would1 like to draw attention to two very celebrated forts at Niagara, Fort George, and Fort Missauga. These forts are opposite the United States frontier where the American forts are kept in good condition. It will be a disgrace to Canada if the forts on the Canadian side are not kept in an equally good state of repair, more especially as it will not require a very large expenditure for that purpose.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: I will take the liberty of bringing the matter to the attention of the Battlefields Commission.

Let me call the attention of the Minister of Militia to the old fortification at Chambly, not very far from my own county of Rouville. This is one of the finest pieces of old military architecture to be found in the country. The fortifications have been well preserved1 up to a few years ago when the government' of Canada spent a few thousand dollars to repair the fortifications, and to restore; the names of the great soldiers and captains
who fought there under the French Regime, but lately I have noticed that the old fort was crumbling and giving signs of decay. I do not think that all the fortifications, all the old landmarks, should be placed1 under the control of the Quebec Battlefields Commission, because that body has one object in view. I believe the time has come when we should take into serious consideration the conditions of all the old military landmarks of the country. I would- mention also the old fortifications at L'lsle-aux-Noix which were beautifully built by the English officers about a century ago, and are very historic. These-fortifications are also crumbling, and I specially draw the attention of the Minister of Militia to the fact. We should not rest satisfied with mere words on this>
matter, because, as the English proverb1 has it, * fine word's butter no parsnips.' . Let the minister act heroically in this matter and see that a sum is placed in the estimates, and that a systematic policy dealing with the preservation of the historic military landmarks of the country, is adopted, for the perpetuation of the memories of the heroes of the past, and for the education of the young men of this country. Some years ago a monument was erected at Chateaugay to commemorate the valorous deeds of Canadians there, and a similar monument was put up at Niagara, but we should not forget that in other sections of the country there are landmarks which also call for consideration and attention.

The [DOT]hon. gentleman would not expect the present government, which has only been in office for a few months, to attempt to perform what he and his colleagues failed to do in 15 years of Liberal administration. He will surely give us breathing space at the beginning of our term of office and allow us time to demonstrate our intentions, if not our promises, in this matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
All that has been said confirms me in the view that this [DOT]matter should be dealt with in a comprehensive manner, either by the Quebec Battlefields Commission or some other commission. The whole question should be taken up and so dealt with, instead of dealing with it piecemeal and in hugger-mugger fashion. I am quite sure the proposal will have the sympathy of every man on this side of the House if treated [DOT]comprehensively. Because this is not a party question, it is a question in which we would all heartily support the government in dealing with it in a proper and comprehensive manner. So far as I am concerned, speaking for myself, I am heartily in sympathy with what has been said. It is only as to the method employed that

there may perhaps he any divergence of opinion. I aim entirely in accord with the idea that legislation should be passed authorizing some commission to take up the whole question, so that it may be dealt with in a thorough and comprehensive way.

The discussion that has taken place this afternoon may be regarded as a basis for further inquiry upon this subject, and I do not wish the Minister of Militia and his colleagues to lose sight of the old fortifications at Louisburg. I was waiting for some other hon. gentleman to mention this grand old fortress, but as nothing has been said, I deem it proper now to bring the fortifications of Louisburg to the notice of the government. The old casements and other parts of those fortifications are just as much intact to-day as they were during the French regime at Botuis-burg, and we should take care that they are preserved as well as can be. An interesting point that I might mention is, that a former captain in the English army Capt. Kennedy, who spent some years of his life at Louisburg and died there, made provision in his will towards the upkeep of the fortification at Louisburg in co-operation with government assistance, so that the conditions as they existed at the time of the siege might be, as far as possible, maintained. I simply mention this matter so that when the government are dealing with this question, Louisburg shall not be forgotten.
Naval Service, including purchase and maintenance of ships, the maintenance and up-keep of dockyards at Esquimalt and and Halifax, and the establishment and maintenance of training school, $1,660,000.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Will the minister please explain this item?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
College	$	5,500
Purchase of new machinery for the dockyards at Halifax and Esquimalt	 19,200
New buildings and other	works..	41,276
