If hon. gentlemen want any further information regarding these different items I have that information under my hand, and will be very glad to give it to them. I may say pending the declaration of what the policy of this government will be touching the naval service-which as my hon. friends know the Prime Minister announced in the debate on the address would not be determined until after full opportunity was had of considering the whole question and of first consulting with the Admiralty authorities in the matter- it has been thought better that the estimates this year should be based on the idea of maintaining the existing ships and the existing establishments, including the Naval College at Halifax, on a proper basis, without adding new ships or adding to the equipment we have at the present time more than is necessary for the purpose of maintaining it in proper condition. It is on that basis entirely that the estimates are made up this year.

I notice that my hon. friends who represent the interests of the province of Quebec in the government have all vanished. They disappeared at the announcement that we might discuss the /Naval service this afternoon. I am sorry for that; I should like to have seen them here. But let me be very frank with my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Hazen) and tell him, notwithstanding the absence of his colleagues .from Quebec, that each and every one of the Quebec ministers, in their respective (constituencies, and at large public meetings in my province during the last election contest, and before that contest, solemnly promised the .people that if a government should be formed under the leadership of the right hon. member from Halifax, (Mr, Borden) then, as soon as parliament should be convened, every sign, every vestige of a Naval service would disappear from the blue-book, that the naval policy of the Laurier government would be wiped o!ut and that we should never hear any thing about it again. Bet me tell my hon. friend also, as I have already stated in his presence elsewhere, that he has no idea of the fight, of the struggle, which took place in our province during the last general election on this naval question. We were told by the Minister of Public works (Mr. ;Monk) by the Postmaster General (Mr. Pelletier) and by the Minister of Inland Revenue (Mr. Nantel) that our policy, was

suicidal, that we were selling our birthright to 'Great Britain, and that the time had come for Canada to assert herself and to do away with all this imperialism and this whole naval expenditure. We on our part, resisted those appeals, appeals of the worst kind, that were made in our province against the naval policy; we stood to our guns like men; and we educated public opinion in the province of Quebec to such an extent that on the 21st of September last we returned a majority of members of that province, pledged to a naval policy. Of course, the members returned in favour of the late government were pledged, I am glad to say to the Liberal policy. I say our campaign was a campaign of education and it was carried on against the declaration on the other side that if we were defeated every vestige of the navy would disappear from the blue-books and that there would be no expenditure whatever on such a service.
Now, I am surprised to see such a large amount of money in the estimates for the maintainance of that naval policy. People are being told every day, in our province, not only in the newspapers but at public meetings, that the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Borden) intends to wipe out the navy from his programme. On the * other hand we read in another section of the press, and learn of speeches on other platforms, that after consultation with the admiralty, a new policy will be evolved which will mean something while the old policy meant nothing.
Now, I want an authoritative statement from the hon. gentleman (Mr. Hazen) who is at the head of the Naval Department. We on this side of the House are not opposed to a Canadian navy; far from it. And in my own province I would be ready to take up the cudgels again to-morrow and fight the same battle that we fought before the 21st of September last. Public education has been eSected in that regard in spite of the Quebec ministers of the government and their followers in the House. I want the hon. gentleman to speak plainly on this question and to say to the country whether we are to have a navy-yes, or no. Whether we are to have a contribution-yes, or no. Then we can debate whether that contribution should be given or not. The naval policy should be above politics. Canada is pledged to do something. Brat there are certain members who represent especially the interests of the province of Quebec, who are pledged against it; and so are their followers in this House. Now, let us be frank about it. Why shillyshally? why speak one way for one province, and another way lor another province? Our words will reach the heart of the empire, and Great Britain will know whether Canada will do something for fcl
maintenance of Britain's supremacy on the seas or not. My hon. friend '(Mr. Hazen) will consult the admiralty. I know Ms fine Imperial spirit. I may disagree with him on the lines of the policy he may pursue. But is it not time to know distinctly whether Canada will do something or not.
I believe that the country has declared in favour of certain aid to be given to Great Britain to maintain her naval supremacy.
I say it would be unbecoming on the part of the Canadian people through their representatives to say that a certain policy was pursued by the late government, but we are going to wipe it out from the statute-book and do notMng. That is what is being said in the province of Quebec today; that is what is being repeated from platform after platform and in every newspaper of a certain stripe in that province. During the last election and since the last election^ they have equivocated as to what they will do and they are equivocating amongst the partisans of the Postmaster General (Mr. Pelletier) in Quebec to-day whether they will do something or nothing. The time has come to speak firmly and plainly. If it is the province of Quebec the hon. gentleman (Mr. Hazen) is afraid of, let him not be afraid. In Quebec he will find a majority of His Majesty's loyal subjects ready'to stand for a Canadian navy that will do its share for the maintenance of the supremacy of Britain on the seas. Those opposed to that principle are but a minority, and a very insignificant minority at that.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: Returning to the House after an absence oi a few minutes, I am told that my hon. friend from Rouville (Mr. Lemieux) has used the same means as were used on a former occasion to say that I was out of the House when this question was discussed. I am never out of the House when my duty calls me here. And I am not afraid to discuss this question with the hon. gentleman now or at any other time.
What are you going to do?

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: I will tell the hon. gentleman if he will wait a minute. In this House I give my mind and .say what I think. But I wish to make clear the point I mentioned first, so that certain newspapers in Montreal to-morrow may have no reason to say that I ran out of the House because I was afraid of what might fall upon me coming from the important member from Rouville. I am going to tell my hon. friend from Rouville (Mr. Lemieux) that he is not stating the facts as they are when he speaks as he has just spoken. I shall ask him to tell me at what public meeting since the elections the stand indicated by him a moment ago was taken.

When my hon. friend was returned by acclamation he made a speech at Lorette in the province of Quebec at which he announced that at last the people would be free from that naval policy that the Borden government has decided not to have any naval question to bother them and that something better than the repeal of the Bill would take place.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: I said then and I say now that I am opposed to the scheme of the late government, that it is a bad thing. I said then as I say now that when the leader of the present government on the debate on the address took up this question he made declarations which were perfectly satisfactory to us and which were satisfactory in the province of Quebec. Those are the facts which wre stated in Quebec.
Not much facts in that.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext:
I am not going to be responsible for people in some quarters-
Mr. iLBMIEUX. In your own paper?

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: The hon. member for Rouville will not find it in my own paper. I have no paper.
Does my hon. friend state he has no paper ?

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: I do.

I must tell my hon. friend that I took the precaution of getting from the court-house in Quebec a declaration of the ownership of ' L'Evenement,'
* of Quebec, and I find the name of my hon. friend the Postmaster General quite prominent amongst the directors and joint owners of ' L'Evenement.'.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: My hon. friend is dealing with ancient history. I was at one time one of the directors of the paper, but I inform my hon. friend that I am not now.
Since when?

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: I do not remember the dates but I can get them for my hon. friend. I thought it was more becoming for a member of this government not to have any interest in any of the newspapers of this country which might be called upon to publish advertisements for this government and I gave away, transferred all my interests in that paper and I think it was the right thing to do. But my hon. friend will not find in that paper anything dike what he has said this afternoon and I defy him to find anything of the kind.
Get me the paper.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: I am not going to look for something that is not there. If he wants it he will have to hunt it up himself.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: We from the province of Quebec have been misrepresented on this question, not only to-day but from the very day the debate in this House began. We have been told that we went around the province of Quebec and declared that we were against any policy at all.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: That is not the stand we have taken. The right hon. the leader o>f the opposition said one day in this House that we had taken the stand that the children of Canadians were going to be disembowelled.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: And that was tantamount to cowardice. I may tell my right hon. 'friend now, that I am against any policy, naval or other, which will put the Canadians of this country who are going to fight for this country in a position to be disembowelled without fighting. I have taken -the stand that the policy of the late government was to send Canadians on such ships, that if they should meet the enemy they would not be within range to fight and that these ships would be sunk before having a chance to fight.

Is my hon. friend aware that at the present moment there are four battleships of the same type <as was proposed by the late government, being built in Great Britain, and that they will be launched during the present season, and added to the navy of Great Britain?

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: Those are the things which we said to the province of Quebec. I do not regret it, I am of that opinion now, but we in the province of Quebec, have been told by the hon. member during the debate on the address that there was an anti-British party in the province of Quebec.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext:
I want to tell him that there is no such thing in the province of Quebec, that the people of our province are British subjects and loyal British subjects-although I am afraid that if this cry goes forth that there is an anti-British party in Quebec, there may be one in some quarters-but the cry to-day is absolutely erroneous, not to say a lie.
We have taken a certain stand on this question. We were absolutely opposed to the naval policy propounded by the late government. What did we find when we came into power with reference to the ten or eleven ships which were to be built on the lines of the ipolicy of my hon. friends opposite? We found that the very men who were in charge of that service, had made reports in which

they stated that [DOT]when the last of these ships would leave the navy yard, they would be obsolete and of no use. Are you surprised that we were opposed to such a policy as that? We were not naval experts but we thought we were telling Quebec what was right in taking that stand, and arriving here, we found that Admiral Kings-mill and Commander Roper were of the same opinion as ourselves. I think that was pretty good justification. Now we are face to face with this question. The government have not had time to go into it, but we have never declared that there would be no policy at all; we adhere, one and all, to the declarations made here by the Prime Minister and those declarations are to the effect that something will be done, that a new policy will be put before this country. With those declarations my right hon. friend has no right to say what he has said. When this policy has been carefully studied, it will be put before parliament, and the country. Those are the declarations made, and it may be that my hon. friends opposite, who had such hopes of seeing this government go to pieces on certain rocks, and who have been disappointed so far, still hope that something might come up to wreck this government. The hon. member for Rouville (Mr. Le-mieux) says that now is the time to speak, that he must know now where this government stands. We are just going to take our time. The government declared that this question should be looked into, and carefully studied, and if the hon. member for Rouville is so impatient about a policy I can only say that the policy which will be put before this country by this government, will be a much better one than the one which he himself, as a member of the late government, put before the country and which was disapnroved.
In the last general election, if it had not been for the appeals which were made to the people of my province that the Prime Minister for (the time being was a French lOanadian and a Catholic, there would not have been a majority in that province of Quebec to approve of the policy which gave us a ' Rainbow ' and a ' Niobe.1

My hon. friend the Postmaster General (Mr. Pelletier) says that the party which he represents in Quebec is not afraid to fight, but that when they fight they want to be in a position to fight and not to fight upon vessels that are so' small and so imperfectly equipped that they will not be within the firing line;. Hoes my hon. friend mean to say-and I hope he will give me an answer to this question-that he and his party will take a vote to provide for efficient vessels that will be in the fight, and that his French friends in Quebec will not De massacred, but will stand up and fight like men ?

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext:
I can tell my hon. friend that when French-Canadians were called upon in the past they did their duty
nobly to their country. That is what they did when they fought at Chateauguay. '
But my hon. friend is not answering the question. Answer the question.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: 1 will answer the question in my own way.
Ah !

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: The hon. gentleman would like me to tell the committee what is going to be the policy of this government when the government has not had time to consider its policy.
I cannot make you answer.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: The hon. gentleman will not make me answer questions which have not been considered by this government. This question has not been considered by the government. My hon. friend may try as much as he likes to make party capital out of it, but this government has taken the stand that there is no policy which it has looked into, but that this matter will be taken up later, at which time a plan governed by the necessities of the question will be considered.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: My hon. friend the Postmaster General has taken refuge on the ground that he was opposed to the Laurier policy. That is the way he put it to-day before the House. He knows as well as I do-and if he denies it I will not bandy words with him-that the position which his party took in the last election, and ever since the Naval Bill was introduced in 1910, was that Canada owed absolutely nothing to England and that there was no need for any policy at all.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: When I heard words to that effect uttered in the province of Quebec I said that for all the years I had lived I had thought it was wrong to say that we owed nothing to England. My hon. friend will never find anything of tbat kind on my lips.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I said a moment ago that I would not bandy words with my hon. friend. I never heard him speak, but I read some speeches upon this point, and I maintain that the policy which was followed by his friends in Quebec during the last campaign and previously, ever since the month of June, 1910, when the Naval Bill was introduced, was that Canada owed nothing to England, that they were against any naval policy and that, if they were not to be disembowelled upon the seas of China and Japan, it was not because they were not to be put upon

imperial ships, but because they were not to be put upon any ships at all. We heard in this very House the declaration that this policy would mean conscription, and the hon. gentleman knows as well as I do that his friends stated during the campaign that the children of the people would be taken by force and put upon the decks of these ships to fight for England. My hon. friend can take any position he likes upon the present occasion as to what he did or did not say-I would not contradict him even if I knew to the contrary, but I leave it to those who heard him and who heard his friends. I hope that his words of to-day will be reported in the province of Quebec just as he has spoken them, for nothing will be better for the peace of the country than that for once we have it from the mouth of himself and his associates that Canada owes something to England. The hon. gentleman says that he was opposed to the Laurier policy. Everybody heard him say that. He and his friends declared themselves as being opposed to that policy and they said that the first thing which would be done would be to repeal it. One of the first things which was done by one of the followers of the present government was to put a question to the leader of the government whether or not the naval law would be repealed during the present session. That was the course advocated by the party in office, or the wing of the party coming from the province of Quebec; they threatened that as soon as the late government had been defeated that policy would be repealed. Well, it is not yet repealed. It is, in part in force. The Minister of Marine and Fisheries, or the Minister of Naval Service (Mr. Hazen) asks for an appropriation of $1,660,000, for what?-to carry on the naval policy of the Laurier government. That is very far from what was expected by the people of Quebec who voted in favour of the members of the government from that province. They never expected that they would be called upon to vote one dollar for the maintenance and support of the naval policy introduced by the Laurier government. They did not suppose that they would be called upon to vote any such money as that, and if anybody in this House had stated to the electors of the county of Quebec or of Champlain county that they would be called upon to vote over a million dollars to carry out the naval law which was then on the statute-book I am satisfied there would have been a different vote in the province of Quebec. But, it was because these promises were made that hon. gentlemen opposite had the measure of success which they achieved in that province. Now, it is indicated in these esti-Sir WILFRID LAURIER.
mates that parliament will appropriate $1,660,000. What for? The naval law asks for the creation of a Naval Department. The Naval Department is maintained. The naval law asks for the creation of a naval college. The naval college is maintained. The only thing that is dropped off is the building of warships for which we had invited tenders. In the course of time I do not know what will be done by the government after they have conferred with Great Britain. But, I know what will be the answer of Great Britain. Whatever answer they will have-in the future, at the present time they are providing the money for carrying out the naval law. What is it that they provide for? They provide for a naval college with a naval staff; they provide for all the frills and feathers of the naval service, but they do not provide for building ships. We shall have no tin-pot navy! But we shall have a. gold lace navy; we shall have an admiral, commodore and' captains, but we shall have no sailors. That is what is provided for by these estimates. I find no fault with the estimates and we are ready to vote the-money. What will the answer of the British government be' when my hon. friend goes over to the other side in order to get that answer? We have it already and we have had it since 1909? At the conference that took place in 1909, which was called' bv the British government and at which all the dominions were represented, Canada, Australia, New Zealand and South Africa, the first thing the British government asked for was a contribution. We were not in favour of a contribution. Whether or not the present government are in favour of a contribution remains to-be seen; we will have to wait for that.
The next thing that was asked for was a fleet unit on the Pacific, and for reasons intimated more than once during last parliament, we did not think it advisable to have a unit on the Pacific only; we thought we must have a service both on the Pacific and the Atlantic-a moderate service to begin because we had to commence in a moderate way-but at all events it was accepted. I shall not anticipate what may be the policy of the present government on the navy but after their return from England we will have an opportunity of judging of it. I have simply to repeat that the naval law is maintained by this government, and that whatever my hon. friend say to the contrary I am glad for my part that he is forced to go back on the language he used last election and to retain the naval policy of the late government.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext:
The right hon. gentleman (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) says he had no occasion to hear what I had to say in the

last election, but if that is so it is his own fault. When the leader of the opposition was going around the province of Quebec he singled out the county I represent to speak in at the last minute, when he knew he could not be answered, and so he called a big meeting in my county on the afternoon of the day before the voting. I then sent a Telegram to the right hon. gentleman (Sir Wilfrid Lauxier) asking him to allow me to appear with my friends at that meeting and I would give him a chance of hearing what I had to say. That request the Tight hon. gentleman refused. Therefore, if the right hon. gentleman had no opportunity to hear me on that occasion, he had nobody to blame but himself for it. I suppose the right hon. the leader of the opposition remembers that incident; at all events I do. I shall not qualify his action in refusing me a hearing but I may say that it is the first time I ever heard of the leader of a great party going, on the eve of an election, into a county, when he could not be answered, and refusing the candidate on the other side an opportunity to speak. If the right hon. gentleman is much surprised to-day in finding a vote for the navy in the estimates, I may tell him that I am not, and I may tell him further that that vote is absolutely logical and consistent with the policy of the Conservative party. Whan we came into power we found certain conditions existing; we found that a naval college had been built at Halifax and that two ships had been purchased. Does the right hon. gentleman mean to say that we should have set fire to that college and sunk those two ships? It is true that one of 'them had met with a bad accident on a certain trip down in Yarmouth, but, nevertheless, we found her there with the other ship, both belonging to Canada. As we had no opportunity to put a naval policy before the country, was it not reasonable and sensible to do as we have done and to say that we would not build these other ten ships which were proposed by the late government, sending back the cheques which had been put in with the tenders and declaring to the country that the ships would not be built? We had under the circumstances to continue what the late government had put into operation. It would have been ridiculokis, even for those so called bad Nationalists in Quebec, without one moment of consideration, to -close the naval college and give the ships to some other country. That would not	be	reasonable. Now, Sir, my hon, and respected friend the leader of the opposition said that the old government had a well defined policy on that subject. The policy may have been well defined, but I submit to this House that it was not well considered, because the policy which they embarked upon and laid before thi9 House was one which, if it had been carried to a conclusion, would have resulted in the expenditure of an enormous amount of money with little or no advantage to Canada or to the empire. Let me say that, there is evidence that the hon. gentlemen themselves must have come to a conclusion of that kind. We find that in the month of February last, tenders were asked for the construction of four cruisers of the 'Bristol' type and six torpedo destroyers. Those tenders were received on the 1st day of May, 1911, five months before the government went out of office; yet during the whole of that time, apparently, the government did nothing with regard to those tenders. Now, Sir, why was it, if the government were convinced of the wisdom of their naval policy, that they did not, on receipt of those tenders, award the contract for the construction of those cruisers and destroyers? Why did they wait for five months, until they went out of power, without having taken a single step in that direction? There were nine tenders. There was the tender of Cammel, Laird & Company, which was the lowest, for $11,280,000. There was the tender of Swan, Hunter & William Richardson for $12,174,000. There were other tenders, ranging from the lowest already mentioned up to $13,055,804. Those tenders did not include the armour plating, the armament, and certain supplies that go with warships of this sort, and which would have considerably augmented the cost.
Now why did the late government, after embarking on that policy, after receiving those tenders on the 1st day of May, allow them to remain in abeyance without taking a single step towards making a contract for the building of those ships? Was it because the hon. gentlemen discovered afterwards that if they had done so they would have simply been throwing away about $15,900,000 of the people's money? Because the fact is, and I have evidence that cannot be contradicted, and which I am prepared to give th:s House at any time if my statement is challenged, I have evidence that those vessels, under that contract, and under the conditions, would not have been completed for six years from .the time the contract was awarded, and by the end of six years those vessels would have been obsolete, entirely unfit for the purposes for which they were designed. I cannot help concluding, therefore, that the late government, after issuing a call for those tenders, discovered the actual facts which I have just stated. Therefore,

thev did not award the contract for the construction of those ships, hut they allowed the matter to stand. When the present government came into power and when I, as Minister of the Naval Service, began to look into the question and found the facts I have just narrated to this House, I would have been entirely failing in my duty as a Minister of the Crown, if I had advised my colleagues in the Council and the Governor General to sign a contract for the construction of those ships which, by the time they were completed, would have been obsolete and valueless for the purpose for which they were intended.
Now, the Minister of Marine in these remarks throws out an intimation that probably the reason the late government did not award the contract for these vessels was because they discovered there had been a mistake and that the expenditure of the money for the purpose would not have been wise. (Left me say to my hon. friend (Mr. Hazen) that he is absolutely and entirely mistaken in that assumption. There were two reasons why the late government did not award the contract. One was, that there was some considerable difficulty in determining as to the firm to whom the contract should be awarded. The lowest tenderers were The Cammell-Laird Company. They are a very reputable ship building firm. They have a very laTge ship building plant at Birkenhead, near Liverpool, and there is no question whatever but that if the contract had been given to them they would have completed it to the entire satisfaction of the government. But one difficulty -and it is the only difficulty I am aware of with regard to the Cammell-Laird Company-was that they coupled with it, a condition of their making an arrangement with one of the tenderers, Norton Griffiths & Company, for the construction of harbour works, including a drydock, in Courtenay bay, St. John. The late Minister of Marine had considerable doubt as to whether that could be regarded as. an unconditional tender, and that was a matter which required the careful consideration he was giving it. But what was of perhaps even more importance than that was (that all the tenderers either had shipyards in Great Britain, or were associated with builders having shipyards in Great Britain, it was considered desirable to take a memorandum of the tenders to England and to confer with the British Admiralty with regard to them, as well as with regard to the different firms who had tendered. Just as soon as it was convenient to do so, the Hon. Mr. Brodeur went to England and conferred with the admiralty. My hon. friend knows what happened after his return to this country. He knows that very shortly after his return it was decided to dissolve parliament and in consequence of that the government did not deal with the matter. After the elections, in consequence of the very great importance of the contract, and of the magnitude of the sum which was involved, it was thought only right to leave the question of awarding the contract to our successors. That is the whole story. Whether rightly or wrongly the late government decided that it would be in the interests of the people of Canada that the ships which were to form the nucleus of the Ganadian navy should be constructed in Canada. The late government felt it would be desirable to encourage the building of ships in Canada that it would give employment to Canadian labour, and as it was necessary to make a beginning at some time, that it would be better to make a beginning in the way in which we proposed it should be made and to enter upon the construction of these war vessels in our own country. So much for that. Now, in consequence of that statement which was made by the Minister of Marine, there was put to him a question later on in the session by myself, which will be found at page 1239 of ' Hansard ', as follows:

Having reference to the statement of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, quoted in Hansard of the present session, page 179, a 9 follows:-
The fact is, and I have evidence that cannot be contradicted and which I am prepared to give this House at any time if my statement is challenged, I have evidence that those vessels, under that contract, (referring to the tenders for the construction of cruisers and torpedo destroyers), and under the conditions, would not have been completed for six years from the time the contract was awarded, and by the end of the six years those vessels would have been obsolete, entirely unfit for the pur poses for which they were designed.
What is the evidence to which the Minister of Marine and Fisheries referred, and will he give the House such evidence in detail?
To that the Minister, Mr. Hazen, answered :-
In the conditions embodied by the late government in their call for tenders for the construction of vessels for the naval service it was stipulated that the time allotted for the construction of the vessels would he six years.
In a memorandum from Admiral Kingsmill, dated October 9, 1911, it is stated that ' owing to the rapidity with which designs change it is anticipated that if it takes six years to complete the programme the ships will be out of date before they are completed/
Then my hon. friend was requested, I think on a motion made by my hon. friend from Rouville, to lay the memorandum on the table of the House, and that was done. I have before me the memorandum of Ad-

miral Kingsmill, which does not at all bear out the statement of my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries. To th)3 Admiral Kingsmill attaches the following memorandum:
With the advent of a minister who is not conversant with naval matters, nor with the requirements of the naval service, it appears desirable to supply information on these points; I therefore forward herewith a few remarks which will tend to enlighten him with regard to immediate requirements with a view to discussion at an early date on the points raised.
This is dated the 9th of October, 1911. Then follows his memorandum, the first clauses of which relate to ship construction. This is what Admiral Kingsmill says:
The programme of new construction adopted by _ the late government consists of: four cruisers of the improved Bristol type; six improved river-class destroyers. Whilst this progamme does not appear an ambitious one, yet it meets present requirements from the fact that ships of this kind do not require very large complements, and we are in a position to train sufficient men to form part of their crews, and will not require the loan of such large numbers of officers and men from the imperial government as would he necessary if large armoured cruisers were included in the programme. The admiralty find, difficulty in keeping their ships fully maimed, and are thus not iu a position to spare large numbers for the Dominions navies.
This statement is an absolute and complete justification of the action of the late government in calling for tenders for this description of war vessel. Admiral Kingsmill entirely approves of the programme of building four cruisers of the improved ' Bristol ' type, and six improved ' river-class ' destroyers. As having a bearing upon this, I would like to read from a report in the 'Montreal Star' of this evening of a speech made by the Rt. Hon. Winston Churchill, First Lord of the Admiralty, in the House of Commons in England, in introducing the naval estimates:
Referring to the building programme, which includes four large armoured ships, eight light armoured cruisers, twenty destroyers and a number of submarines, Mr. Churchill said that $3,500,000 was to be expended on the construction of submarines this year, and as regards the light armoured cruisers the admiralty had decided to return to a smaller type of vessels as being more useful than the recently built vessels of the Chatham class of 5,400 tons. These eight armoured cruisers will be the smallest, cheapest and fastest vessels protected with vertical armour ever projected for the British Navy. They will be strong enough and fast enough to overhaul and cut down any destroyer.
We have here the very strongest approval by Admiral Kingsmill of the programme Mr. PUGSLEY.
undertaken by the late government. The remainder of his memorandum relates to the place where it would be best to have these vessels constructed-whether it would be better to build them all in Canada or to have some of them built in Canada and some in the shipyards of the mother country. This is what he says on that point:
Tenders were called for and have been received by the government for the construction of these vessels in Canada; whilst it may be desirable to encourage a firm or firms to establish shipyards in Canada, the interests and efficiency of the naval service would be better served if some portion of the ships, one or two of the cruisers, and two destroyers were constructed in England, orders being placed without delay. We should thus he able to obtain delivery of one destroyer within a year and one cruiser and a second destroyer within eighteen months; by that time a' sufficient number of men will have been trained to form a nucleus of the crews, and training will be more efficiently and expeditiously carried out with the advent of modern ships. In the meantime a shipyard can be established in Canada and the remainder of the ships constructed in this yard; the whole of the programme would thus be completed in four years instead of in six as at present arranged. Owing to the rapidity with which designs change it is anticipated that, if it takes six years to complete the programme, the ships will be out of date before they are completed. Even in the short period which has elapsed since the present designs were adopted, the typical destroyers have increased in displacement and the machinery arrangement has been re-designed, which may make it desirable to negotiate with the firm who undertakes the work for an improved destroyer.
The committee will see that Admiral Kingsmill draws a distinction between the advantage of having these ships constructed in four years, and having them constructed in six years, as was proposed in the programme of the late government. But he has overlooked this important fact, that while the contracting firm had six years in which to build all the ships, that did not mean that they would delay for six years the 'building of any one vessel. They were to begin the work within a time specified, and would be obliged, in order to complete the contract within six years, to build two war vessels in every eighteen months, and hand them over complete to the Canadian government. That is what the specifications called for. Has my hon. friend the tenders and specifications here?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I have not the specifications.

That is what would be provided for by the Naval Department. Then Admiral Kingsmill suggests that probably the department sholuld have the right to make the changes in accordance with changes which might be suggested by the

o334
British admiralty. I venture to say that would be in the contract, as it is in all contracts, that the minister should have the right to make alterations which might be recommended by the engineers oi the department, and that the contractor would be obliged to make those alterations, and in case of decreased expenditure, he would make a reduction, while in case of increased expenditure, he would be allowed an increase in cost. The memorandum of Admiral Kings-mill does not at all bear out the statement that was made by my hon. friend. What does my hon. friend propose to do about the building of the Canadian navy? Does the hon. minister contend, does Admiral Kingsmill contend or do the o.fficers of his department contend that these vessels were not of the very best type existing in the British navy at the time those officers gave their approval to the government for their construction? There is no question that was the case. If the vessels of a different type had been designed, the same remark would apply. If a country entered on a naval programme which would run over six years or ten or fifteen or twenty years, it might well be that before the whole programme was completed, the vessels of earlier construction would be out of date.
But that is a difficulty which always presents itself to any nation which undertakes the building of a navy. If my hon. friend is right then the United States could never, with any degree of wisdom, have started to construct a navy. Nor could Japan, nor any country in the world, because when they start they start with a programme which will extend in most cases over a great many years, and of course after the lapse of a numbeT of years the vessels which are constructed in the first place would become obsolete. But surely this remark -would not apply to a contract such as the late government proposed to give which wduld allow the contractors to take six years for the building af all these vessels, yet would have required them to construct at least two of the vessels during every 18 months in order to complete the contract within the prescribed period. Now this is a matter of very great importance to the people of Canada, and it seems to me that the committee has a right to know if, when my hon. friend gave that reason for not awarding these contracts, the government concurred with Admiral Kingsmill that two or three of .these ships should be built in England. Surely my hon. friend and his colleagues did not take the important step of delaying the commencement of a Canadian navy without either agreeing or disagreeing with Admiral Kingsmill. If they agreed with Admiral Kingsmill then they should have at once placed an order for the construction, as he says, of one or two of the cruisers and two destroyers in England without delay, and the contract for the remainder of the vessels should have been awarded to a firm for construction in Canada, so that that firm could proceed with the building of its shipyard and get to work on the construction of the additional ships. But the government has done nothing. Notwithstanding there was a unanimous opinion expressed by this House as long ago as 1909, that it was desirable to proceed with the least possible delay to provide a Canadian navy which would be available for the defence of Canada, and which would also be available to assist in the defence of the empire in time of peril, the government simply withdrew from the matter, returned the deposits, and decided not to go on with the contracts, and so far as we have been informed the government have not decided whether they will adopt the view of Admiral Kingsmill: that is to have two or three of these ships built in England and proceed in Canada with the construction of the remaining vessels which would form part of the navy. If the contract had been let to the lowest tenderers Cammell, Liard & Company, early last October when the government came into power and when they had authority to deal with the matter, and if they had also acted upon the tenders which were received for the construction of a dry dock at the harbour of St. John, instead of delaying for many months before taking action, by this time the construction of a dry dock and a ship yard would have been under way, it would not be many months before the keel of the first vessel would have be.en laid in Canada, and it would not have been many years before all the ten vessels would have been constructed and available for the defence of the country and for the defence of the empire. But nothing is being done, and my hon. friend (Mr. Hazen) proposes to go home to England to consult the admiralty. What does he intend to recommend to the admiralty? He has stopped all action upon these tenders, he has not acted upon the advice of Admiral Kingsmill and given an order for two or three vessels in England, he has taken no steps whatever. Nevertheless he is going home to consult the British authorities. Well, we know What their opinion is. We know perfectly well that what they would prefer iwould be a money contribution. They would prefer that Canada should contribute a good many million dollars every year, place it at the disposal of the admiralty and let them build, man and control the ships. Does my hon. friend prefer to act upon the advice which the British admiralty may give him, if it is in that direction? The next thing the admiralty would prefer, and it is all on re-

cord, is that Canada should build a fleet unit to be placed entirely in Pacific waters. Is this government prepared to act on that suggestion, or has it any opinion upon the subject at all? It seems to me they ought to know whether, in their opinion, the proposition would be acceptable to the people of Canada or not. I think it would not be, but that it would be wholly unacceptable to the people of this country. Then there is the third suggestion, and this is the last which the British government made, their views upon the matter being well known: That we undertake to do the next best thing which could be done for the benefit of Canada and for the benefit of the empire; and my hon. friends may dally months and months and even years, and they may make trips to London in order to consult the British admirailty as often as they like, and they will find I think those are the views which will be .presented to them by the British government. It seems to me it is idle for my hon. friend to say that they want to get he opinion of the British admiralty when, as I have said, we have it already clearly expressed in terms with regard to which there can be no doubt whatever. I felt, Mr. Chairman it was my duty to bring this matter before the committee, because whatever others may have thought, I certainly understood my hon. friend to convey the impression that none of these ships were to be completed for six years, and that perhaps by reason of the type of vessels they would become obsolete. But if you read carefully Admiral Kingsmill's memorandum his remarks would -apply as much to any class of vessels the construction of which might be undertaken, as it would to these vessels which were proposed as part of the programme of the late government. He admits that they are the best type which can be designed for the purpose for which Canada required them. He admits th-at it would be better to build vessels of this class at the outset, than to build vessels of different design; and the only respect in which he differs from the late government is that he thinks these vessels ought to be constructed in four years instead of in six years, and that in order to do so it would be better to place an order for one or two cruisers and two destroyers in England, and then proceed with the establishment of a ship-yard in Canada and award the -contract for the construction here of the additional vessels.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman from the city of -St. John has at last thought it necessary, that somebody should give some explanation to this House and the country as to why it was that the government of which he w-as a member delayed for so long a time without taking any action on the tenders that were submitted in answer Mr. PUGSLEY.
to the call for tenders for the building of certain cruisers of the ' Bristol ' type, and certain torpedo destroyers, for the purpose of constituting the nucleus of a Canacdan navy. I might -remind the House of the fact that these tenders were received on the 1st day of May last. The firms who tendered were:	Caramel! Laird & Company, $11,280,000; Swan, Hunter & Wig-ham Richardson, $12,174,000; nearly $1,000,000 more; the British Canadian Ship Building & Dock Company, $12,464,000; Vickers Sons and Maxim, $12,712,000; Sir William G. Armstrong, Whitworth & Company, $12,842,000; William Beardmore & Company, $13,055,000; and the Thames Ironworks Shipbuilding & Engineering Company, $8,532,000. The last mentioned tender, whi-ch is $3,000,000 less in round figures than the lowest of the other tenders, provided that the ships should be built in England and, therefore, was- not open to consideration under the call for tenders which was that the ships were to be built in Canada. The tender of Cammed Laird & Company w-as nearly $1,000,000 lower than the tender of Swan, Hunter & Wigham Richardson. These tenders were received on the first day of May in the year 1911 and, beyond opening the tenders and tabulating them, there is not a scratch of a pen to show that any action was taken, or any thought given to the tenders until the 5th of October, 1911, two weeks after the general elections, and more than five week-s after these tenders had been received by the Department of Marine and Fisheries in Ottawa.
The first record we have of anything being done with regard to these tenders is in a memorandum that was submitted to -council on the 5th of October, 1911, more than five months after they were received by my hon. friend from Rouville (Mr. Lemieux), who at that time was in charge of the Department of the Naval Service.
Not over six months- five months.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Yes, a little over five months. The memorandum of my hon. friend says.
Under existing circumstances, and having regard to the magnitude of the transaction, the undersigned is of opinion that the question of awarding the contract may probably be left to the incoming administration and has the honour so to advise council.
So, for a period of five months after tenders were received, nothing was done with regard to the -matter, so far as the record shows, by my hon. friend (Mr. Lemieux) or the members of the government to which he belonged. But on the 5th of October, shortly before they handed over the seals of office, my hon. friend reports to council that the matter should

be left to the incoming administration. My bon. friend, who to-night is in such a tremendous hurry that something should be done, has, I think the House will admit, entirely failed to give to the House any good reason why five months should have elapsed after tenders were called for before any action was taken. I feel that I was amply justified in saying, when speaking on the address, that the reason that appeared to actuate my hon. friend was that after the tenders were received it was felt that even if the contracts were awarded and carried out, before the contracts could be completed the vessels constructed would be useless, being out of date, and that the $15,000,000 or thereabouts spent in their construction would be spent to no good purpose, and be actually lost money so far as the interest of Canada; or of the empire was concerned. I mentioned the sum of $15,000,000, for although the lowest tender amounted to between $11,000,000 and $12,000,000, it did not include the armour-plate or armour and certain other portions necessary to a war vessel which would have to be bought and paid for entirely outside the contract price, and these would have added very materially to the cost of these ships.
The hon. gentleman has said that I was not justified in drawing the conclusion I did from the report made to me as Minister of the Naval Service by Admiral Kings-mill. Let us look at the report of Admiral Kingsmill as read by my hon. friend. The hon. gentleman lias said that the first clause affords absolute and complete justification for rwhat the government did, for its whole course in regard to this naval matter. What is the first paragraph? He first refers to the fact of the programme of new construction adopted by the late government which consists of:
4. Cruisers of the improved 'Bristol' type.
6. Improved ' river-class ' destroyers.
And says:
Whilst this programme does not appear an ambitious one, yet it meets present requirements from the fact that ships of this type do not require very large complements, and we are in a position to train sufficient men to form part of their crew, and will not require to obtain the loan of such large numbers of officers and men from the imperial government as would be necessary if large armoured cruisers were included in the programme.
In other words, Admiral Kingsmill says that the programme might meet present requirements, and this opinion is based solely on the ground that for these ships we might get	the sailors in
Canada without having to go to England to get men to man the ships and make them effective. That is the only reason given in the memorandum prepared by Admiral Kingsmill as to this programme being sufficient for the requirements; and on that the hon. gentleman bases the assertion that Admiral Kingsmill's statement shows that the course taken by the government was absolutely and completely justified. And here is what Admiral Kingsmill says with regard to these vessels, after first recomanending that they should be allowed to be built in England:
In the meantime a shipyard can -be established in Canada and the remainder of the programme would -thus -be completed in four years
I desire to ask a question. Does the hon. gentleman know how long it would take even the best shipyards in England to build the ships as mentioned in the naval programme of last year?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Admiral Kingsmill, who was an authority on matters of this sort, who was selected as the Admiral of the Canadian navy by my hon. friends-and a very proper appointment and selection no doubt-calls attention to this in these words:
Tenders were called for and have been received by the government for the construction of these vessels in Canada; whilst it may be desirable to encourage a firm or firms to establish shipyards in Canada, the interests and efficiency of the naval service would be better served if some portion of the ships, one or two of the cruisers, and two destroyers, were constructed in England, orders being placed without delay. We should thus be_ able to obtain delivery of one destroyer within eighteen months; by that time a sufficient number of men will have been trained to form the nucleus of -the crews and training will be m<^re efficiently and expeditiously carried out with the advent of modern ships.
Evidently Admiral Kingsmill believes that if the contract were placed in England one destroyer and one cruiser could be delivered this year and a second destroyer within eighteen months, but that if we followed the programme laid down by hon. gentlemen opposite and if the contract had been awarded to Cammel, Laird & Co., the lowest tenderers, or to any of these other firms, the contract could not have been completed within six years from the time it was awarded and by that time the ships would be completely obsolete and out of date.
Does the hon. gentleman understand Admiral Kingsmill to mean that all the ships will be built in six years? Does he deny that two ships will be completed in eighteen months?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I do deny that two ships could be completed in eighteen months. It would be absolutely impossible to have a Canadian shipyard established, the plant, materials and men assembled to do the work and to complete any one of the vessels in eighteen months. The language of Admiral Kingsmill's report is plain and clear, that having regard to the whole contract it could only be completed in six years and at the end of six years we would have ships delivered to us obsolete and practically fit for the scrap heap.
Within what time does a first-class warship become obsolete?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Judging from Admiral Kingsmill's report, in about six years. Owing to the rapi^ improvements and new inventions a ship ceases to become an effective fighting machine in a very short time. Having regard to that set of facts, I do not believe there is a man in Canada unless, he is speaking from some political standpoint, who would for a moment advo-

cate that it was desirable to enter into this contract and on the other hand I believe that the people of Canada would almost unanimously have condemned any government that would enter into a contract under which they would receive ships obsolete at the time they were built. I think I was placing the most charitable construction possible on the action of hon. gentlemen opposite who for six months and over after the receipt of these tenders did nothing, apparently did not even give serious consideration to the matter and took no action, when I say I believe their action was prompted by the realization that the contract into which they proposed to enter was improvident and not in the interests of the taxpayers; that they would be spending a large sum without getting an adequate return to the people of Canada or rendering service and assistance to Great Britain in case she became involved in a war with a foreign power.
_ My hon. friend to-nigho asked what we intended to do when we consult with the admiralty. The Prime Minister in adressing this House during the debate on the address stated plainly that it was our intention not to rush into a scheme as hon.. gentlemen opposite did which was not well considered but to carefully consider all the different interests involved and after consultation with the admiralty, to formulate and bring before this House a naval policy that we believe will meet with the approval of the people of Canada irrespective of the province from which they come and also of the empire whose interests we want to protect with those of Canada in the framing of any naval policy or any navy that we may have.
With reference to some remarks made by the hon. member for Rouville (Mr. Lemieux), I would say that I am not afraid in any respect of the people of the province of Quebec. I have the very greatest respect and admiration for the patriotism and loyalty of the people of the province from which my hon. friend comes, and I believe that the people of Quebec, in common with the people from the rest of Canada, realize that it is a duty that we owe to the empire to take some effective means not only for the protection of our own ports and shipping, but also that we join hand in hand in promoting the interest and defending the cause of the British Empire as well .
This naval question undoubtedly is a question of very great importance in this country. We are gaining in Canada a position of wealth and importance as one of the sisters beyond the seas of the British Empire. I believe that there is-not a self-respecting citizen of Canada who does not feel that the position we occupy to-day, allowing the taxpayers of Great Britain without any assistance on our part

to continue as in the years when we were in our infancy to maintain the British navy for the support and protection not only of the British Isles but of the British Colonial possessions beyond the seas, is rather humiliating to us as a self-respecting people and that it is our duty plainly, clearly, and manifestly, to contribute our fair share towards national defence.	[DOT]
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I believe that throughout Canada that is the strong sentiment of the people, but while that is the general feeling, while we feel that we have outgrown our swaddling clothes, and are standing on strong ground financially and in every other respect, it is humiliating to us as a nation to go on and allow the mother country to continue to pay all the expense of the support of the navy that has done so much for us in the past, and must be maintained if the British Empire of which we are an integral part is to maintain its supremacy in the future. Therefore, I say it is our duty to contribute our share fairly to the support of the British navy ; but while I say that I think our contribution must be on grounds that will meet with the approval of our citizens and will be consistent with our position as a iselfr-especting part of the British Empire. A navy to be effective must be for the purposes of the empire. If we are to continue as an empire we cannot have one navy for New Zealand, another for Australia, another for South Africa, another in Canada, and another for the British Isles. A navy which exists for the purpose of the general defence of the empire must be a navy concerning which there shall not be a divided control which would destroy its usefulness and efficiency in tiime of trouble. As General Botha, Prime Minister of South Africa, said soon after the imperial conference: I fail to see how South Africa can fail _ to be at war if any other part of the British Empire is; it is not consistent with the idea of empire, that ont part can be at war without the other parts assisting and rendering effective aid. That must be the feeling and ambition so far as the navy is concerned, and whatever navy is designed-and for the moment I am not considering whether each portion of the empire should have representation on the board controlling that navy-must be a navy concerning which there will not be a divided control and must be prepared to act and strike as an effective whole when necessary in defence of the flag.
This question has been discussed to-day largely from the standpoint of the effect of the naval policy of the recent government upon the province of Quebec. Let me say to hon. gentlemen opposite that I believe that naval policy as enunciated
by hon. gentlemen opposite was not any more popular in the other provinces; I believe that the general feeling in Canada was largely adverse to the scheme which was embarked on hurriedly without carefully considering the consequences. We hope and believe that the government of the day will be able to formulate and lay before parliament at a not far distant date a proposal in regard to the important question now under consideration that will meet with the enthusiastic support not only of the English provinces but of Quebec as well, and that will prove itself in the future a very great force for the preservation of the. peace and for the security of the whole British Empire.

Has my hon. friend the
tenders and, if so, will he kindly send them over to me?

speechtext: The tenders I read were contained in the report made to council by my hon. friend who sits opposite to me, the hon. member for Rouville (Mr. Lemieux). The tenders were laid before the House. I think the papers can be got.

speechtext: I have not the call for tenders; all I have is a list of the amounts of each tender. I may be able to get the information without any great delay.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: We will get it for the hon. gentleman in a moment. The deputy minister of Naval Affairs tells me that the call for tenders required the delivery of one cruiser and two destroyers within three years of the date of the awarding of the contract; after that one cruiser every year and one destroyer every nine months.
Only one cruiser would have been obsolete.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: They would all have been obsolete at the end of six years.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: As a matter of fact, the British admiralty have abandoned this type of vessel alogether during the present year.

I agree with what has been said by my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Hazen) that something ought to be done for the naval defence of Canada and we must all join hands in maintaining the supremacy of Great Britain in case of danger. There

has never been any difference of opinion between this side of the House and the other as to that material point in the discussion, namely, the defence of the Brit-itsh flag and the maintenance of British supremacy over the seas. Let that be clearly understood throughout the country. The words we are speaking this evening will, I hope, be repeated by the press throughout Canada. The issue was obscured during the election. My hon. friend must be aware, that in certain provinces the policy of my right hon. friend the leader of the opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) was assailed, because, forsooth, his policy did not go far enough, and in the province of Quebec it was assailed, because, forsooth, it went too far. Now, I admit we suffered heavily from the joint attacks of the extremists on both sides during the election. I have no doubt whatever that on the 21st September last many constituencies were lost to the government of the day because the .policy of my right hon. friend had been represented as being a little Canadian policy, whilst in the province of Quebec it was represented as being too much of a British policy. Now, after the defeat the late government could not consistently give the contract for the carrying out of the naval programme that had been elaborated before the elections. We thought, and properly so, that the question should be left to our successors who had defeated us on that very question because, let there be no mistake about it, while we may talk about reciprocity and other issues that were involved during the last campaign, I can assure the Minister of Marine and Fisheries and the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Borden), that in our province we were simply pilloried on the naval question, because, indeed we had gone too far. I repeat again to my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries that the majority of the people in the province of Quebec, in spite of the appeals there were made, pronounced themselves in favour of the naval defence and of the maintenance of the supremacy of Great Britain upon the seas and in the world at large. The question has been solved There is a majority amongst the people in favour of that policy. Now, it remains for my hon. friend to evolve a new programme. He is going to consult with the admiralty, he says. I am glad of the words he has spoken this evening. He does not speak this evening in the back concession of the county of Quebec; he speaks on the floor of the House of Commons, to the Canadian people, and his words to-morrow will be re-echoed in Great (Britain, in the heart of the empire. We are going to have a naval policy. That naval policy, from what I understand from the hon. gentleman, will be a policy which Mr. LEMIEDX.
will take one of two forms, either a contribution in money to the British exchequer, or the construction of cruisers, of destroyers, perhaps of Dreadnoughts in Canada or Great Britain. Have I understood the hon. gentleman rightly?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I did not say what form it would take.

the construction of a Canadian navy will make a new Halifax of the old Halifax. Then, the hon. member for North Toronto during the recess also went around the country delivering many speeches, and at many places again declared himself in favour of a Canadian navy, built in Canada, and manned by Canadians. Thank Heaven, the Conservative party was once true to its colours; it was a Canadian party. On that question of a navy, evolved on the very pretext, the obvious pretext, of helping the mother country it put that question above party lines. It did not want to play the politicai game with that national question. But that mood did not last many months. An election took place in the county of Drummond and Arth-abaska. The firebrands, the Minister of Public Works, Mr. Bourassa, Mr. Armand Lavergne, the Postmaster General saw an occasion to create troubles for the Liberal government. They could not well attack the Liberal government on its general policy; but they went before the people of Drummond and Arthabaska on the naval question; and what did they say there? My hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries in those days was quietly presiding over the affairs of New Brunswick at Fredericton, honestiy administering the affairs of his province. The right hon. the Prime Minister was away somewhere else, perhaps outside of Canada-If I remember well. At all events, although about half the electors in the county of Drummond and Arthabaska are English-speaking and the other half French, my right hon. friend the leader of the government kept away from the constituency; so did the Minister of Trade and Commerce; although some years ago I remember, when there was a by-election in the country of Sherbrooke, we met there the Prime Minister and the Minister of Trade and Commerce-it was not then too far for them to come and visit ns. But on that very serious occasion of a iby-election in Drummond and Arthalbaska, they kept away from the country. There we saw the Postmaster General, the Minister of Public Works, you, Mr. Chairman, the member for Dorchester (Mr. Sevigny), Mr. Bourassa and the Beau Brum-mall of the Nationalist party, the young man of the red necktie, Mr. Armand La-vengne. And what appeals did they make?

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: Will my hon. friend allow me?

My hon. friend may answer me by-and-by. They all came to the constituency, and there we know what incendiary appeals they made. We know

that an hon. gentleman spoke of certain holes in the British flag. _ Another gentleman appealed to Divinity itself. The Canadian nationality, meaning the French Canadian, he said, was being crucified on the Golgotha of militarism, and the crucifi-ers were the Liberal ministers and their right hon. leader. The Judases of the nationalise were the Liberal ministers; the traitors were the Liberal ministers; yes, we in their estimation, were selling our birthright for a mess of pottage. Great Britain was encroaching on the rights of Canada, and we were mean enough, we were unpatriotic enough, we were anglicised enough, to forget our own blood, our traditions, to our aspirations, our ideals, and we were playing into the hands of John Bull.
Sir, we know the result : They went from concession to concession, people with brass buttons knocked at the door of Jean Baptiste the farmer, and said to the mother in that household:	' Mother, how many
sons have you?' ' What is the (matter with you?' ' Well, have you got any sons?' 'Yes.' 'Then you had better give me their names, because Laurier is going to take them and enlist them' in the navy, they will be sent from Quebec to the China seas, or to India, or to Japan, and they will be disembowelled. Laurier wants them to fight for the British flag for an unknown cause. The Postmaster General, was he then Zandrang? I do not know. The Minister of Public Works, the Minister of Inland Revenue, and you, Mr. Chairman, were all there; and the people of Drummond and Arthabaska in a moment of weakness, to quote an historical phrase, were so upset as to believe in what the hon. gentlemen said. Thank heaven the people of Drummond and Arthabaska were found on their way to Damascus at the last election. They paused, they reflected, they read, they listened, and they saw the light and they sent back to his farm that modern Cincinnatus Mr. Gilbert. Now, Sir, to be serious.
Hear, hear.

I am only repeating the arguments used in Drummond and Arthabaska. My hon. friends on the other side-and I have many there I know- my Tory friends, for whom I have great respect, frankly applaud the appeals made by the Postmaster General when he turns to them and says: 'Yes we are ready to fight for the British flag. We adore the same God, we Catholics and Protestants.' He newer misses that- peroration; 'but if they knew him as I know him, if they could have listened to him in the county of Quebec, in the county of Lotbiniere and in the county of Drummond and Arthabaska, they would find, not the Britisher who appeals to their noblest passions and 170
looks for their applause in this House, but the very worst firebrand this country has ever known.
Order.

Now to be serious again. I say to my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries: He has taken my portfolio-I was Minister of Marine and Fisheries for two months, and I know that there has been no mistake in that department-and he will find the department clean and unsullied, and even the honest Ducharme will find nothing to investigate there. My hon. friend (Mr. Hazen) will go to England. Let me tell him in all seriousness that he carries with him the best wishes of the Canadian people, whether Conservative or Liberal. He will consult the admiralty; behind him will stand the Canadian people. There in conjunction with the British statesmen he will evolve a new policy. Whatever that policy may be, if it is all accepted, it will be the policy of the Canadian people, and I can tell him this further:	The Liberal party in this House,
composed not only of English speaking Liberals, but French Canadian Liberals, will stand behind the government when that policy is put before the House. We will not make a party question of the defence of the empire.
Oh, oh.

No, we will not make a party question of the defence of the empire, of the defence of the British flag and the supremacy of the mother country over the sea. This is a national question. That is how we put it before the people of the province of Quebec, in spite of the vicious appeals made by the friend of the Minister of Marine who is sitting to his left, in spite of the passions roused by his colleagues in the cabinet. We stood firmly by the Canadian police during the last elections, and we intend to stand for it in the future, as in the past. We stand by the mother country when the government's naval policy is brought before parliament.

My dear Colleague,-

very heart of the matter; and that before we entered into any arrangement of that kind we must know where we were standing within this empire. So, we propose that the naval policy of the late government should not be continued, and we do propose before any naval policy is entered upon that some of those matters shall be considered, and when that policy is brought down it shall be presented to parliament, and the people of this country shall be given an opportunity to pronounce upon it.
So far as the future policy of this government is concerned, we propose to formulate it after careful consideration and attention to the problems which I have mentioned here to-night. We propose to give to those problems our very best consideration. We propose, so far as the technical question is concerned, to be guided by the empire's experts, because he was not guided because the admiralty must be better informed upon the technical side of this question than any man in this country can possibly be.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: For my part, and I believe for the whole House also, the discussion we have had is most instructive and will bear excellent fruit. At last we know where we are On this question of the naval policy. We know that it is the policy of this government to-have a naval service. We know that it is-their intention, somehow or other-I do net know how-they do not themselves know exactly-to take part in the defence of the empire, but whether by a contribution or whether by maintaining a fleet of their own is a matter to be decided, very properly, in the future. The present government took issue with that policy, the policy we laid down, and for which we had the approval of the last parliament. I have no fault to find with those who condemned that policy from the point of view represented by my hon. friend opposite. He was not satisfied with the line which we took, nor were his friends behind satisfied with it. In their view we had kept too much autonomy in our policy. In so far as I remember the discussion during the last parliament, the reproach of my right hon. friend and his friends from all the provinces, except the province of Quebec, was that there was too much autonomy in our policy. But everybody knows in the province of Quebec that for eighteen months and more, from the month of January, 1910, when we introduced the naval policy Bill, up to the 21st September, 1911, the gentlemen who support the present administration, the gentlemen who represent the province of Quebec in this administration, one and all, upon all the hustings in Quebec, upon every stump upon which they could plant their feet, stated that we owed absolutely nothing to-England, that we should not have a ship to assist in her defence and that we should never give a penny for that defence. I suppose that I am not to bring proof of what I say, but if that statement is denied upon the present occasion
They cannot deny it.
