Well, these gentlemen are lonesome in the cold shades of opposition, but let me tell them that this government is quite capable of taking caTe of its own policy. Let me tell them further that if any good policy is submitted to this country we will always find these gentlemen opposite taking a stand, as they have always done, against the public interest, or else behind the lines of Torres Vedras. Let us compare for a moment the patriotic principles and lofty sentiments of the member for Rouville to-day, when he has become a great imperialist, with the platform of his party years ago. Let us compare his utterances to-day with the programme his party had in the province of Quebec when they came into power in 1896. The member for Rouville, I think-I do not make assertions as he does without being perfectly sure- but I am informed he was one of the founders of a paper called ' Le Soir.'
No.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: The hon. member (Mr. Lemieux) says ' No,' but he also says I was in Drummond-Arthabaska during the last election, when I was not there. There was in Quebec a paper which my right hon. friend the leader of the opposition-who by his courtesy always gives a good example to the young fellow from Rouville- there was in Quebec a paper which the right hon. leader of the opposition had written articles for and which was his organ.
I rise to a point of order. My hon. friend (Mr. Pelletier) is rather too cheeky.
Order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Will the hon. gentleman state his point of order?

The hon. gentleman
(Mr. Pelletier) speaks of the ' young fellow ' from Rouville, He may apeak that way in the county of Quebec, but not in this House. He must speak of the hon. gentleman from Rouville.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: The rules of parliament do not oblige me to say more than the hon. member for Rouville.

The hon. gentleman will have to be polite in spite of himself. I do not lose my temper, but I say the hon. gentleman has no right to make that remark. The rules of the House will compel him to refer to another member as the ' hon. gentleman.'

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext:
The ' hon. member ' will do. Well the hon. member says he is

not losing his temper, but if we saw him when he really lost his tempper >he must lose control of himself altogether. There wag a newspaper in Quebec in which the leader of the opposition sometimes wrote very good articles and which was known as his party organ.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I am responsible for the articles I wrote myself.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: Yes, and there were other articles written in support of the policy of my right hon. friend which he never repudiated.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Life is too short.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext:
I will read what one of these articles now, and we will see what these great imperialists said when they wanted to reach power. This is from the Liberal organ in Quebec:
Do you want war; thence million dollars in guns, cannons and bayonets; imminent danger for you farmers.
These are the head lines and here is the article:
One of old Tapper's dreams was imperial federation. Imperial federation means a closer alliance between England and her colonies generally and Canada in particular. Ono condition of such an alliance would be that in time of war Canada would he called upon to pay its share of the cost in money and in men. And, as England is nearly always at war with somebody we would be continually taxing ourselves to find money, always drawing lots to raise men. In return England would make these fakirs baronets, knights of this, commanders of that. But the people would remain food for cannon.- Hardly had Sir Charles Topper returned from England than he began to pave the way for the realization of his awful plan. England was threatened with a difficulty with the United States over a few acres of mining land which she claimed in Venezuela, thousands of miles away from our country, in Central America. Immediately Sir Charles Tnpper, to be officious hastened to Order the purchase in England of guns, cannon, &c. to the extent of $1,800,000, in the midst of a session without consulting the House. That was not enough for him. He wanted three millions. Mr. Foster proposed on April 21st, 1806, '(Hansard/ page 16902) a resolution authorizing a loan of $3,000, 000 to pay for the purchases made and to he made. There had then been ordered 40,000 Lee-Enfield rifles and 23,000 carbines of the same make for the cavalry. There have been ordered four batteries of six cannon, 12 pounders with the (accessary ammunition. The riflles cost $18 each.
Now I come to the climax, and when I read this, let it not be forgotten that these were the words spoken to the public by the party organ in Quebec:

speakerposition: Postmaster General

speechtext: No, Mr. Chairman, the country does not know them now. The country may know one side, but it does not know the other side. Let us see a little what the country will think of the other side-at least, a portion of the other side; because I know my hon. friends opposite; I know there is no mistake about them; they are staunch Tories, staunch Conservatives. But these words do not apply to my hon. friend, and I wish to reply at once to the question that was put to me a moment ago. It is good for the House, it is good for the country, that this ultra imperialist, this ultra Tory, should be known-not by us; we know him; but by his own friends. My hon. friend said a moment ago that he did not go to Drummond and Arthabaska. He did not, and I will explain to the House why.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: You said three times that I went.

Listen to the reason why the hon. gentleman did not go to Drummond and Arthabaska. The hon. gentleman, I stated to the House the other day, has changed colours as often as the sky changes. In 1886 he was a Rielist candidate in the county of Temis-couata against the Ross government. In 1887 he was a Liberal candidate in the

county of Three Rivers. In 1888 or 1889 he was elected in the county of Dorchester, succeeding his bosom friend, Mr. Laro-ehelle. In 1890 he was again a Liberal candidate. In 1891 that stalwart loyalist, who would not stand for reciprocity in 1911, supported unrestricted reciprocity.
Mr. Chairman, I rise to a point of order. The hon. gentleman is not discussing any issue bearing on the question before the committee.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think certainly that the committee is wandering far from the item under discussion.

My hon. friend spoke of articles published in 1896 and before 1896 to explain his stand, and I think I am entitled to answer him to show him before the country and before his own friends. I was just saying that in 1891 the hon. gentleman stood firmly in favour of unrestricted reciprocity as a straight Liberal in the county of Dorchester. A few months afterwards
I rise to a point of order. The hon. gentleman is now entering upon an issue
I am coming to the point.

I quite understand that I am not entitled to make my point of order without being interrupted. It seems to me that the House is degenerating to a pretty low standard. The hon. gentleman is entering upon a discussion of unrestricted reciprocity. What that has to do with the naval question I cannot see. I ask your ruling.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I must repeat that the hon. member has gone far from the question under discussion. Both sides of the House have done so. I would invite the hon. member to come back to the point under discussion.

I am nearing the point, Mr. Chairman. I was just saying that in 1891 the hon. gentleman stood with this party. In 1896 he stood with the other party, but in 1904 he had a quarrel with the other party, and that is how ' Zand-rang ' comes in. He wanted to know why I should call him ' Zandrang.' He had a quarrel with his party on that very point; that is why
Order.
Mr. Chairman, I cannot see that the hon. member is coming to the point.
I am coming to the point.
Order.
Order.

And to-day he stands in this House ready to support anything emanating from the government. The other day on another question the hon. gentleman said to tlhe faithful of the county of Quebec that there were times in the life of a public man when it was more difficult for him to keep his portfolio than to throw it aside. He decided, however, to ,keep his portfolio on the school question, and make sure, Mr. Chairman, he will again keep his portfolio on the naval question also.

It may bean advantage, or a disadvantage, but I happened to sit in this House in 1896, and it would be hard to reconcile the voluble gentleman who has just taken his seat with the same gentleman who sat here silent as the tomb on a certain occasion. What was that occasion? The Postmaster General quoted to-night utterances from newspapers published in the province of Quebec prior to the elections of 1896. There happened to sit in this House at that time a gentleman who stood prominently high in the opinion of both sides in his reputation for fairness, and his splendid character in the province of Quebec. I refer to the Hon. John McIntosh who had the honour of representing the city of Sherbrooke, which city did ' itself credit in electing him as its member. I remember seeing then a blanched face which held a palsied tongue, and it was the face and the tongue of the hon. member for Rouville on the occasion of a scathing denunciation by Mr. McIntosh. Sir, the occasion of criticism were the speeches uttered by the hon. member for Rouville

who paraded from one end of the province of Quebec to the other making denunciation of 'Old Tupper'. The hon. gentleman did not even have that respect which he should have had for the grey hairs of that distinguished statesman as to term him by his title of 'Sir Charles'. That is the taste which the hon. gentleman displays for a man in public life. Did that hon. gentleman dare to deny one word uttered by the hon. John McIntosh on that occasion? No, Sir, not a single word. And his leader and the ministers sitting with him on that side of the House hung down their ,very heads for shame of him. The statement which Mr. McIntosh made at that time, at the same time .enumerating the different places where the hon. gentleman had made the speeches complained of, was that he was a man wiho instead of being in the Canadian parliament, should have been prosecuted for treason to the British Crown. That is the hon. gentleman who has been prating here to-night, and presenting his views on imperialism as to the views that should be entertained by the hon. gentlemen on both sides of this House.
Save the mark.

The wreck in the shape of His Majesty's loyal opposition which sit on the opposite side are at such variance with each other that they do not know in what direction they are going. I have been in this House, with a slight interruption, for which hon. gentlemen opposite devoutly prayed, for three parliaments, and in that period who ever saw such a spectacle as was presented1 in this House on the Manitoba school question the other night? Sir, it is a well known rule in the British navy that when a ship sinks owing to the blunder of the commander, that commander like a man goes down with his ship. That has not been done by the leader of the opposition. He is still clinging to the ship, and if any man should be humiliated how must the leader of the opposition have been humiliated the other night. He took a stand on the school question, in connection with the Manitoba boundaries extension Bill, and1 I give him credit for being conscientious; but if he was conscientious in his attitude with respect to that question, then he stands in the unenviable position that he no longer leads his compatriots from Quebec, but they lead him. Under these circumstances the time has come in the province of Quebec when the right hon. gentleman cannot lead his own following. Sir, the public are getting tired and sick of these hon. gentlemen prating about race and religion.
Hear, hear.

I represent a constituency in the province of Ontario where there are 1,500 French .Canadian voters, and in the last election what was the whole issue in that French Canadian settlement? Was it the question of reciprocity or the question of the navy? No, Sir, but the bosom friend1 of the leader of the opposition, the creature of his hand, the putty which he moulded, Senator Cas-grain, travelled all the way from Montreal to the riding of East Simcoe, and for two hours harangued at different points French Canadian audiences. What was the subject? Was it reciprocity, was it the question of the navy, was it the economic question? No, Sir, it was: 'Vote for the old man because he is a French Canadian and a Catholic.' That was the whole cry raised during the last election amongst the French Canadians in my riding. And, Sir, in making that statement I do not go behind Senator Casgrain's back, I am a personal friend of his-at least I hope I am-and I saw him after the opening of the session, and said to him: ' You ought to be ashamed of yourself. The idea of a man of your intelligence going into that riding and endeavouring for two hours to excite the people on questions of race and1 creed in a county where the people were intelligent enough to deal with questions on their merits, and on their merits alone.' Senator Casgrain admitted the very statement that I attributed to him, that the whole trend of his speech was, ' vote for Laurier because he is a Roman Catholic anu a Frenchman.' What happened? An intelligent French Canadian elector said: 'We know Sir Wilfrid is a Frenchman and a Roman Catholic. Tell us about reciprocity.' Senator Casgrain's response to that question was: ' That has nothing to do with it. Vote for Laurier, because he is a Frenchman and a Catholic.' Sir, that policy was not only carried1 on in East Simcoe, it was carried on in other ridings, and what was the result? Why, Sir, the returns show it. The county of Prescott, in Ontario, went Liberal in answer to the appeal along those lines. Glengarry with its large French vote, went Liberal in response to the same appeal. South Essex, the two Kents, and Russell were all carried in the same manner, I repeat that people are sick and tired) of these eternal howls from hon. gentleman opposite, and from their leader, on this question of race and religion. However, it has stood them in good stead. The leader of the opposition has never thought it was not the proper thing to do it himself. I sat in this House during the session of 1896, and what happened when his Chicoutimi speech was attributed to him? The leader of the opposition had there made the

statement ' that he thanked God there was not an Orangeman in the Liberal party, and yet, sitting right behind him at the time, was the Grand Master of Eastern Ontario, the hon. member for Addington.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: The Orange order never so far disgraced itself.

And then Mr. Bellay, member for Chicoutimi and Saguenay, made the statement repeatedly from his place in the House, and produced a bunch of affidavits in support of it
The right hon. gentleman who leads me opposition did not dare deny that he had made the statement attributed to him, anil ' Hansard ' will prove it. It was a pituul sight, and for this reason, that though the right hon. gentleman did not deny it hun self, it fell to the lot of two gentlemen to stand up-two of his own supporters, Mr Carroll and the present Senator Choquette -and declare that they were present ana *had not heard it said, and it could not have been said. But, as I have said, the right hon. gentleman himself would not make the denial, and I do not suppose he would deny it to-night even after twenty years. That is the style of election cries that we have been subjected to in the riding of East Simcoe and in all the ridings in Ontario in which there are many French Canadians. And I want to tell hon. gfit-tlemen opposite that had they eliminated that feature from the discussion in these contests the French vote in their ridings would have been much broken up, but instead of that it was a solid mass, and that by reason of the appeals that have been made from time to time. As to the member from Renville (Mr. Lemieux), I do not suppose that the House is very much concerned with his personal troubles. I have beard the adage that fools rush in where angels fear to tread, and also that people who live in glass houses should not throw stones. If the hon. gentleman had come at me personally as he cape at the Postmaster General (Mr. Pelletier), I would refer to a debate which took place in this House in .relation to certain actions .in the county of Gaspe that did not redound to the credit of the hon. member and to some person very near to him. And on that occasion, what did the right lion, gentleman (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) plead for him? Why, it was enough to melt one to tears to hear the defence put up by the leader of the opposition for the hon. member for Rouville and a certain other person in connection with certain occurrences in one of the ridings in the province of Quebec. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Lemieux) talks about the Postmaster General (Mr. Pelletier) as being a firebrand. Well, there is one thing about a man who carries a firebrand- you can always see him coming. But this
darkdantern brigade gentry who infest the French settlements are not always to be caught. For my part, I prefer the man with the flaming torch to the man who arms himself with a dark lantern.
These hon. gentlemen are in opposition, and I think before many years are passed exposures will be made in this House of the way millions of dollars were frittered away and stolen from the public treasury, anid the result will be to keep them where they are for many years to come. They may as well accept the inevitable. They are in opposition, and they are in opposition to stay for many years. But all this talking of the hon. member for Rouville may be summed up in this:	He is very
busy about nothing and out of wind to no purpose.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I desire to ask the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Hazen) for 'information as to the ships included in this item. What is the nature of these ships?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
It is not expected to purchase any ships with this vote. The total amount is $1,660,000, and it is divided under the following heads:
To pay the officers and men of 'the ' Niobe ' and 'Rainbow' and of the Naval College, $583,080.
Stores for the two boats, and guns, $533,900. Repairs to ships and vessels (nearly all for repairs of damages to the ' Niobe '), $200,000.
Repairs to the dockyards machinery at Halifax and Esquimau, $13,260.
Miscellaneous dockyard services at Halifax und Esquimalt, $44,444.
Miscellaneous other services, $118,600.
Repairs and maintenance of buildings, provision of additional improvements for the college, $5,500.	,
Purchase of new machinery for dockyards at Halifax and Esquimalt, $19,200.
Hew buildings and other works, $4,276. Construction of lighters, water-tank and service boats, $64,500.
That makes the total of the vote. I would be glad to give the right hon. gentleman details of any of these subdivisions if he desires.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: No, I only wished to know if new boats were to be purchased. I understand it is not intended to make such purchases.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Nothing except lighters, _ a water-tank and service boats. Nothing in the way of what might be called boats for the navy.
Are men being recruited for the service?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes, from time to time, to keep the number on the 'Niobe' and the ' Rainbow ' up to strength.
How many men on each of these ships?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The authorized numbers are: .For the 'Niobe,' 60 officers and 630 men; for the 'Rainbow,' 18 officers and 251 men; Royal Naval College at Halifax, naval officers, 8; civilian officers, 4; cadets, 45; naval men, 40; civilians, 10. This makes a total of 1,068. That is the authorized strength, but I do not think we are up to strength at the present time. For instance, there is accommodation in the naval college for 45 cadets, and I think that at the present time there are only about 30.
Would the hon. minister sum up the services which are being rendered now by . these two ships?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Those upon the ships, of course, are enlisted for the purpose of receiving instruction. The course of instruction is similar to that on board the ships of the British navy; and the intention was, in the scheme proposed, that after taking a certain course of instruction they should be shipped into other vessels actually engaged in outside waters instead of doing the work among the harbours which the ' Niobe ' and ' Rainbow ' are doing. The training summary included the British navy instruction in gunnery, the management of a ship and other matters to make them efficient seamen for a man of war.

I have seen it stated in the papers that certain of the cadets had been sent to England aboard of some of the ships there. How many young Canadians have been sent to the other side? And will they come back?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Thirteen have been sent to continue there the work of their course of training that they could not get on board the ship here.
Who commands the ' Rainbow '?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Commander Holmes.

And on board the
' Niobe ' Commander Macdonald?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes.

When I was Postmaster General, I was asked by the Minister of Marine and Fisheries of that time, to ask the postmasters throughout the country to recruit men for the navy. Are the postmasters continuing that work? Are they continuing to recruit?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: That is continued, those instructions to the postmasters have never been cancelled.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service

speechtext: Are you recruiting men?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: We are getting men from time to time, there is no very active recruiting going on.
Would the minister give some further information about the college at Halifax?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The college is the old hospital building in the navy-yard. The cadets are instructed by a staff of instructors in different branches of education necessary to fit them for the navy. They are also instructed in mechanical work, there is a machine shop and carpenter shop and they receive manual training. In fact they receive the sort of training for the navy that 'is given at the college at Kingston for life in the army.
Do they all receive the same kind of training? '

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes.
What is the length of the course?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: About two years.
Do they spend part of that time on the ships?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Not until they are through with the college. Then if they want to continue a naval career they go on board a
ship and continue their course.
What qualifications must a cadet possess?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: He has to pass a preliminary examination such as a 'boy would get at the common schools of the country, but although the examination is simple some boys fail. The boys are usually about 17 years of age. It is found impossible to get the boys to go to school as young as they do in Great Britain.
The idea of the minister undoubtedly is to have these men who are trained on those ships serve on the new navy he is going to devise when he goes and consults with the admiralty?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
That, of course, was the idea, object and purpose of establishing the college just as with the college at Kingston, but many of those who graduated from the college at Kingston do not go into the army or even take out commissions in the militia; the education they receive fits them for engineering or any other calling because of the very excellent training they get. The same thing is true of the naval college at Halifax. I visited it last autumn and was very much pleased with what I saw. I thought the discipline was excellent and the training good. It would be a benefit to a boy even if he did not enter the navy as a profession. Of

course if we are going to have a navy in Canada and to have naval officers we must have means to properly educate them. In England they have the naval colleges and a naval college is an essential and necessary part of the naval system.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I am not prepared to tell my hon. friend at this moment what the policy of the government will be in that respect.

The minister is not even in a position to say whether he will adhere to the resolution which was adopted unanimously in this House and in the wording of which his own leader, then the leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden), participated.
I am sure of that because I was present in the House when this resolution was adopted with the participation of both parties and with both leaders sharing in the framing of it. It has one paragraph which is important. The minister is not in a position to say whether he will' adhere to the resolution which was adopted here unanimously not two years ago-may I ask?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: That is correct.

The minister, a few minutes ago, said, if I understood him correctly, that the scheme propounded by the late government had been hurriedly conceived. This resolution was adopted almost three years ago. It was adopted in March. 1909, and the Bill was presented to this House for the carrvinsr out of the policy regarding naval defence on the 3rd February, 1910. That is almost one year later, and, in the meantime, there was a
conference in London between two ministers, at least, of the late government and the Brisish admiralty. I do not wish to delay the House at all, but this is a subject in which I am very much interested. I have been discussing it a good deal with gentlemen who sit behind the minister. One paragraph of this most important resolution reads as follows:-
The House will cordially approve of any necessary expenditure designed to promote the *speedy organization of a Canadian Naval *Service in co-operation with and in close relation to the Imperial navy, along the lines suggested, by the admiralty at the last Imperial Conference, and in full sympathy with *the view

And so on. We have contended that the policy, inaugurated by the late administration was exactly on the line of this part of the resolution. We have been contending that in the province of Quebec, and I think we were right. The naval policy which was adopted provided for the building in this country of a certain number of ships, the control of which was to be in the hands of the Canadian government, but it was provided in a certain clause-I do not remember the number of it-that if it was judged necessary, this Canadian navy could share in the defence of the empire and be a part at a given moment of the imperial navy. We have been condemned in the province of Quebec, by the Postmaster General, because this scheme was in too close co-operation with the imperial navy, whilst, if I am well informed, in the province of Ontario we have been condemned because it was not in cooperation sufficiently with the mother country.	[DOT]

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: In defence of the Naval Bill, did not the hon. member for Beauce, in the counties of Montmagny and Beauce where he ran, tell the people that this navy was not so bad as it looked because it was for the protection of the export of cheese and butter?

Certainly, and in saying that I was repeating the very words of the right hon. gentleman who leads the government. He expressed that in the seat which is now occupied by my right hon. friend the leader of the opposition when he said that this naval organization would provide for the protection of commerce. Are cheese and butter not important factors in our commerce, I would ask my hon. friend?

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext:
Certainly, but what I meant to suggest was that the hon. member for Beauce, as a minister of the Crown, told the audience which he addresser! during the eleotion, that there was no danger at all of anybody being hurt by those poor ships, because they were not

going to wage war, but were merely for the protection of cheese and butter.

I never stood for an academic resolution to protect the country but I always stood for a navy to protect our coast and trade and how could we protect the country when we went to war unless we fired guns? I see that the Postmaster General is right when he says that he was not in Drummond and Arthabaska; otherwise he would have known what I said there.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: I am told that it was about the same thing.

Yes. this navy was to be a Canadian navy under the control of the Canadian government for the protection of our ports, coasts, trade and commerce, and sharing with the mother country in the moment of need. Those are the words I used in Drummond Arthabaska.
And the Postmaster General said that it was a crime to do that.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: The hon. .member for Rouville does not know anything about it.

I never heard the Postmaster General on a. platform in the last election. I have read some of his speeches in a paper which is supposed to be friendly to him and one paragraph conveyed to me the idea that this navy was condemned very severely and that any participation whatever in defence of the empire would be a national crime. Of course, to-day it is changed as on the school question everything is changed. We have gained to-day the knowledge that everybody in this House is in favour of this country sharing in defence of the empire. Is there anybody in the House against it?
Speak now.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: I will speak.
Speak now.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: Would the hon. member for Rouville try and take some advice from his leader and be somewhat more calm? I will speak when my leader speaks on this question and when we have formulated a policy. Let my hon. friend wait a little.
You cannot speak.
In the meantime the hon. gentleman is within the lines of Torres Vedras.
Do you mean Mr. Lavergne or your present leader?

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: Let the hon. member for Beauce speak.

As far as I was personally concerned I had not taken very strong-Mr. PELLETIER..
ly to the idea of the organization of the Canadian navy until the 29t/i March, 1909. But on that occasion |we witnessed the great spectacle of both readers and both parties uniting on the one idea that the time had come when we should organize, in so far as naval defence was concerned, and the word 'speedy* was included in this paragraph at the suggestion of the leader of the opposition of that time. My hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries claims that it was conceived hurriedly, that we were too quick, that we were too fast, too swift, too speedy and yet this word 'speedy' was included at the suggestion of the right hon. gentleman who now leads the government. Since then I have been a fervent adherent of the idea of naval organization in Canada. I realize that it is necessary, that it is a duty, an obligation, and I take this opportunity to say that I believe there is a difference, at least in .French, between the word 'duty' and the word 'obligation'. There is a big difference between the word 'duty' and the word 'obligation' and I am sorry that I have to differ from the right hon. gentleman who leads the House in that regard. I have done my best to have the people in Quebec come to the idea that the time has arrived when we should organize a naval defence.
The minister stated to-night that when in six years the ships would be built, they would be obsolete, but if such an opinion were ever given by any, gallant admiral it would be a suprise to me because a good 'many British ships are older than six years and yet they are in effective service in the navy. I tell the minister :	I still
adhere to the resolution adopted on the 29th of March, 1909, I adhere to every "word of it and I trust that when he goes to England-and this country will be well represented by him-he will emphasize the fact that this Parliament was unanimous in passing this resolution, and that direct and periodical contributions to the British admiralty are not allowed by this resolution of the Canadian parliament, but that a speedy organization of a naval service in co-operation with the mother country is ordered by the resolution. The Liberal, party has been doing its best to carry out that resolution as fast as possible, and we have been blamed for it. We now await the policy of the government, and I trust that whatever the minister proposes will be well devised and well planned, as the result of these negotiations with the home authorities and the experts of the British navy. I hope that every man in this House, not only the minister and his leader, not only the gentlemen who sit behind him, not only the Liberal party as a whole, but even those whom you, Mr. Chairman, know so well and who have been denouncing any naval

organization in this country, will support the policy the minister submits. Then will be done away with these vicious appeals
that have been made in the Drovince of Quebec especially, and even in Ontario and the other provinces on exactly opposite grounds.

I realize that it is perhaps in the interests of the country that we should get quickly through with the estimates, but I must say a few words upon the resolution now before us. It seems to be well understood that the policy of both political parties in this country is to contribute some aid, in whatever shape it may be, to the defence of the empire. It may he that in the heat of a political combat things have been said which would not be said on the floor of this parliament, but taking the discussion we have had in this House to-day, we may fairly come to the conclusion that the Canadian Parliament endorses some contribution towards imperial naval defence. I think we may also draw the conclusion from the discussion that the present government does not intend to give a money contribution to the British admiralty. I take it that that contribution will be in the shape of ships, because _ otherwise the government would not be maintaining what naval defence service we have in Canada at the present time. Of course, it must be supposed that if the government had the intention of doing anything else than supplying ships, which may be built either in this country or in England, it would be absurd for the government to be voting imoney to keep up the two ships we now have. Much has been said about the delay that has taken place in reference to this question of contribution to our naval defence, but it must not be forgotten that much has been done in Canada towards helping out the British Empire in connection with the defence of pur country. It takes a long time to work out a plan of this kind; it took a long time to work out a plan for taking over the fortifications at Halifax and Esquimalt, but, in this as in other cases, the longer it takes the better may be the final result. / Much has been said about the delay on the part of the late government in providing for our defence, but it seems -to me that the present government is not in any great hurry, and the best we have heard from the Minister of Marine is1 that in the not far distant future there will be something done in the matter. We are led to understand that the Minister of Marine is going to England to discuss the question with the home authorities, and as this is a business government and supposing as a business government it will not contribute money towards naval defence, but that it will build ships, then the question arises
as to whether ships should be built in Canada or in the mother country. From the mere standpoint of loyalty alone, and without considering anything else, it would of course be just as loyal for the Canadian government to give the money to the British admiralty to supply itself with these ships, as for the Canadian government to build the ships in our own country. But, there are other things which may be considered. The man who takes the ground that we would not, in the course of a few years, be able to build as good ships in Canada as they can build in the English dockyard is not a true Canadian, because he underrates the skill and the industry and the ability of Canadian workmen. I believe it to be the sentiment in the province from which I come, that if there is going to be a contribution to naval defence, then that money should be spent in Nova Scotia, in New Brunswick, in Prince Edward Island or in British Columbia, as the case may be. If we go into the building of these ships, the British workman can come here and earn Canadian dollars if he will, but the people of Canada who are putting their hands into their pockets should have the right to earn these dollars if dollars are to be earned. I look upon this matter from a business standpoint, and I say that in the course of a few years we will be able to build just as good ships on this side of the water as they can in Great Britain. We may talk as we like about conferring with the admiralty, but as I understand it the admiralty has already concurred in the naval policy of the late government.
But the principal point that I wish to lay stress on is this, that the hon. Minister of Marine, when he goes to England to confer with the admiralty on this question, should not forget that there is a sentiment in this country, especially in the maritime provinces, in which I include British Columbia, that if we are going to contribute ships-and I believe we should contribute nothing but ships-those ships should be built by Canadian workmen, of Canadian material, and with Canadian dollars. That is the stand that I believe every maritime man will take. They may tell us: Yes, the people of Nova Scotia, the people of New Brunswick and the people of British Columbia will' have a chance to obtain some graft from such government expenditure. Surely every government that comes into power in this -country has enough business capacity to see to it that there is no such thing as that. That is an argument that is put up by the ' Montreal Star '-that our people yho ask for money to be spent in this country are people who have some axe to grind. There is no one in this parliament who has not some axe to grind, and the axe

that we should grind is to see that our workmen are protected, that if money is to be spent, we should take a strong Canadian, business view, that it should be spent on this side of the water.

And I for one will not harbour any grudge against them, nor hold an account against them, if they will even at this late day stand loyally behind the Minister of .Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Hazen) in carrying out the policy of the resolution read a moment ago by the hon. member for Beauee (Mr. Beland) and adopt the imperial resolution of 1907 which is the standard adopted by themselves, ana go forward with the policy and let us no longer remain under the condemnation meted out by the Prime Minister to any class who are not willing to .contribute to their own support an/d defence in 'this empire of which we are so proud to form a part.

I wish to add ijust one word of exhortation to the Minister of Marine and Fisheries. Two days ago the hon. member for Yamaska (Mr. Mondou) asked a question:
Does the government intend to propose the repeal of the Naval Act?
And the answer was 'Yes', and then the Minister of Marine and Fisheries went on to explain some kind'of .policy that is to be adopted by the present government and *said that policy would undoubtedly require legislation, which legislation would involve the repeal of the present Naval Act. I took the trouble to look up the Naval Service. Act to find what in it could be objectionable t-o the minister. I find that the first section is the title. Sec. 2 and 3 refer to interpretation. Sec. 4 provides that the King is to be commander-in-chief of the Canadian navy. I suppose that will not be objectionable to my hon. friend?
It is objectionable to the hon. member for Dorchester (Mr. Sevigny).
What good would they be without the Dreadnoughts?
If they -were no good the British admiralty would not build them.
They .are good with the others, but what wo-uld be the use of them without the others?

They are the kind of ships used for the protection of the trade routes. They are swift ships, battleships. They are building also 20 destroyers, 6 submarines, 2 river gun-boats, 1 department ship and 1 hospital ship. We proposed 4 of these cruisers of the ' Bristol ' type and 6 torpedo destroyers to begin with, the very kind of ships they are building in England. They are building these constantly. One of them was launched in June last, and they are proposing to launch one on the 18th of June this year.
They are proposing to launch another on the 19th of August, a third on the 31st of August and a fourth in September. During the past two years the British government has built in British yards the following protected cruisers:	Five of the
Bristol type (that is the type we are proposing to build); four of the Dartmouth type; three of the Dublin class; three improved of the Dublin class, and three for the Australian government, making in all 18, and we are told by the Minister of Marine and by the Prime Minister that these vessels will be useless in time of war. Then 18 of these useless vessels have been built by the British Admiralty within the last two years, or are now building, apd they are also being built by every civilized country in the world. There is a dispute among experts as to the best type of ship. There is no doubt that the strongest and most effective ship is the Dreadnought, but these other ships are being built by every civilized and progressive nation in the world. The British government to-day own 92 protected cruisers, Germany 41, Japan 16, United States 14, Austria 9, Russia 8, Italy 7, France 5. The last proposal of the British admiralty was that they would build five in Great Britain each year and if they were the kind of ships my horn, friend says they are, I submit that the British admiralty would not be building them at all. A _ couple of years ago the government of Australia asked for an expert to be sent out to make some investigations and give them some advice and -then the report of -Sir Reginald -Henderson the expert who went there recommends within the next 22 years the -construction of the following vessels: Eight battleships, 10 protected cruisers, 18
destroyers, and 12 submarines. I can understand my ihon. friend saying we ought to have some Dreadnoughts. If that is his policy why -does he' not announce it? If the only difference between the two parties is that we on this side of -the House believe in protected -cruisers to begin with and th-ose on the other side in Dreadnoughts, it -should be easily -settled, but the postmaster -General and the Nationalist party have not made that demand, and they are not in favour of any kind of ship. These are the questions with which the Minister of Marine will be met when -he reaches London, and I submit he will have either to pay a cash contribution or to adopt some policy verv close to the policy of the late government.

The protection of the fisheries along the coast from Canso around to Cape Breton as soon as the drift ice is gone is very important, because we have many American vessels around the coast at that time, and it is highly necessary that the three-mile limit should be enforced. Is there any system by which the ships will be in readiness to go to that part of the province as early as they will be required?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I entirely concur in what my hon. friend has said. We have three steamers in the service on the coast men-

tinned, the ' Canada,' the 'Constance,' and the ' Petrel.' They will all be put in commission when the season opens and their services are required.

It is reported on the coast that the laws are not well enforced in regard to steam trawling, that in the Gulf of St. Lawrence the steam trawlers have been working inside the three-mile limit. Some doubt has been expressed as to what is a bay in all parts of our waters. The steam trawler is prohibited from working in bays or harbours or within three miles of the coast line. In the gulf between Cape Breton and Cape Jack some fishermen contend that they should be kept out of that place altogether.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: How wide is the bay at the mouth?
Perhaps ten or twelve miles.
Twenty miles.

I am not quite sure about the width of the bay; at all events, I think the minister should have some authority that would define the bays along the coast that are excluded from the operations of the steam trawler, and also the instructions to the protective agents to look out for these steam trawlers and see that they observe the law.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
This question with regard to bays was dealt with at the arbitration which took place at The Hague two years acr0 when Sir Charles Fitzpatrick was the representative of the. Canadian government, and Sir Allen Aylesworth was the agent of His Britannic Majesty. The tribunal at the Hague practically adopted the rule in regard to bays that was adopted in the treaty of 1888, spoken of as the Blaine-Chamberlain treaty, which was negotiated by Sir Charles Tupper, and which was subsequently thrown out by the Senate of the United States. It defines, except in the case o.f the Bay of Fundy, which is not considered * at a.11, where the three mile limit shall be with regard to bays. In bays that are not more than ten miles in width it shall be a line from headland to headland at the point where the bay ceases to have the conformation of a bay,_ and at other places it -shall be three miles from the shore. But, there are bays in Prince Edward Island, New Brunswick, like Mira-michi Bay and the Baie des Chaleurs, in Nova Scotia and Newfoundland, more than ten miles in width, in regard to which it is expressly provided that the line shall be diawn from headland to headland at the point where it ceases to have the conformation of a bay. There is a general clause in other cases to the effect that the line Mr. HAZEN.
shall be drawn from the first point _ at which the bay is not more than ten miles ir width. A treaty has been agreed to practically in so far as Canada is concerned, -and Newfoundland is now about to do the same, but there must be a reference to the United States Senate fox confirmation. The deputy minister tells me that the department has been unable to get any evidence whatever that isteam trawlers have be-en^ fishing within the three mile limit in the waters mentioned by the hon. member for Gnysborough. The Naval Department has been unable to find steam trawlers, whether from the United States or France, inside the three mile limit. I will ask the deputy minister to give instructions to the commanders of these vessels to take more particular pains this year, to watch out and see that no trawlers are allowed within the district referred to by my hon. friend.

Might I suggest that the deputy minister will ask the protection vessels to lay out at nights when the trawler is in the vicinity. I am told that it is at night that the damage is done. The trawler works at might, and as a rule the cruiser goes into some snug harbour where they can have a nice easy time, and they do not see anything, of course. If the protection vessel would lay out at night and watch the trawler perhaps it could get at the difficulty.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Commander Wakeham is nut in the naval service, hut in the service of the Marine and Fisheries Department, No application, in so far as I know, has been made by Commander Wakeham for superannuation and no application has been made to me from any source to superannuate him. I do not know of any reason

for superannuating him. He 'has been a very capable officer 'and I am sure that I have not the slightest intention of superannuating him at present.

Befoie we leave this question with regard to steam trawlers, which has been introduced by the hon. member for Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair), I wish to say a word with respect to it. The hon. member for Guysborough, during last session, introduced a resolution, on this question which resulted in a very full and free discussion. I spoke upon that occasion and I condemned very strongly the system of taking fish by means of beam iand otter trawlers. I entertain today exactly the same opinion in regard to the matter as I did upon that occasion. On that occasion there were statements made by various gentlemen supporting the administration of that day which effectually evidenced the fact that these trawlers were operated within the three-mile limit. I dare say that the hon, member for Guysborough will recollect that such was the case. The subject is one which is of very vital importance to the fishermen not only of Nova Scotia, but to all the maritime provinces, and is one which might very well engage the serious attention of the officers of the Department of Marine | and Fisheries. For two or three years in i the reports of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries of the late government some reference to these beam and otter trawlers was made and in each case the intimation was thrown out that beam trawling had come to 'stay, that it was something which might as well be accepted because it was inevitable. For my own part I think that it would be a very serious thing if it were allowed to go on unchecked. If large sums of money were permitted to be invested in these [DOT]trawlers it might be said later on that there was a vested interest and that it would be improper to interfere with the operation of them. I think that the government should now do all that it possibly can to check the operation of these trawlers. Of course, in the case of trawlers operating in the North Sea, there is a very different condition prevailing from that which prevails in this 'country. In the maritime provinces the government has expended millions of dollars in constructing breakwaters, wharfs and aids of that character to the fishermen and the fishermen have invested large sums of money in high-class fishing boats and vessels.
If these trawlers are permitted to carry on their operations in our waters, it will mean that the money invested in our ordinary fisheries will be very largely wasted. That is to say, the tendency will be to drive the fishermen who are now prosecuting their calling by the ordinary method,
out of that business and compel them to engage in some other, while the steam trawlers will themselves carry on the operation of taking fish. That may be profitable perhaps in countries where there is a very large population and having many industries, such as Great Britain,. but in this country I think it would be a most serious thing, and everything that we can do should be done to prevent the operation of these steam trawlers. I took the view at that time, and I think the hon. member (Mr. Sinclair) also entertained a similar view, that if possible these steam trawlers should be debarred the use of our harbours, that they should not be permitted to enter our ports for the purpose of landing their fish or for coaling. In that way they would be excluded from the benefit of the ports in the maritime provinces and the prosecution of this business would be discouraged.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Would that in any way interfere with the trawlers coming from France and operating from St. Pierre-Miquelon?

I quite understand that difficulties might arise In that way, but that is a matter that might be dealt with by diplomatic negotiations with the United States and with France. I believe that if the United States and Canada agree that there shall be no beam trawling in the waters of the North Atlantic, there will be none. I furthermore believe that the conditions are such upon this side of the Atlantic that it would he manifestly in the interests of those who have large sums of money invested in the fisheries, and in the interest of the fisheries themselves, that efforts to suppress and discourage steam trawling should be made. Something has been said lately with respect to the steps which the late government took in respect to the suppression of steam trawling. They passed regulations preventing the operations of beam trawlers within the three mile limit. Regulations were passed preventing the operations of these beam trawlers within the territorial waters of Canada, but in so far as the payment of bounties to the steam trawlers was concerned, I know that bounties were paid. For instance, they paid to the trawler ' Wren ' the amount of $111.50 in one year, and it was not until a question was asked by myself in this House in'1911, and the matter thus brought to the attention of the administration, that regulations were passed by which beam trawlers were excluded from the benefit of these bounties. To-day we find that although, this government and the Minister of Marine have been charged by certain gentlemen, who are not upon this side of the House, with being in favour of the operation of the beam trawler, the fact is

that the government has taken a firm stand in regard to the enforcement of the regulations with respect to the three-mile limit, and also with regard to the nonpayment of bounties to these steam trawlers. I am assured by the minister that he has gone a step further, and has already opened up Correspondence which may lead perhaps to some arrangement being arrived at whereby the United States and Canada will stand together in preventing in future the operations of these trawlers in the North Atlantic waters. I trust it will not be thought that we on this side of the House are in favour of the operation of the steam trawlers, because .we are not. For my own part I am as strongly opposed to them to-day as I was a year ago, and I believe that all those who take an interest in the fisheries of our country feel that the best interests of the fisheries, and the best interests of the fishermen themselves, will be conserved and advanced by preventing, so far as possible, the operation of trawlers in the North Atlantic waters.

The question to which my hon. friend (Mr. Jameson) refers is a very interesting one on the coast of Nova Scotia. I have not much to say against what my hon. friend has said; I think he and I agree as to what ought to be done in regard to these steam trawlers. I will not call it a ' beam5 trawler, because I understand there is no such ship now in use as a ' beam1 trawler. There was a good many years ago a ship of that kind used in the North Seas but a new type of ship has been adopted called the ' otter ' trawler, and is now in use. In order to distinguish what I mean I call this kind of trawler a steam trawler to distinguish it from the usual line trawls. My hon. friend (Mr. Jameson) has given a little credit to the late government, although it seems to hurt his feelings to do so. He has admitted that the late government did prohibit this kind of fishing and did so very promptly a few weeks after the arrival of the first steam trawler in Canadian waters. He also admits that when he brought the question of payment of the bounties to the attention of the late government, at once the regulation in regard to the bounty was repealed and a new regulation was adopted by which the steam trawler is in future to get no bounty. I do not admit that he was at all instrumental in bringing about this change. Although it has been drawn out of him to a certain extent he is compelled to admit that the attitude of the late government was decidedly against this mode of fishing, and if the present government is able to do as much as the late government to show its sincerity in this matter 1 think Mr. JAMESON
we will have reason to be pretty well pleased. My hon. friend (Mr. Jameson) has suggested some method by which this could be done, and perhaps it is the best method. If it can be carried out I shall certainly give it my support. I had the pleasure of travelling yesterday to Ottawa with certain gentlemen who have come from Nova Scotia to interview the government in regard to this matter. A number _ of them are captains of schooners sailing out of the port of Lunenburg and fishing on the banks. They are what we call deep-sea fishermen; splendid fellows; some of them are in the gallery to-night listening to the speeches. They have come here supported with affidavits showing the destruction of their gear on the banks by these ships, and they have sulfinm; proof in their pockets to show the government that the fishermen cannot carry on their business at all on the Grand Banks if the steam trawler is to be allowed to work in those waters. This means the rapid destruction of the inshore fisheries and of the deep sea fisheries of Canada in which eleven millions or twelve millions of money has been invested. And not only will the money be lost, but the best type of men we have on our coast will disappear; the men who we will have to draw on to man our navy if we are to have a navy in the future. I say that we should stand by these men because it is quite certain that if this kind of fishing is allowed to become a rule on the coast of Canada the ^ ordinary fisherman who now owns his ship and is his own master, will be wiped out and he will have to work for some capitalist who will own the steam or beam trawler.
I trust, therefore, that the Minister of Marine will take this matter to heart, and give it his best consideration. My hon. friend from Digby (Mr. Jameson), said that if we could exclude the steam trawler from the ports of the United States, and also from the ports of Canada, that would perhaps settle the business. I know that it would be difficult to get the assent of European governments to the prohibition of the steam trawler in these waters, from the fact that it is the usual mode of fishing in France, and has come to be the mode of fishing in Great Britain. The trawler has driven the ordinary fishing vessel out of the North Sea, and if that mode of fishing is carried on for many years longer, there will not be any fishing worth anything left there. On the coasts of Canada we have a great fishing industry, and we should do what is neccessary to preserve it. I think my hon. friend will find a good deal of sympathy at Washington with the proposal that something drastic should be done, and if the two governments unite, I

think something can be done. I would1 like, however, to have the policy of the government from the minister himself rather than from the hon. member for Digby. I have no doubt that the hon. member knows what he is talking about, but when this matter was discussed a few days ago, the attitude of the government did not seem to be what the hon. member for Digby says it is. If the minister is opposed to steam trawling in these waters, and is ready to advocate regulations under which fish caught in steam trawlers cannot be allowed to land1 on the coasts of Canada, and steam trawlers engaged in this industry cannot receive coal from the coal mines of Canada, it will be interesting for the House to know it.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I am surprised that in some quarters an endeavour has been made to create the impression, in consequence of some remarks that I made in the House a few weeks ago, that I was not in favour of the suppression of the steam trawler. I made a statement to the House, prepared for me by the officers of the department, dealing with this question, and1 showing the pros and cons of it-a statement very similar to one made a few years ago by my predecessor in office, the Hon. Mr. Brodeur; and an attempt was made for political reasons to create the impression that I was not in favour of suppressing steam trawling if it could be suppressed. Nothing could be farther from the truth. I am convinced, from what I have read on the subject, that steam trawling is a Serious menace and danger to our fisheries on the Atlantic coast, and I presume on the Pacific coast as well, and if persisted in must lead to the destruction of the fisheries. The difficulty in the matter, however, is this. Steam trawling is not now permitted inside of our territorial waters; no trawler can operate in Canada within the three-mile limit. The vessels engaged in trawling come chiefly from France, and the United States. In the North Sea steam trawling is carried on very extensively. There are probably over 2,000 steam trawlers carrying on operations there now, and1 it is impossible for Canada to get the support of the [British government in any attempt to prohibit steam trawling, so long as Great Britain is a party to the arrangement under which it is carried on in the North sea by the people of the different countries engaged in fishing in those waters. In fact, the government of Great Britain will not take any steps to prevent steam trawling on the Atlantic coast, and cannot do so consistently so long as she is a party to that arrangement. There does appear, however to be some reason for hope that the government of the
United States will be willing to join with the government of Canada in endeavouring to do something to prevent this mode of fishing being carried on, as there is, among the fishermen who go out from the port of Gloucester, at the present moment a very determined agitation in favour of the suppression of fishing in this way. The difficulty that arises, however, is this:	The United States and Canada
may enter into an agreement providing that neither country should engage in steam trawling. But that will not control France, which sends steam trawlers close to the three-mile limit and makes Pierre and Miquelon their base of operations; and if we adopted regulations providing that steam trawlers should not land their fish or buy coal at a Canadian port, that would not prevent the trawlers from France from carrying on their operations. Perhaps, however, if the United States and Canada came to an agreement on this subject, they might bring moral pressure enough to bear on other countries to induce them not to allow steam trawlers to carry on these operations in future. I have taken up this question with the authorities at Washington, and I am carrying on a correspondence of an informal character through Mr. Bryce, the British Ambassador, which may lead to something later on. I am not in a position to inform the House what that correspondence amounts to; but I can assure the hon. member for Guysborough, the hon. member for Digby and other hon. members who are interested, that, if it is possible to do so, effective steps will be taken to prevent steam trawling being carried on. The question is whether we should prohibit at once steam trawlers, shipping fish or buying supplies from Canadian ports. Suppose we made that regulation, is it going to assist us at the present time? I do not say whether it is or not. If we made that regulation, and steam trawlers continue to come from France, while American trawlers will be able to take their catch to the American market, and probably bring enough coal for the round voyage. The only way to make such a regulation effective would be to prevent steam trawlers from carrying on their operations outside of the three-mile limit; otherwise you might have the spectacle of an American trawler coming to the three-mile limit and carrying on operations while ours would1 be unable to carry on a similar business. There are, I believe, only two steam trawlers operating from Canada, a large number from the United States, and a larger number from France. That is the situation. No matter how strongly any Canadian government might be in favour of preventing the operations of steam trawlers, there are great difficulties in the way, that will have to be over-

come before anything can be accomplished. I am having the matter given consideration in the department, I am carrying on correspondence with Washington through the British Ambassador, and I hope we may be able to accomplish something in the direction desired.
The responsibility of introducing this matter into politics does not lie with this side of the House, but with the other side.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I do not think either side of the House is above making political capital out of anything of that kind.

The minister said a few minutes ago, that some person had
been endeavouring to make political capital out of this question.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I noticed that in some extracts from the press of the province from
which the hon. gentleman comes.

It has been one of the chief planks in the platform of my hon. friend opposite representing the eastern part of Nova Scotia during the last few elections. I was accused of owning a share in a steam trawler. When my opponents discovered that they could not find out any other way of trying to prejudice the fishermen in the county I have the honour to represent against me, they told a false story round the shore that I was a shareholder in the steam trawler that was working in that vicinity. This question has been a political one in that province for the last four or five years, and when the late government had taken the step to abolish steam trawling in Canadian waters, the provincial convention of the Conservative party, at a meeting held -in Truro some years ago, passed a resolution condemning that government for not doing more in connection with this question. You will therefore see that no person on this side of the House is. responsible for introducing this question into the political arena, but that it is owing to hon. friends from Nova Scotia, who were trying to harass and annoy the late government over this question, that their chickens are now coming home to roost, that they have to deal with this question themselves.

The hon. gentleman said that I somewhat grudgingly admitted the late government had taken certain steps for the prevention of steam trawling within the three-mile limit. I do not grudgingly admit it, I say it is a matter of record that on the 9th September. 1908, an order in council was passed which reads as follows:-
The use or operation of vessels known as steam trawlers, operating beam, otter, or other trawls for the purpose of catching fish Mr. HAZEN.
is prohibited within the three mile limit and in the hays and harbours of Canada.
I do not make that at all as a grudging admission. I say that it is a matter of record, and the hon. gentleman, I dare say, was very well informed with regard to it himself. Now, let us see what the late government did under that regulation, and T will quote for that purpose from the debate which took place last session on the resolution of my hon. friend from Guys-borough. That question was discussed in this House on the 6th February, 1911, and I will quote from the remarks of one of the hon. gentleman's own friends on the subject, the hon. member for Inverness (Mr. Chisholm) which are to be found on page 3116 of ' Hansard.' This is what the hon. gentleman in question said:
I have just a word or two to say with regard to the operations of steam trawlers within the three-mile limit. I am of the opinion that the steam trawlers do operate within that limit.
This, be it remembered, was over two years after the enactment, by the late government, of the regulation prohibiting the operation of steam trawls within the three-mile limit.
On more occasions than one that famous beam'traiwler the 'Wren,' and another whose name I do not remember, operated off the coast of Inverness last year.
That would be in the year 1910, a year and upwards after the passage of this regulation.
This steam trawler would come about dark, move along aimlessly, and just as soon as night fell they would drop their nets and steam on. That I hare from the fishermen of Inverness, who have watched their movements. From their statements I am satisfied that their steam trawler did operate within the three-mile limit.
'So that while I am perfectly satisfied to admit that the late government passed a regulation prohibiting the operation of steam trawlers within the three-mile limit,
I put the hon. member for Inverness in the witness-box and proved out of his own mouth, that the late government did not enforce that regulation and did not protect the fishermen.

The late government, it was shown over and over again, had given instructions to the vessels to watch the steam trawlers, and see that the regulation was not violated. They also challenged the parties who were making those statements to produce proof, and if they did so prosecutions would be conducted. Those parties, however, failed to produce the proof called for, and the government is not responsible in that case.

The hon. member for Guysborough may not be prepared.to take

the statement of bis colleague the member for Inverness in that regard, but it certainly went unchallenged in this House when the question was debated in 1911, and I believe it will be unchallenged by any member who is cognizant of the state of affairs as they were. The hon. member for Guysborough states that we are attempting to make political capital out of this, and insinuates that the government which came into power on the 10th October last are responsible for the present condition of affairs.
I do not wish to labour the question, but I think it is very obvious that the late government only trifled with the matter, that *they were not serious at ad'i in their 'attempts to deal with it. They went on and paid a bounty to steam trawlers after the regulations had been passed prohibiting the operation of steam trawlers within the three-mile limit. It was not until some days after I had brought the matter to the attention of the late government by placing a question on the order paDer with regard to the payment of these bounties, that on the 22nd of February, 1911, an order in council was passed which prevented steam trawlers from sharing in the bounties paid to fishing vessels. Therefore, I do not think it comes with very good grace from the hon. member for Guysborough to cast insinuations upon either the Minister of Marine and Fisheries,or this administration, with respect to the steam trawlers or intimate that they are favouring them. 'The hon. gentleman has gone a step further and said that the Conservative party in Nova Scotia pitch-forked this question into the political arena by passing a resolution in respect to the matter, after, as I understood him, the late government had passed a regulation by which they debarred the steam trawlers from' participating in the bounties paid to them. That regulation, as I have said was passed on the 22nd of February, 1911, and the resolution to which he refers was passed, if my memory serves me, in June or July, in 1909, almost two years before the late government had taken the stand with regard to these bounties to which I have jusi alluded, and one year after they had passed the regulation prohibiting the operation of these steam trawlers within the three-mile limit, during which time they had actually permitted such operation by steam trawlers. So that when the matter is looked at from a fair and reasonable point of view, it will be seen that the late government only trifled with the situation and never dealt with it energetically. Either they disregarded the interests of the fishermen, or they stood in with those gentlemen who were operating the steam trawlers. I drew attention on more than one occasion, in this House to reports of officers of the Department of Marine and Fisheries, suggesting
that the steam trawlers had come to stay, and when the question was being discussed in the House I quoted on the 6th of February, 1911, from the report of Mr. Cowie, an officer of the department, an officer engaged by the late government and who I believe is yet in the government employ. I quoted from the statement made by that officer at page 377 of the report of the Marine and Fisheries Department for 1910, and this is what-he says:
I think it is now beyond a doubt that trawling ha9 come to stay here, and although its development will, of necessity, be slow, nevertheless, looking to the time when Canada will have many more millions of people within her borders than she now ihas, when railway rates have been reduced, and the distributing facilities will have been increased to keep pace with the expanding trade, I believe there will he seen a fleet of Canadian steam trawlers running in from the Atlantic grounds with daily supplies of wholesome fresh food fish.
That was the statement which appeared in the report of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries for the year 1910. Does not that seem to have favoured the operation of these steam trawlers? And yet when the present Minister of Marine and Fisheries a few days ago read a report prepared by officers of his department-officers not of his own selection, but officers that were in the department when he came into office-that is along somewhat similar lines, the Liberal newspapers in Nova Scotia attribute to him the views that are expressed in the report and my hon. friend from Guysborough is not fair enough to admit that the statement was not one made by the minister, but was a statement made by men, whom he found in office when he took charge of the department over which he has now the honour to preside.
Hydrographic surveys, including survey of Hudson bay, $320,000.
Has this anything to do with the work of the ' Arctic? 5

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No, that is in the main estimates which were passed the other night. This is divided as follows: Lake Superior, $30,000; Lake Ontario, $30,000; Atlantic coast, $40,000; Pacific coast, $90,000; Hudson bay, $100,000; Harbour surveys, $20,000; general account, including engraving and printing, $10,000-total, $320,000; the same amount as voted for the service last year.

I do not wish to detain the House, but I was not here when the question of the Arctic came up, and perhaps I may be permitted to say here that the government ought to recognize the work done by Captain Bernier in the far north. The Captain ought to receive

through the recommendation of his minister the recognition generally given to an old officer of the Crown. Had I been here the other evening I would have spoken more of the merits of Captain Bernier. But I would ask the minister to bear in mind the service that Captain Beirnier has rendered to Canada and the empire.
Hydrographic purveys-bo provide for a new vessel required for surveying the Atlantic coast, $200,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes.
Has the contract been given?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No, tenders have not been asked for yet.
Are tenders to be asked for as soon as possible?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes.
Does the Minister intend to build the vessel in this country?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I prefer to have it built in this country if possible. I think the old government had a rule in regard to vessels of this sort that if the tender put in from Canada did not exceed that from outside, by more than a certain percentage, the contract was awarded here. I would like to have it built in Canada, but sometimes our shipyards are so busy that it is almost impossible to have vessels built.
Radiotelegraphio service-to provide for the building and maintenance of wireless stations, $271,500.

Is the hon. minister aware of what is taking place in England in connection with the wireless system? I see it stated that the British government have decided upon a policy on this subject, .and that they are arranging to girdle the whole globe with the wireless system, connecting the various colonies. Has the hon. gentleman been in communication with the home government on this .subject? The naval service being established, would not this be a timely subject for discussion at future naval conferences by my hon. friend with the British admirafty?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: That, I believe, was agreed upon at the Colonial conference. We have practically bridged the Atlantic with the wireless. The idea then is to reach Australia, but I do not think that up to the present time they have been able to get messages acrosis the Pacific ocean. Of course, we have the cable on the Pacific.

Before we leave the large amount in which the Hudson Bay is involved-I do not wish to detain the House-but I would ask the privilege when the Hudson Bay Railway is under discussion to ask my hon. friend .some questions about this survey o>f the Hudson Bay as it will affect the question of the railway.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I shall be happy to give my hon. friend (Mr. Graham) information at any time.

It is connected with the Hudson Bay route, and the discussion will naturally come up on the railway item.
